title: Chapter One
paragraphs: Sargodha, 1971
The House That Made Him
Before Hina. Before the wedding I refused to attend. Before any of what comes next.
Part I — Inheriting
Kiraman Kataybein
The Noble Scribes
My flaws my own
I'm carved from family stone
Roots run deep like ancient trees
I am trying to bank good deeds
Kiraman Kataybein
Keeping track of every dip every slip
I fall — get up, begin again
fearing the final accounting
Huqq colossal as the cosmos — quiet as a prayer
Rare as truth in a world of flair
I cut through like a surgical tear —
Precise — slicing through despair
I am trying to ascend
Seize every second
Reckon with my record
Remembering & beckoning every blessing
Prayer the only weapon
Purposeless pursuits make me nervous
My dhikr verses — like nurses — healing what the hurt is
Courageous as currents — burning like a furnace
Certain in my purpose
Underneath the surface, Huqq is workin
Qaram un Kataybein — catching it all on film
Every whim, every hymn, every sin
But still therein remains a flickering
Dim light I carry within
Yā Allah, shine light on these dreams that dimmed

The angels keep the record. Kiraman Kataybein. One on the right, one on the left, writing it all down. Every dip, every slip. The Quran says they sit with you whether you notice them or not. I have noticed them my whole life. I was born into a house that already knew their names.

Sargodha, Pakistan. November 8, 1971. The third of four children. Two older brothers — Basit, Assad. A sister coming thirteen months later — Saima. A father who did not yet know he would move us all to America. A mother who did not yet know how much of her would be needed to hold the move together. The third child arrives quiet into a country at war with itself again. I would not remember any of this. But the angels would.

This chapter is about the house that made me. Before Hina. Before the wedding I refused to attend. Before any of what comes next. Just the house — its two sources of weather, my father and my mother — and what they each handed me without ever sitting me down to explain.
Crept quiet like tsunamis,
raising the ships of the entire community.
A Father's Footprints · on Ikram
My Mother
A firecracker. A pioneer. A double-edged sword.

In order to understand what I am saying, a person has to have the ability to think at various levels. And be able to navigate multiple layers of thought, relationships and concepts. Life is not one, two or three dimensional. There are numerous dimensions, of which I myself only consciously understand a few to some extent.
My mother was overall not an easy person to deal with. Most of my life, my stances were in large part against her, causing much friction in many relationships and people's lives.

On one hand she was extremely hardworking, giving, caring, open hearted, courageous, supportive — had a love for Islam, Allah(swt) and our beloved Prophet, and thereby the Muslim community. So much more should and inshaAllah will be said on these wonderful, positive-energy traits my mother possessed. She adored her family and kids. And she is a humongous factor in who we are and became — and who my father was.
On the other hand, my mother was controlling, spiteful, and wanted to contain, direct, manipulate, and influence her circles. She was a very strong personality.

She was far ahead of her contemporaries in terms of thinking and understanding even though she was not formally educated. She was and is a very positive influence in who I am, and I am lucky and blessed to have such a woman for a mother. However, I cannot deny that much of the toxicity in the environment around me was in large part due to her vision and desires for how and what should be.

This is true of all of us. As much of toxicity in others' lives must be attributed to myself to certain degrees. I know it must — but its impact, or how much, I would not know. But each of us, especially those with strong personalities, are usually a double-edged sword.
She was a pioneer
in breaking out of the bad cultural norms,
while holding on to many of the good ones.
on his mother
A du'a · for what was inherited
رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ وَعَلَىٰ وَالِدَيَّ
Rabbi awziʿnī an ashkura niʿmataka allatī anʿamta ʿalayya wa ʿalā wālidayya.
My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor that You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.

Surah Al-Naml 27:19. The du’a Sulaiman (as) made when he understood the speech of the ant. The boy who would later read this book began praying it before he could write his own name. He had been bestowed with two parents who, with all their weather, were his first proof that goodness existed.
A Beginning · January 1, 2022
Justified Belief versus Opinion
All the angels are gathered up. Adam is introduced to them. Iblis is amongst the angels. God shares with the gathering some thoughts. Iblis has his own opinion.
All the angels took and processed the thoughts, information shared, and responded, interacted accordingly. Iblis processed and did the same.

You have a beginning — but from there you are eternal. You will never cease to exist. Live like that. Live your life knowing you are eternal. Those that know this live a little differently. Love a little differently. The things they love are a little different.
— II —
My Father, and the House
The first man in our family line to attend college. He did not narrate his reasons out loud — he just packed.

My father was Muhammad Ikram Koshul. Born October 5, 1935, in Jalandhar, before there was a Pakistan. His own father — my grandfather — was Chaudary Daulat Khan, who watched much of his family killed during Partition and walked the survivors across the new border in 1947 when my father was eleven, twelve. The first man in our family line to attend college. A veterinarian by training. The kind of man who looked out for his extended family and his community as a default setting, the way other men breathe. He did not spend money on himself. He brought us to America in 1976 because his work brought us, and because Allah's plan brought us, and he did not narrate either reason out loud — he just packed.

My mother was Shagufta. Eight or nine years younger than my father. A firecracker. A seamstress with no formal training who could put a meal on the table for ten people from scratch on a moment's notice while running three other things at the same time. Hospitality was her religion's outward shape — feeding people, hosting people, dressing well, designing the room. The sharp tongue that comes with all of that, used to keep people in line. The big heart underneath that meant the line was drawn around them, not against them.

The house in New Jersey held both of them. My father's quiet. My mother's weather. And in the quiet between the weather, on a shelf, was a book called Bahishti Zewar — the manual the cultural revisionists used to teach Muslim women of the Indian subcontinent who they were supposed to be. I will not write its full sentence here yet. That belongs to the next chapter. But the book was on the shelf. And at ten or eleven, I looked up.
Inshallah, from his progeny
will come the new Salahudeen.
We say ameen.
on his father · Ikram-portrait fragment
Have you ever rolled with Huqq?
Have you ever strolled with Huqq?
If you have, stand up and say so.
on his father
— III —
A Note on Time
The same Hijri date for two children, on the day Allah sent down the Qur'an.
Artifact · From Hina's Hand
A Hijri Ledger, in Hina's Handwriting
Hina's handwritten Islamic Birthdays ledger

Hina kept this single sheet her whole life. Hina: Sunday, January 1, 1967 — Ramadan 19, 1386. Abrar: Monday, November 8, 1971 — Ramadan 19, 1391. The Islamic lunar calendar depends on moon sighting; throughout this book, the family's shared anchor is given as Ramadan 20.
— IV —
A Gift, in Ramadan of 1981
A pendant, a pair of foldable sunglasses, a broach. The gift came first.

In Ramadan of 1402 AH, in the summer of 1981, a nine-year-old kid gives a fourteen-year-old young lady three things: a crystal heart pendant on a gold chain, a pair of foldable sunglasses, and a broach.

I do not, at nine, understand what I am doing. I understand only that this person is a person, and that there are gifts I have, and that they are hers. The gift in three pieces will travel. The crystal heart pendant will travel to South Carolina with her in 1984 inside a marriage that should never have happened, and it will return to New Jersey at the end of 1986 when that marriage falls apart. She will wear it daily, every day, after she returns. The pendant will break in two pieces in 2018 — one year before she passes. I will write about that in its own chapter, much later in this book.
What I want noted here, on this page, in this chapter: the gift is given. At nine. Before any of it. Before the wedding I refused. Before the marriage we built. Before any of the rest.

By 1982, the friction between the two mothers had begun — Shagufta and Nusrat, the two women running the two houses. The fathers stayed brothers the way they had been on the soccer field in Jalandhar. The mothers were a different weather. Nobody named the friction then. The gift had already been given.
The gift came first.
He been on the run tryin to find us,
to blind us with his demonic stuff —
he can't harm us.
Like the sun, we got our own back.
on his father · final fragment
A Scrap of Paper
February 14, 1983. She kept it for thirty-six years.

Hina kept a scrap of paper her whole life. On it, in handwriting, were three short verses — Surah Al-Asr, the chapter of the Qur'an about time, about loss, about the people who do good and remind one another to be patient. The scrap is signed at the bottom:
— Abrar Koshul, 2/14/83 —

I did not send it. I have learned, much later in life and in this work, that I did not send it. She got it from somewhere. I do not know how, after all these years, the scrap with my name on it ended up in her hands. I know only that she kept it. That it was in her things when she died. That whatever the wiring of that summer was — the gift, the gathering at the picnic, the wedding to follow — somewhere on a shelf in someone's house, my eleven-year-old hand had written her name on a piece of the Qur'an, and signed it Abrar.

Five months later, on July 17, 1983, the community would gather for an Eid picnic at Ringwood Manor. Hina, age sixteen, would be sitting in a Mustard Yellow Datsun B210 with her younger sister. Her fiancé would drop a cricket bat three hundred yards away and run toward the parking lot. What happens next belongs to the next chapter.
The scrap of paper sat on a shelf for thirty-six years. The angels kept the record.
Artifact · Bridge to Chapter Two
Surah Al-Asr, 2/14/83
Surah Al-Asr scrap signed Abrar Koshul 2/14/83

Three verses of Surah Al-Asr — the chapter on time, on loss, on those who do good and remind one another to truth and patience. English translation in one hand, Arabic in another, signed at the bottom: Abrar Koshul, 2/14/83. Hina kept it among her things until her death in 2019.

title: Chapter Two — The First Marriage, 1983
paragraphs: The First Marriage
A wedding I refused to attend at twelve. The act I am proudest of in my life. Nobody noticed.
Part I — Inheriting
A Beginning
January 1, 2022 · in his own hand
I believe in love as I believe in God — you can't touch it, see it, but you can feel its wrath and awe.
In the summer of 1982, during the later part of Ramadan, a ten-year-old kid gifts a young fifteen-year-old lady a crystal heart pendant and gold chain, a pair of foldable sunglasses, and a broach.
In 1984 the young lady, because of a patriarchal upbringing, society, and many other various elements, is married off to a man ten years her senior.
The kid does not attend the wedding as a silent protest, as the actions, decisions do not reconcile with his understanding of things — epistemology.
That heart pendant travels to South Carolina as one of her possessions, returns to New Jersey in late 1986 as that marriage is falling apart.
She's wearing the heart pendant daily — everyday.
They get married in November 1989.
The both of their birthdays are Ramadan 20.
The Spine
The kid does not attend the wedding
as a silent protest.
The actions, decisions do not reconcile
with his understanding of things.

This is the chapter where I want you to slow down. The events of 1983 are the ones I have been writing toward my entire adult life. The wedding I refused to attend at twelve is the foundation of every act of moral architecture I have built since. It changed nothing externally. Nobody noticed. I sat on the grass at the edge of an empty soccer field while it happened. That is the one act in my life I am proud of.

Hina Beg was fifteen years old in 1981 when I sent her my first letter through Cris Caves. I was ten, almost eleven. I copied out the lyrics to Fame — Irene Cara, 1980 movie, 1981 still on the radio — and folded the paper and gave it to Cris because Cris lived on Alicia Avenue and Cris understood what I was asking him to do without my having to explain it. Cris waited for her on the way to school. When she came into eyesight he handed her my letter. Then he walked away. Then I waited.

How I found the courage to send a fifteen-year-old girl somebody else's song lyrics — by God, I do not know. I was a child. I had no business doing it. I did it anyway. The doing-it-anyway is the thing. I have spent forty-four years doing things I had no business doing, and the first one was sending Irene Cara to a girl who would later become my wife.
The words were not mine. The sending was.

Notes came back. Sometimes. Not every time. Her handwriting. Mine going out, hers coming back, Cris in the middle. Each day in 1981 was a lifetime. I want you to understand this. I am not being figurative. A child of ten and eleven, waiting for a note from a girl of fifteen, lives a lifetime per day. The anticipation is a kind of suffering. It is also a kind of joy. They are the same thing. I learned that at ten. I have never unlearned it.
From Hina's Hand · July 7, 1982 · age 15.5
Author: Dye (Hina Beg)
"I, Hina Beg, always enjoyed poetry. I loved to listen to the blending of two words. I just enjoyed the rhythmic verses."

"Living as a youngster in Dar-ul-Islah, we — the youth — have had speech competitions, question and answer competitions, and original poetry competitions. It was due to the competitions I got down to writing poetry, and enjoyed it."
"My earlier poems obviously were written with the help of my great father, Dr. Khalid Beg. But by the age of nine I wrote my very first poem, entitled The Walk on Buraq."
"Since I had written quite a few poems by the age of fifteen I planned to compile them in this book, for the reading of others. To whom it may concern: I hope you enjoy."
The Necklace
Ramadan 1982. He was eleven. She was fifteen. The pendant would travel everywhere she went for the next thirty-seven years.
Ibought her a necklace at Queen Anne Pharmacy on Queen Anne Road. The pharmacy is gone now. A Papa John's sits where it stood. The pharmacy disappeared. The necklace did not.

It was a heart. Glass. White stripes running through it. Beautiful. Tasteful. Something a fifteen-year-old girl might actually wear. There is a photograph of it. You can see it for yourself when this book is published, if her children agree.

I gave it to her. I will not tell you how. The how is between her and me. I will tell you only that without the necklace, what came after would have seemed to be a dream. I would have woken up at fifty-four and not been certain any of it was real. The necklace was the proof. She kept it.

She wore it through her first marriage. She wore it through the beating at the Eid picnic at Ringwood Manor, July 17, 1983, in the back of a mustard yellow Datsun B210. She wore it through the trajectory — Newark, Franklin Road, South Carolina, Ohio. She wore it through the divorce. She wore it after. She wore it after she married me. She wore it at her fiftieth birthday in Saudi Arabia. She wore it through her last year.
She's wearing the heart pendant daily —
everyday.
a fragment, in his hand

Six months before she died, the heart broke in half. Glass does that. Glass knows. The same week the heart broke I was writing emails to her siblings. Begging them to stop. I was telling them in writing, because there was nothing else left to do, that if they did not stop fighting over the house and the money and the inheritance, their sister, my wife, was going to die.
The emails exist. I have them. They will be in the book.
The half-heart exists. I have it. It will be in the book if her children allow it.
For some reason, artifacts survive. Life does not. The necklace broke at the same hour the marriage was being broken from the outside, and I do not believe in coincidence and I never have.
When the world turned its back on you —
God sent me.
I Adore Her · plants for chapter eight
— II —
August 19, 1983
Hina was sixteen. Yasin Qamaruddin was twenty-five. Her father, Khalid Beg, officiated his own daughter's wedding. The kid did not attend.

She was engaged at fifteen. Late 1982. The man was Yasin Qamaruddin, ten years her senior, no legal standing, no relationship with the family of any sort. His father was Sheikh Maj S. Qamaruddin. The engagement was arranged the way these things were arranged — by adults, in a framework, through lines of authority that ran through her father, who was the imam of our community, and through her mother, who was responsible for the things mothers in that framework are responsible for, and through a book on a shelf called Bahishti Zewar which I will get to.

There were beatings before the nikah. The parents knew. The community knew. A picnic was held on July 17, 1983, at Ringwood Manor State Park to celebrate Eid-ul-Fitr — the flyer survives, signed by Br. Syed Mohammed Tahir as secretary of Dar-ul-Islah. Marinated chicken. Eight homemade burgers. Bring your own rolls. Two bottles of soda. The flyer is a Xerox of an ordinary community announcement. I will reproduce it in this book because it is the document that exists from the day my wife was beaten in public at sixteen years old in front of a parking lot full of cars.

What happened at Ringwood Manor that day is in the essay you are about to read, written by me, the year she died. I am going to drop it in whole. There is no way to paraphrase it. It is the centerpiece of this chapter. Her name was Hina Beg. She was the loveliest of her generation. Decency emanated from her very being. She was sixteen.
The Documents
The wedding papers, 1983

— III —
This Lady, Your Mother, My Wife
Written in 2019, the year she died. The centerpiece of this chapter. Drops in whole.

Abeautiful, dynamic, fifteen-year-old. A dignified and pure young lady. Decency and goodness emanated from her very being. She had the loveliest of eyes and a smile such that the world has never seen. A vibrant personality, innocent and at the same time distinguished. Her purity and simplicity were coupled with flare because of her strong convictions and beliefs. These qualities came across to some of the Aunties as abrasive, because she spoke honestly, innocently, and directly, though meaning no disrespect.

Her love for her father was unparalleled. A daughter fully and completely captivated with the honor, dignity, decency and warmth of this man. She saw her father as a loving, compassionate, patient, intellectual giant, a pioneer and iconic figure in the Muslim community. He was well spoken, knowledgeable, intelligent, and had the character of a selfless saint. He experienced heroic success in academia, as well as in the spectrum of religion in the midst of New York City. The epicenter of the western world, New York City was seen as both the financial capital and a cultural capital of western values. To a young lady with the purest of hearts her father stood in the shadows and belly of the beast. And this child of grace, dignity, honor, respect and charisma would always be obedient to him, and to her mother.

She was in the lap of the truest, most pristine, divine religion that the world has known. She was safeguarded by the truest book ever to be written. She was in the arms of the most wonderful father, family and community possible. And lived in a society of law and order. Her future would inevitably be full of learning, education, compassion, caring, safety and all the beautiful and pure things the world has to offer. What could possibly go wrong?

At this tender age, rather than furthering her education, beginning on the path to increased learning, maturity and self-sufficiency, her father, with all of his positions, experience, intelligence and wisdom felt the "right way" was to entrust her to another man to be lord and sustainer over her. For this young lady, her father was not just her father, but the religious icon, Islam and Quran, community and family, all in one. That's what her young captivated eyes saw, but it didn't sit right in her heart. But what's a little girl's heart compared to all else.

If her father were to say this is the right and proper thing, and she lives in his house, eats his food, wears clothes bought by him and has no means to sustain her own life, it is not for her to disagree. Coupled with the material evidence is the respect and obedience she feels for her parents. She must acquiesce to their suggestions and wishes. This is what Islam and Quran say is the right way and, to this point, it has been Islam, Quran and Moashara islamiya that have been the foundation for everything.

So, she is engaged to a man, ten years her senior, with a hideous complexion and darkness written in his very expression. An individual with no legal standing and no bonds or relationships with the family of any sort.

During this engagement, the community has a barbecue picnic to celebrate Eid-Ul-Fitr on July 17th, 1983 at Ringwood Manor State Park. It's a beautiful sunny day. Attendees are asked to bring one marinated chicken, and eight homemade burgers, rolls and a couple of bottles of soda. Some Uncles are barbecuing, ladies are chit chatting, children are playing games, some girls jumping rope, and everyone is having a great time. Young men are playing cricket on a field about three hundred yards from the parking lot which is filled with parked cars. Her younger sister hurts herself jumping rope and she takes her to sit in the Mustard Yellow Datsun B210. A family friend stops by to say "Hello".

At this point her fiancé is playing cricket nearby. He suddenly drops the cricket bat and begins on a full sprint towards the parking lot. Naturally, this catches everyone's attention, those on the field and those in the nearby areas. They watch as he reaches the car, grabs a handful of her hair and smashes her head against the open car door and the side of the car. Her hair was yanked with so much force and torque that it is ripped from her scalp and left in his hands. He runs back to the cricket game.

No one moves. Everyone is stunned and she sits quietly and gathers herself. Her mother is called over by someone. She joins the ladies some time later, and there is an eerie silence as whispers and glances are shared between the Aunties. There is a plethora of thoughts and emotions running through the community. Shock, sorrow, disgust, embarrassment, shame, and so many more.

There are private beatings and she is raped prior to the nikah. The parents are aware of these transgressions, yet no one comes to her defense, no one comes to her aid. Somehow it is her who is shamed. It is her who must be doing something wrong, that this man feels the need to be physical with her at such an early stage. The wedding goes forward on August 19, 1983 in Teaneck, New Jersey. Mehr: $1,000. Khalid Beg signs as the officiant.

The trajectory of the next three years takes her from Newark to South Carolina to Durham, North Carolina, to Lima, Ohio at her uncle Akmal Beg's house in refuge, and back to Franklin Road in November 1985. She is nineteen, going on twenty, and has come home a beaten and defeated woman. Her father's phrase, in his own writing, in a letter that survives. I will reproduce that letter elsewhere in this book.
This Lady. Your Mother. My Wife.
The kid does not attend the wedding
as a silent protest.
A Beginning · the spine, plainly stated
— IV —
What She Was Writing
She was a poet from age nine. By the time her father arranged the engagement, she had been writing for six years.
Hina's handwritten poem 'Pick Your Path,' October 31, 1982
October 31, 1982 · age 15.5
Pick Your Path
I listened to Rock & Roll —
then I'd hear my father talk.
Saying we're bad —
I'd listen, cause he's my dad.
But then I said something
which made me ring.
I said living here in the U.S. of A.
You have to do something,
if you aren't astray.
He said why don't you listen to ghazal or qawali —
I said Abajee but golly
I don't listen to something that doesn't make sense.
— Now you can push your kids in whatever way.
And only time will show.
You shall have no say.
Hina's handwritten poem refusing forced abortion, November 24, 1984
November 24, 1984 · 11:24 AM · age 17
Murder I Can't Do
Murder I can't do, it is totally Haram —
I have been blessed with a life inside of me.
A life if it were to live,
give birth to it I can.
Either I can pay for such a great big sin,
or go ahead with the tortures.
To kill a baby is something I can't do.
Ya Allah, that is what I do dua to you.
If the choice was mine alone —
work I would do.
And within nine months,
I would deliver the baby too.
A blessing this big neither of us deserve,
at least on this earth.
If murdered this baby is —
never ever shall I give birth.
Two poems · seven months apart · 1984
The Collapse and the Return

Oh ya Allah! I'm going astray. I've quit on Quraan, nor do I pray. I want to follow my Rasool, but don't know how. Please guide me the way and show me now... Oh help me, help me, ya merciful — ya kind. Truly I'm lost, I feel as if I'm blind.
SEPTEMBER 7, 1984 —

Ya Allah, you've given me the guide. Now with your laws help me to abide. Humbly I turn towards you and pray... I want to go forward like a train on the track. My destination's exact name I do not know — wherever my Rasool is, I want to go.

She was seventeen. Married a year. The first poem written four months before her father's letter would arrive in Durham. The second written ten weeks before the forced-abortion refusal. The arc of one summer, in her own handwriting, on facing pages of a notebook.
Her Father's Letter
November 1984. From Khalid Beg to his nineteen-year-old daughter in Durham, North Carolina. Reproduced in full elsewhere in this book.

My father-in-law, Dr. Khalid Beg, was a man I loved. I want that on the record before what comes next. He was the imam of our community. He was tall, gentle, intellectual, articulate, dignified, kind. He was the first imam at Dar-ul-Islah. He co-founded the masjid with my own father, Ikram, and five or six other families. He had walked into America with a PhD and a job as a research scientist, and he had walked out of academia into being a high school teacher because the masjid was a more important obligation to him than his own career. He was a saint to almost everyone who ever met him. And in November 1984 he sat down at a desk and wrote his nineteen-year-old daughter a letter that I am not going to paraphrase here. The letter is in this book in its entirety. Read it for yourself. It is the most painful document in this archive — not because it is cruel, but because the man writing it is good, and the framework he is operating inside is the one that broke his daughter, and he can see her drowning in the framework he himself helped build, and he cannot — at the end — find a way to take her out of it.
He calls her, in his own hand, a beaten and defeated woman.
That is his daughter. At nineteen. In her father's handwriting.
I am angry at him. I will be angry at him for the rest of my life. I loved him. Both things are true. The book will hold them both at once.
Artifact · From Khalid Beg's Hand
The Letter to His Daughter, November 1984
[Khalid Beg's handwritten letter to Hina · Drive ID 1y3aCeMdv7hS5qQ_ShNLc9Rp3mnWj_jOQTt9RXCfoLMo · scan available · placement here is the artifact reproduction]
Khalid Beg, in his own hand, to his nineteen-year-old daughter in Durham, North Carolina. The full letter is reproduced in Appendix E.
— VI —
Newark · South Carolina · Durham · Lima
November 1985: she comes home. February 1986: she starts at the flower shop. October 1, 1987: the divorce decree is final.

The trajectory in those three years is a list of cities and an undocumented amount of damage. Newark first. Then South Carolina. Then 1801 Williamsburg Road, Apartment 37-A in Durham, North Carolina. Then Lima, Ohio, to her uncle Akmal Beg's house — the one branch of the Beg family that took her in when she ran. Then back to Franklin Road, in November 1985, going on nineteen.

She did not come home with anything. They had taken everything. Her money, her keys, her checks, her sense of herself. The forced-abortion refusal poem from November 24, 1984 was written from inside that confinement. So were the seven NC letters that survive. So was the collapse-and-return arc, July through September of that same year — the spiritual collapse and the spiritual return, written four months apart in the same notebook. She held herself together with poetry and prayer. There were no other resources available to her.

In February 1986 she got a job at Teaneck Flower Shop, where Peter Tournas was the owner. She was nineteen. She would be there alone for two years before I joined her. In September 1986 she retained a lawyer. The papers from Goldsmith Law Firm survive. The fee agreement is on file. Five hundred dollars retainer, one thousand dollars minimum fee, $125 an hour. The lawyer's note in the margin says the case may go to annulment. October 1, 1987, the divorce decree was final. She was twenty.
I was sixteen. I had been homeless since March of that year. We caught up to each other at the masjid during Ramadan in 1987. She got me a job at the flower shop. February 1988, I started.
What happened next is the next chapter. This one ends here.
A wife is everything.
No regret. No second guess.
The one to whom we turn at the time of need,
"till death we part."
My true wife — her name is Hina.
She is the girl I grew up with.
The lady I love.
The woman who is now, my wife.
A True Wife · August 13, 1991 · in his hand at twenty

"Issued to Minor"
Marriage license stamp, August 1983, Bergen County, New Jersey

The State of New Jersey, Bergen County, Township of Teaneck, August 11, 1983. License number 168. The stamp at the top reads ISSUED TO MINOR. The bride: age 16. The groom: age 27. The mehr: $1,000. The officiant, listed under "Title": IMAM. The officiant, listed under "Name of person performing ceremony": Khalid Beg.
A du'a · from the wreckage
لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنْتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ
Lā ilāha illā anta, subḥānaka, innī kuntu min al-ẓālimīn.
There is no god but You. Glory be to You. Indeed I was among the wrongdoers.

The du’a of Yunus (as) from inside the belly of the whale. Surah Al-Anbiya 21:87. Said by every Muslim who has ever found themselves inside a darkness that was not entirely of their own making, but for which they will still ask forgiveness because asking is the only door out. Hina was sixteen. The du’a was older than she was.

title: Chapter Three — Dar-ul-Islah, the Two Patriarchs, Homelessness
paragraphs: The House of Reform
Dar ul Islah, the Two Patriarchs, and the Boy They Caught
A masjid built by two men from a soccer field in Jalandhar. The boy who fell out of the world they built. The young woman who caught him.
Part I — Inheriting
Surah al-Ra’d
The Thunder · 13:11
إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ
Inna Allāha lā yughayyiru mā bi-qawmin
ḥattā yughayyirū mā bi-anfusihim.
Allah does not change the condition of a people
until they change what is within themselves.

What follows is not my story. I was a child on the periphery of it, but I was ever present for it. The men who built this thing are not the men I am writing about in this book. They built the place inside which the rest of this book happens. I owe them the truth of what I saw — and I owe them the discipline not to claim more than what I saw.

Some of them are still alive. Some have passed. The ones who remain are old men now. The ones who were young men when I was a boy at their elbows would not recognize me on the street. That is the nature of children at the edges of a community. You see everything. You are seen by no one in particular. You inherit the work of men who do not know they are teaching you anything.
This chapter is for them. And for the boy who fell out of the world they built, and for the young woman who caught him.
Two Boys on a Soccer Field
Jalandhar, before there was a Pakistan. Brooklyn, decades after the world they knew had ended.

In 1947, on a soccer field in Jalandhar, two boys ran toward the same ball. One was Muhammad Ikram. The other was Khalid Beg. They were eleven, twelve. They were friends the way boys who play together every afternoon are friends, without ever having to name it.

That summer the partition came. Trains left the cities packed and arrived empty. A million died. Both families lost much of themselves on the road south. Both boys survived. Neither saw Jalandhar again.
For thirty years, they did not see each other.

Immigrants do a thing the country they have come to does not always notice. They search. They sit at each other’s tables on Friday evenings and ask, where are you from, what part of Pakistan, what village, what school, who do you know — and through the asking, families that were torn apart by the partition try to find the threads of themselves again. Maybe it is a habit. Maybe it is grief that never stopped looking. Either way, the men kept asking.

It was through those conversations, in someone’s living room in Brooklyn or Queens, that my father first heard the name Khalid Beg again. Dr. Beg was already in the country. The two men eventually met — at the masjid where my father’s family had come to live on the second floor while the prayers happened on the first. They talked the way men who have not seen each other in thirty years talk. Through Dr. Beg, my father learned about Teaneck. A few months later, the family moved.
Two boys from a soccer field in Punjab built a mosque together in New Jersey. The mosque they built is the inheritance this chapter is about.
Artifact · The Bloodline
Beg Family Tree, in Khalid Beg’s Records
Beg Family Tree, scanned from Khalid Beg's papers

The family tree Khalid Beg kept among his papers. Jalandhar before partition. Hamilton, Ontario. Then New Jersey. The line that walked away from the soccer field in 1947 and walked back to it, through three countries and forty-two years, on November 10, 1989.
Two boys from a city they could no longer go home to.
And then — my father’s son married Khalid’s daughter.
Their bloodlines, broken open in 1947,
came back together.
on the patriarchs
— II —
Uncle Nader’s Garage
Before there was a building. Before there was a sign. The cooing of pigeons through the wall during khutbah.
Before there was a building, there was a garage on Copley Avenue in Teaneck.

The boy is eight. Maybe nine. His father has packed him and his brothers into the car on a Friday afternoon, and they have driven the few blocks to a house belonging to a man called Uncle Nader. The garage door is open. Rugs have been laid down on the concrete floor. The smell of motor oil has not left the room. Underneath the smell of motor oil is the smell of attar from the bottles the men have brought, and underneath that, the warm bread smell of the neighbor’s kitchen drifting through the open windows.

In the backyard there is a pigeon coop. The boy can hear the pigeons cooing through the walls of the garage all through the khutbah. Uncle Nader is a soft-hearted man with a Trinidadian accent — the kind of voice that people from the islands carry with them, smooth and warm, the kind of voice that makes you feel at home in a garage that smells like motor oil. The boy will remember the cooing of the pigeons before he remembers what the imam said.

A handful of families. Eight or ten men. Their wives in another part of the house. Children threading between adult legs to find each other. Someone calls the iqamah. The men line up. The boy takes his place at the back, between his father’s hand and his brother Assad’s elbow.
This is the first place he ever heard the word community used about people he could see.

The garage will not last. Uncle Nader will move out of the area within a year or two. Other families will offer their houses temporarily. Someone’s basement. Someone else’s living room. The prayers will keep happening because the prayers do not need a building. But the men who are now coming together every Friday have started to look at each other and ask whether they could build something more permanent.

My father is not the kind of man who lets a thought go once it has entered him. He starts doing the work in the shadows. Not in the meetings, not at the front, but in the phone calls, in the conversations with the brothers and uncles, in the moving and the asking and the small acts of getting things ready for the men who will be in the forefront.

The boy does not know this at the time. The boy only knows that his father keeps having long phone calls in the evenings, and that more men are starting to come to the house, and that something — the boy cannot name what — is being decided in rooms he is not allowed in.

He will be allowed in soon enough. Once the families had decided to put an offer on the property, the boys — my brothers and I — were taken to see it. From that day forward, we were in the rooms where the discussions happened and the work was being done. The men who moved the chairs around the table were us.
— III —
The Little Old Lady’s Garden
A small lot. A hut. Neat rows of vegetables behind it. The man with the pen was Khalid Beg. My father was the engine.
The boy was perhaps ten when his father drove him out one Saturday to look at the lot.

It was small. A small hut sat on it. Behind the hut, an old woman had a garden — neat rows of vegetables and flowers, the way a woman who has lived alone for a long time keeps her garden. The little old lady met them at the door. She had agreed to sell.

The men who would buy the property were not Ikram. They were Dr. Khalid Beg and Masoom Jaleel. Dr. Beg signed the first check. Masoom Jaleel was at his side. They were the visible founders. They were the names that would be on the deed, the names that would later be on the imam’s nameplate, the names that the New York Times would print in 1991 when the article ran.
Ikram was in the room.

He had been in the room for the meetings that decided to look for property in the first place. He would be in the room for every meeting that followed for the next several years. He had picked up the phone and called the man who knew about this lot. He had driven to look at it before anyone else. He had spoken to his wife at the kitchen table about whether the families could afford what was being asked. But he was not the man with the pen.

The project itself had been talked about since 1975. The property was purchased in 1979. The building would not be finished until 1985. Ten years from idea to dome. Ten years of phone calls and arguments and weekend drives to see lots that did not work out. My father was in nearly every one of those years.
This was his pattern.

In 1977, in the family’s first apartment in Queens, his family had been one of the families whose house became the first floor of a mosque — Masjid al-Falah, which still stands and which has become the headquarters of an entire revivalist movement. Ikram had not been the imam there either. He had been the man on the second floor. The engine.

His wife called him the engine. His children, later in life, would call him the unseen motor. He was the man who quietly bought the house, signed his name on the papers, made the phone calls to the men who would become founders.

The boy, watching, did not understand at ten that this was rare. He thought all fathers were like this. He thought this was what men did. It would take him another twenty years and his own attempts at building to understand that men who do this are unusual, and that men who do this without bitterness are more unusual still.
— IV —
What the Wives Built
The husbands signed the checks. The wives held the people. Between Shagufta and Nusrat, the social fabric of the community was woven.
There is a sentence in something the boy will write decades later, as a grown man, in a foreward to a packet of records he wants the next generation to have:
This was only possible
with the unwavering support of their wives.
Who undoubtedly played a major if not majority role
in pulling the social circles, and thus community, together.
Foreward Dar Ul Islah · 2021
He means it as a thank-you. It is also a fact.

His own mother — Shagufta — was the firecracker. Energy, hospitality, food from scratch at a moment’s notice, sharp tongue to keep people in line, big heart to help anyone who came through the door. There was no one like her in the community. When other women came to visit, they came to her kitchen. The kitchen was the room where the actual decisions about how the community functioned were made, even though the men sat in the living room and thought they were the ones deciding.

Auntie Beg — Nusrat — Hina’s mother — held the same role on the other side. She was the gentle one. Where Shagufta pushed, Nusrat held. The women who would not have followed Shagufta would follow Nusrat. The women who would not have followed Nusrat would follow Shagufta. Between them, the social fabric of the community was woven. The husbands signed the checks. The wives held the people.

The boy does not yet know that this is the pattern of every community that ever survived. He will learn it later. He will learn it slowly, and he will learn it inadequately, because he is a boy. But the women in the kitchen were already teaching him.
The Tent, the First Sign, the Uncles
A catalog of what the boy saw. Wooden arrows painted red and white. A Black American convert’s sign on a chain-link fence.
What follows is the boy’s catalog of what he saw.

He remembers Uncle Tahir and Uncle Masoom picking him and his brothers up every morning for Fajr. Sometimes in a green station wagon. Sometimes in a red firebird. The detail of the cars matters. These were not solemn old men. These were men with cars they loved. The masjid had texture.
He remembers Uncle Hameedudin throwing the football around with the boys on the property after Fajr was done. The masjid was not only solemnity. There were footballs.

He remembers Uncle Suri cutting wooden arrows by hand and painting them red and white to point the cars to where they should park. Buyahka before Buyahka had a name. A man building a parking system out of wood and house paint because no one was going to come do it for them.
He remembers Uncle Bajwa running a small backhoe to move and level the land. The labor.
He remembers Azmat Rehmat, who was the cool one. Cool cars. Cool clothes. The community had glamour too. Not all uncles. Some young men.

He remembers the Ramadan tent that went up every year before there was a permanent building. The tent was the masjid in its larval form. A stretched piece of canvas, prayer rugs underneath, and a hundred and fifty people who behaved as if it were a marble courtyard in Damascus. They were practicing.
He remembers Ajaz saab making huge pots of tea for everyone because someone had to make the tea, and Ajaz saab had decided it would be him.
He remembers Brother Jess and Brother Osman, two Malaysian students from FDU, taking the boys to the park and on outings, and being the first non-Pakistani Muslims he ever called brother.

He remembers going with the Catovic family to ISNA conventions and seeing, for the first time, that the Muslim community in America was much bigger than the few families who had become his weekly Friday.
He remembers the first sign for the masjid.

It was painted by a man named Mr. Wilbur, the African American art teacher at Longfellow School. Mr. Wilbur was Muslim. He had become Muslim in the way that many Black Americans had become Muslim through the long arc of the twentieth century — through the Nation, through Malcolm, through Imam W.D. Mohammed, through the slow rediscovery of an Islam that had always belonged to them even when the world said otherwise. Mr. Wilbur painted the sign that said Dar-ul-Islah, and it was hung on the chain-link fence that surrounded the property, and it was there for years.

The boy did not know at ten what it meant that the first public face of a mosque founded by Indo-Pak immigrants was a sign painted by a Black American convert. He would understand it later. He would understand it as the rebuke to every person who has ever told him that Islam is a foreign religion in America. The first sign of the first masjid he ever knew was painted by an American.

In the same years, on a burnt orange couch a few miles away, the boy was reading Bahishti Zewar. The two facts sit together. Bahishti Zewar was the manual one community had carried with it across the ocean. Mr. Wilbur’s sign was a different thing entirely. Both were called Islam. The boy already, at ten, had begun the work of figuring out which one to keep.
Tip of the spear —
the men who put their bodies first
so the rest could pray under a roof.
on the founders
— VI —
The Name, the Vote
House of Reform. They named it after its limitation, not its triumph.
When the elders sat down to choose a name for the community, they chose Dar ul Islah.

House of Reform. Abode of Reform. The translation matters. They did not name it Dar ul Iman, House of Faith. They did not name it Dar us Salam, House of Peace. They named it after its limitation, not its triumph. They knew, even as they were buying the property, that the community would need to keep reforming itself. That what they were building was not a finished thing but a workshop.

The boy did not catch this at the time. He caught it decades later, when he understood that almost no one names a thing after its weakness on purpose. The elders who named Dar ul Islah were either unusually humble or unusually clear-eyed. He thinks now, looking back, that they were both.
Then came the vote.

The architects had drawn up two designs. One was a simple structure, something like four hundred thousand dollars to build. The other was an ambitious design — a dome, a minaret, a courtyard — closer to one point two million. The elders argued. They argued in meetings the boy was sometimes allowed into and sometimes was not. They argued in living rooms after dinner. They argued in cars on the way home. Some men felt the simple structure was more Islamic — modest, sufficient, not given to ostentation. Some men felt the larger design was the right thing for the community Bergen County would become — a building that would be visible from the turnpike, that would announce that Muslims belonged here, that would be there for the grandchildren.
Both positions were sincere. Both positions had Islamic backing. This is what community-building actually looks like — not unity, but disagreement, held inside a shared project.

The vote went to the larger design. The dome and the minaret were built. The New York Times would write about the building in 1991. The MIT Aga Khan Visual Archive would later photograph it. The seventy-foot minaret would be visible from the New Jersey Turnpike, exactly as the men who voted for it had hoped.

The boy was a teenager by the time the building was finished in 1985. He remembers walking through it the first time. He remembers thinking that buildings are heavy, and that the men who had built it were tired.
— VII —
The Splintering
The men who built Dar ul Islah did not stay together. The case began in 1986. A boy sat in the courtroom and listened.
I am going to tell you something I do not want to tell you. I am going to tell you anyway because the book does not work without it.

The men who built Dar ul Islah did not stay together. The community split. The split was not theological in the way an outsider might imagine — Sunni against Shia, or this madhhab against that one. It was something more granular and more honest than that. The Indo-Pak subcontinent, which produced almost all of these men, contains within it twenty or thirty regions, each with its own language and food and customs. Inside each region are the village people, the farmers, the laborers, the educated and the uneducated, the aristocrats, the high society, and every gradation in between. There are madrasa traditions that have shaped some men’s reading of Islam and not others. There are disagreements about how a community should fund itself — whether the money should come only from the families inside the room or whether it could come from overseas backers, and what came with each kind of money. There are men who had been working on this project since 1975, when it was only an idea on a kitchen table, and there are men who moved into the area in the early 1980s when the building was already going up and who arrived with their own ideas about what it should become.

The split was about whose manner of thinking would guide the masjid forward. That was the truth of it. Not money exactly, not ego exactly, though those were present too. It was about which tradition would set the tone for the next generation. Two groups of sincere men disagreed about that, and the disagreement hardened, and the hardening became a lawsuit, and the lawsuit went to court.

The groundwork for the case began in 1984. The case itself did not start until 1986. By then I was fourteen, fifteen years old. Old enough to sit in the courtroom. Old enough to understand some of what was being said, though not all.

My father was a witness. He was on Dr. Beg’s side, and on Masoom Jaleel’s side, and on the side of the men who had founded the place. He sat where they sat. He testified to what he had seen. The man who had spent his entire adult life staying out of the photograph sat in the front row of a courtroom because, this once, the question being asked was a question he could not stay quiet on.

The other side had its own good men. I want to be clear about that. They were not villains. Some of them I had loved as uncles. Some of them I still love. They believed what they believed and they had reasons. The case was not about who was a good Muslim and who was not. The case was about who had what right, and who owed what duty, and who could be trusted to hold what.
A boy sat there and listened.

I will not tell you what was said. I will tell you what I learned. I learned that building something sacred does not protect you from breaking it. I learned that sincerity is not enough — that two men can both be sincere and still end up on opposite sides of a courtroom, and that the universe does not always sort out who is right. I learned that the same hands that lay a foundation can later sue over the deed. I learned that a community is not a permanent thing. It is a thing that has to be remade every year, every Friday, every time two men disagree and have to choose whether to keep walking the same road or to part.
My father and my father-in-law were on the side that lost.
I want you to read that sentence again.
They lost.
the splintering

The men who had thought about this project since 1975, who had bought the property in 1979, who had held the meetings and made the phone calls and signed the checks and built the building and chosen the name — they lost the case that decided whose vision would guide what they had built. They were told, in effect, by a court of law: the masjid you built is no longer yours to steer.

What did they do? They did what no one had any right to expect. The next Friday they were at the masjid. They prayed the way they had always prayed, as if no court had ever existed. My father did not raise his voice about it at the dinner table. Dr. Beg did not give a sermon about it from the floor. They lost the case, and for a long time, they kept showing up.

How long is a long time? A few years. Long enough to model for me what dignity in defeat looks like. Long enough that I would carry the lesson the rest of my life. But the practical truth is harder than the spiritual one. The court did not just take the steering. Over time, the new leadership took the building. The Begs no longer had a masjid that was theirs to use the way a family uses its masjid — for a daughter’s wedding, for a grandfather’s janazah, for the small private rituals that make a building yours. The next chapter shows you what that meant. Hina’s wedding to me, in 1989, was not held in the masjid her father had founded. It was held in his living room. The men who built Dar ul Islah eventually had to bring their own daughters’ weddings home.
I have thought about this for forty years. I do not know how they carried it. I have carried smaller things worse.
There is a du’a the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to say often, more often than any other du’a according to the narration that has come down to us:
يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ
Yā Muqallibal-qulūb, thabbit qalbī ‘alā dīnik
O Turner of hearts, keep my heart firm upon Your religion.

I think my father said this du’a. I do not know that he said it. I never heard him say it out loud. But I think he must have said it. Because to walk back into the same building the week after you have lost the right to shape it, and to pray the way you have always prayed, is to have a heart that has been kept firm by someone other than you. No man does that on his own.
— VIII —
The Boy in the Entryway
A blue shalwar kameez. A long overcoat almost reaching her ankles. The most particular thing he had ever seen.

Before there was the dome and the minaret, there was the small hut on the property — the same hut that had stood there when the little old lady had her garden behind it. The community used the hut as the everything-room. Wudu happened there. Tea happened there. The men sat there between salat. The women sometimes used it when the weather drove them in from outside. Children came in and out the way children do, without permission and without notice.

It was 1981. I was ten, maybe a touch older. I was coming out of the hut and a young woman was coming in. We met in the entryway. We knew each other. Our families had known each other for thirty-four years, since the soccer field in Jalandhar.
She was Hina. She was older than me by five years.

I remember saying salam. I remember her radiant self the way she always was. I remember a blue shalwar kameez and earrings that matched the blue, and a long overcoat over the kameez — the kind of overcoat Boy George of Culture Club used to wear, though I would not have known to call it that at the time. I just knew that no one else in the masjid dressed like her, and that no one else in the masjid carried herself like her, and that something about the way she was standing in the doorway with the overcoat almost reaching her ankles was the most particular thing I had ever seen.

We spoke briefly. I do not remember what we said. I doubt either of us thought, at that moment, that we would one day be married, that we would have three children together, that I would bury her in 2019, that I would write a book in 2026 in which this moment would appear as a hinge. We were two children of the community whose fathers had built the place we were standing in. That was all.
The masjid that my father and Dr. Beg
and Masoom Jaleel and the other families had built
produced this entryway.
The entryway produced the meeting.
on the hinge
— IX —
March 1987
The boy fell out of the world the men had built. The young woman who had walked through the entryway in 1981 caught him.

I want to tell you about the spring after they lost the case. The masjid had a new leadership. The fathers kept showing up. And the boy — the boy who is me, the same boy who watched it all from the back of the room — was no longer at home.

Iwill not lay out the inside of my parents’ house here. That is not what this chapter is about and the people inside that house are still living. What I will tell you is this: in March 1987, at the age of fifteen, I was no longer welcome under my father’s roof. The reasons sit in the territory my sister has her own version of, and that version is true to her in ways I do not need to fight here. I have included her account elsewhere. The fact, on the ground, was simple. I had a duffel bag. I did not have a place.

Friends of mine had houses that took me in for a night, two nights, three. Their parents fed me. Their parents looked the other way when I slept on a couch that was not theirs to give. I do not have words for what those families did. I have not paid them back. I do not think I can.

Hina was twenty. She had been home from her own marriage for about a year and a half. She had retained a lawyer in September 1986. The divorce decree would not come until October 1987. She was in the middle of her own salvage. She had no business taking on someone else’s.
She took it on anyway.
Artifact · September 5, 1986
The Lawyer’s Fee Agreement
Goldsmith Law Firm fee agreement, retained by Hina, September 5, 1986

The retainer Hina signed at the Goldsmith Law Firm to begin the proceedings that would end her first marriage. September 5, 1986. She was nineteen. The decree itself would not come until October 1, 1987. In the spring between those two dates, the boy turned up with a duffel bag and she made room for him.

What that looked like was not romantic in the way a movie would film it. It looked like a job. She got me a foothold at The Flower Shop. Work I could do. A reason to get up in the morning. She fed me. She helped me figure out where I would sleep that week and the week after. She was not, in 1987, my girlfriend. We were not engaged. We were not anything that needed a name. She was a young woman who had been broken open and put back together by her own three years in another state, and she looked at a fifteen-year-old boy with a duffel bag and decided he would not be left to figure it out alone.
I did not understand at the time what she was doing. I understand now.
She was a teenager and the only adult in my life.

I have written that sentence in this book before. I will write it again before the book is done. It is the load-bearing sentence of how I read her, and how I read myself, and how I read the marriage we eventually built. She was a teenager and the only adult in my life. The men I have spent this chapter naming — Ikram, Khalid Beg, Masoom Jaleel, Uncle Nader, Uncle Hameedudin, Uncle Bajwa, Mr. Wilbur — built the masjid. The masjid produced the entryway. The entryway produced the meeting. And six years after the meeting, when the boy fell out of the world the men had built, the young woman who had walked through that entryway in 1981 caught him.

You will hear me say, later in this book, that Hina and I built each other. That neither of us was the hero. That goodness, decency, faith, love — these are not rankable, and a marriage is not a transaction. All of that is true.
And it is also true that she went first.

Before there was a marriage between us, before there was a child, before there was a flower shop with our names on it, before there was anything I could give her in return — she gave me food, she gave me work, she gave me a foothold. She gave me a reason to keep being. The shade I would later give her was structural. She was a woman, and I was a man in a world that listened differently to men. I do not take credit for what the world handed me to hand to her. The shade she gave me was something else. It was hers. She had nothing to give and she gave it. She had no shelter to share and she shared it.

That is one of the four ways she saved me. There are three others, and they will come in their own chapters. But this is the one Chapter 3 has to carry, because Chapter 3 is the chapter where the inheritance the men built becomes the place inside which a particular boy fell, and Chapter 3 has no honest ending without naming the person who caught him.
A version not mine · in my sister’s own framing
What my sister would say

My sister’s version and recollection of events would taint towards my mother, and reflect much of her mindset and personality. The narrative is along these lines: my parents were dead against the marriage; I would not listen and was smitten by Hina; Hina was a type of vixen and seductress, taking advantage of an underage kid; my parents repeatedly summoned me home, but I would not return because I had found shelter and comfort in Hina; the two of us were having our cakes and eating them as well.

It is a neatly packaged and perfectly sensible narrative. How or who can argue such a narrative — it is all self-evident and clear. In all of this of course the Koshul family is and was a beacon of light, of hope, of goodness and all the rest. There existed just a couple of black sheep. And black marks on the family which would be Hina and Abrar.

This topic has never been spoken upon between my sister and I. From 1987 until January 2024. Never once has it been spoken about. This reflects our personalities, or at least in part each of our personalities.

I by no means was an angel, have been an angel, am without deficiencies. But things along the lines of drugs, robberies, alcohol, casual sex, shirk, blatant lying, slandering of others — these I do not recall egregiously. As for Hina being a vixen: please. She was and is a simple, beautiful, pure soul who was caught in a dirty, nasty world with all its games, hustles and traps. The woman was a sweetheart of a woman. In truth, one this world and community and her own family did not deserve.
After God, who would know her better than I. But there is a possibility that I am a blatant liar and have fights I need to finish or win. Perhaps that possibility remains.

I tell you all of this because the rest of the book happens in the shadow of what I have just named. The masjid that my father and Dr. Beg and Masoom Jaleel and the other families had built — the masjid named after its limitation, the masjid that split and went to court and was lost in court and was rebuilt anyway, the masjid with the Black American convert’s sign on the fence — that masjid produced the entryway. The entryway produced the meeting. The meeting, six years later, produced the rescue. The rescue, two years after that, produced the wedding the boy actually attended.

I did not lay the brick. I did not write the check. I did not testify in court. I did not catch myself when I fell. I was the boy in the entryway, already, without knowing it, in the right place. The men I have named in this chapter built the masjid. The masjid built me. And in the entryway, in a blue kameez and a long overcoat in 1981, was the woman who would build the rest.

I owe them all. I owe the men I named. I owe the men I did not name. I owe the wives in the kitchens whose names I am still learning. I owe Hina most of all. The book that follows is, in its own slow way, the receipt.

title: Chapter Four — November 10, 1989: Love Forged in Fire
paragraphs: November 10, 1989
Love Forged in Fire

The wedding I attended. Her father walked her down the aisle the second time. The mehr was one thousand dollars — everything I had. We had nothing else to give each other but ourselves, and we gave it.
Part I — Inheriting
In the still of the night
From the chapals fragments · on Hina
In the still of the night, in its peaceful bliss
It’s in the air tonight.
Don’t put your feet on the floor.
Please, stay here for a while.
Allow me to place the stars on your walkway.
I’ll light up my heart to brighten up your path.
What’s a night without the moon?
It can’t breathe without the moon.
How do you think I sufficed.

Six years after the kid refused to attend Hina’s first wedding, he attended her second. He was eighteen. She was twenty-two. Her father walked her down the aisle this time. The mehr was one thousand dollars — every dollar the kid had. We had nothing else to give each other — not money, not a settled future, not the approval of every person in the room. So we gave each other ourselves. And the angels, who had been keeping the record, wrote it down.

November 10, 1989. A Friday. Two days after my eighteenth birthday. The nikah was performed in the living room at 89 Franklin Road — in Khalid Beg’s house, the same room where he had received me and turned me away two years earlier. The same armchair. The same room. He had not changed his furniture. He had changed his mind.

I want to tell you why we were not at a masjid. The simple answer is that the side of the family running the nikah did not have one. The Beg family had spent their adult lives building Dar ul Islah and had lost the lawsuit two years before, in 1987. The building still stood — the dome and the minaret, visible from the turnpike, exactly as the men had voted in 1979. But the building was no longer the Begs’ to use the way a family uses a masjid for its own daughter’s wedding. They had lost the steering and, in the practical sense that families know about and outsiders do not, they had lost the building too. A new leadership had it. A new tone shaped what happened inside its walls. You did not bring your daughter’s nikah into a building whose direction you no longer trusted.

So Khalid Beg did what fathers do when the institutions fail them. He brought the nikah home. He cleared the living room. He arranged the chairs. He asked an imam who would come to come. The whole ceremony fit in the room where the family lived — where the daughters had grown up, where the conversations of thirty years had happened, where I had sat across from him at fifteen and at sixteen and at seventeen as he tried to figure out who I was and whether to let me near his daughter. By eighteen the question had answered itself, on his furniture, in his room.

In our culture, the bride’s side runs the nikah. The groom’s side runs the walimah. The nikah belongs to the woman’s family because the woman is the one who is moving, structurally and ritually, from one household to another. Her father walks her in. Her father gives her away. Her father’s living room is the right room. That part of the day belonged to Khalid Beg, and he carried it.

Of my own family, only my father came. Ikram Koshul came. My mother did not. Shagufta was angry. Some of the anger was for the marriage. Some of it was for the years I had not been her son. Some of it was for the years she did not know how to talk about. Whatever it was, she was not at the nikah. I noticed.

I have written elsewhere that we were the first couple in the community that got married. I want to qualify that. We were not the first couple in the community to have a nikah. We were the first couple in the community where the bride and groom had each grown up inside the community as children of the founders — the first generation marrying back into itself. The aunties had watched us across thirty Fridays a year for a decade. The uncles had watched. We were the first homegrown wedding, and the community knew it whether they would admit the meaning of it or not.

Not everyone in the community was happy. They were not. Some had stories about Hina they had carried since 1983. Some had stories about me they had carried since 1987. Some had taken sides during the splintering and could not look at my father’s face without remembering. Weddings in this community were never just two people. The room was small and the family ran it, but the community knew, and the community had its opinions.
What I Promised
A nikah is a contract. It is also a promise made out loud, in front of God, before the witnesses you owe the rest of your life to.

Anikah is a contract. The mehr is set, the wali consents, the bride consents three times, the witnesses sign. It is not a sacrament in the Catholic sense. It is a promise made out loud, in the language of property and rights, because the deen takes property and rights seriously and refuses to pretend that love is enough.
My mehr to Hina was one thousand dollars.

It was every dollar I had. I was eighteen. I had been working at the flower shop since I was fifteen and a half, since the spring of 1987 when she had first put me on the payroll because I had nowhere else to go. I had been saving in the way a kid saves — without a plan, without a wedding in view, just because saving was what you did when you had been homeless once and did not intend to be homeless again. By November 1989 the savings had reached one thousand dollars. I gave them all to her, in the form of a promise on paper, in front of the imam and the witnesses and the room.

I want her sons to read this and know exactly what their father gave their mother that afternoon. He gave her everything. Not a number large enough to mean security. A number small enough to mean this is the floor of who I am right now and I am giving you the whole floor. The kid had nothing else. He gave the nothing.

Hina’s first mehr, in 1983, had also been one thousand dollars. I have written about that license in the previous chapter. The license itself sits in the appendix of this book. I want you to look at the two pieces of paper next to each other and notice that they say the same number.
One thousand dollars in 1983. One thousand dollars in 1989.
Same number. Different meanings.

In 1983, the man writing the number was twenty-seven years old. He had a profession. He had a family with money. The thousand dollars was what he and the men around him decided a sixteen-year-old girl was worth as a wife. They could have written more. They wrote one thousand. The number was a ceiling. It was the most they thought they had to commit, and they committed exactly that much, and not a dollar more.

In 1989, the man writing the number was eighteen years old. He had no profession. He had no family money to draw on. The thousand dollars was every dollar he had on earth, accumulated through three years of work that had begun as survival and ended as a wage. The number was not a ceiling. It was a floor with nothing under it. He was not committing to a percentage of what he had. He was committing to the whole of what he had.

I do not say this to elevate myself. I say it because the contract that afternoon was real, and the meaning of the contract depends on what the man writing it had to give. The first man had more than a thousand dollars and gave a thousand. The second man had a thousand dollars and gave a thousand. The same paper. Two different deals.
The promise was the point. The mehr was the form the promise took. The form mattered. The number mattered less than what the number was a proportion of.

Years later, when we had something, I would put more on paper for her in other ways. I would buy her things. I would sign the lease at Teaneck Flower Shop. I would do what husbands do when the years bring resources. But the day of the wedding, the kid had a thousand dollars and a duffel bag of clothes from the previous chapter, and he gave her the thousand dollars and kept the duffel bag, and the witnesses signed.
Like my chapals at the masjid,
my heart has been stolen and forever gone.
Like chapals at the masjid —
heart gets stolen and forever gone.
on the nikah · chapals fragment
— II —
Pakiza Mohabbat
A clean love. There is a phrase for it in Urdu that English does not quite carry.

There is a phrase in Urdu that I want here. The English does not carry it. Pakiza mohabbat. Clean love. Pure love. A love made of wudu. A love that you bring to God before you bring it to the beloved, because the beloved is a trust from God before she is anything else.
Pakiza mohabbat karna chata hain.
Tilawat-e-Qur’an bhi karne chata hain.
Aur aap ke saath ek umar guzarni chata hain.

I want to love you cleanly. I want to also recite the Qur’an. And I want to spend a lifetime with you. The three desires sit on the same shelf. The Urdu does not separate them and I will not separate them here. The marriage I was committing to that afternoon was not a separate compartment from the rest of my life with Allah. It was the same building. Different rooms.
Mera aik chota sa kam kar do.
Ek nikahnama lekar khud ko mere naam kar do.

Do this one small thing for me. Take a nikahnama and put yourself in my name. The Urdu is courtship language and contract language at once, the way Urdu often is. The same word for name carries the legal weight and the love song. The man asking is asking with both hands.
I had been asking with both hands since I was twelve. The wedding was where the asking finally found the right room.
What is salat without wudu?
Pakiza mohabbat.
Tilawat-e-Qur’an bhi karne chata hain.
on the nikah
— III —
The Walimah
In our culture the bride’s side runs the nikah and the groom’s side runs the walimah. I was the groom’s side. I ran it on my own.

In our culture the bride’s side runs the nikah and the groom’s side runs the walimah. The walimah is the public celebration the day after — the meal the new husband puts on for the community as the first act of his marriage. It is, structurally, the husband announcing himself to the world as a husband. It is supposed to be the groom’s family carrying the weight.

I did not have a family carrying the weight. I had a father who came to the nikah and a mother who did not. I had two older brothers and a younger sister and a household I had not lived in for two years. The groom’s side, in the structural sense, was me. The kid was the groom’s side.
I ran the walimah on my own.

Every dollar I had saved at the flower shop and at every job I had had since I was fifteen, I spent on the walimah. I rented a hall. I hired a caterer. I hired an MC. I got a sound system. I ordered a wedding cake. I put flowers on every table. I chose tablecloths. I picked out wedding favors. In Pakistani-Muslim weddings in Bergen County in 1989, no one was doing this. Walimas were food and a little speaking. The boy was doing a wedding the way he had seen weddings done in films and at the country clubs where he had worked the kitchen. He was doing it because he wanted Hina to have the wedding she should have had the first time and didn’t.

I hired a photographer. I hired a videographer. I paid them in full. I want you to read those two sentences and notice what they say. The kid had decided, at eighteen, that this day would be witnessed by professionals because the family witnesses were not all going to come, and because Hina deserved a record of being the bride at a wedding she actually wanted, and because the angels who keep the record are real but the videotape and the photographs are real too, and the eighteen-year-old kid running the walimah on his own believed in records.

Every anniversary, for the rest of her life, we sat on the couch in the den and watched the videotape of the walimah together. We laughed at how thin I was. We marveled at how she looked. We said to each other, in the way long-married couples say things without quite saying them, look what we did. Look what we did.

The pictures from that day are somewhere in the boxes of this house. The videotape too. By the time you read this book, in the version that goes to the family, those pictures will be in the appendix. The kid in them is barely recognizable to me now — thinner than any of my sons have ever been, in a suit he could not afford, standing next to a woman in a kameez she had chosen herself, smiling like a man who had pulled off a thing nobody had asked him to pull off.

He had pulled it off. He had spent every dollar he had on the day his wife should have had the first time. The walimah was a receipt for the marriage that had not been allowed to happen six years before. He was eighteen and broke the next morning. He did not regret it.
Placeholder · v2 photographs
The Walimah, November 11, 1989
Photographs and videotape of the walimah, paid for by the kid himself. To be inserted in the v2 build once the prints and tape are located and digitized.
— IV —
The Khabaa Letter
August 1991. Twenty-one months in. A man writes his wife a five-page letter from a hotel room and does not finish it the way the first four pages would have led you to expect.

In August 1991, twenty-one months into the marriage, I wrote Hina a five-page letter from a Khabaa hotel room. I was twenty. We had a son who was eight months old. The letter was a long meditation on the marriage, on the deen, on the man I was trying to be, on the ways I was failing at it. The first four pages read like a young husband sermon — earnest, a little overwrought, full of references to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and his wives, full of resolutions about how I would do better. The kind of letter a young man writes to convince himself first and his wife second.
The fifth page broke the frame.

I will not paraphrase what page five says. I want it reproduced inside this book the way I wrote it that night, on hotel stationery, in handwriting that has not aged well. The four pages before it have to be there too — without them, the fifth page is just a fragment. With them, the fifth page is the moment a young man stopped writing the sermon and started telling the truth.
Placeholder · v2 reproduction
The Khabaa Letter, August 1991
Five pages, on hotel stationery. Pages 1–4 reproduced in facsimile. Page 5 reproduced overleaf as the reveal. To be inserted in the v2 build once the scans are uploaded.
What We Built in Each Other
She did not save me by being a saint. I did not save her by being a hero. We saved each other by being honest, in private, when nobody was watching.

Ihave been writing this book a long time, and one of the things I have had to decide is how to talk about the marriage without lying. The lie that comes most easily is the one that says she saved me. The other lie that comes most easily is the one that says I saved her. Both are short. Both are false. The truth is longer and harder to say without sounding like I am hedging.
We built each other.

Not metaphorically. Materially. She was the proof to me, when I was a child, that the dignified Muslim woman the Qur’an described actually walked around in the world — in a blue overcoat at the masjid, in the way she carried her body in a community that did not know what to do with her. I was the proof to her, when she was a young woman who had been broken and put back together, that the man the Qur’an described — the husband who is a garment to his wife, the man who is gentle with his women — was not a fairy tale. We were each other’s evidence. Without that evidence, neither of us would have believed.

She was the incubator of my critical thinking. I have written this elsewhere and I will write it again because it is true and the book has to carry it. What I saw happen to Hina between 1982 and 1986 made the seed my parents had planted in me — the small intuitions about right and wrong, the ten-year-old’s questions on a burnt orange couch — germinate. Without her, the seed might have stayed a seed. The questions might have stayed questions. I might have become a comfortable man.
