I was — and this is the harder thing to say — one of the places she was able to stand for truth. The 1984 forced-abortion refusal poem. The “Alone I have been” letter. The 2014 letter that begins I cannot fight it alone. She was a writer her whole life, but the writing she did in our marriage was different from the writing she had done before. She had a witness. The witness made some things sayable that had not been sayable before.

And then the shelter. In 1987 she gave me a foothold when I had none. She was twenty. She had no business saving anyone. She did it anyway. From 1989 forward I gave her structural shelter in return — the shelter of being a man in a world that listened differently to men. I do not romanticize that shelter. I did not earn it. The world handed it to me at birth because of my chromosomes and I handed it onward to her because she should not have needed it and the world had failed to see her without it. The shelter she gave me in 1987 was hers. The shelter I gave her was the world’s, on loan.

Goodness, decency, faith, love — these are not rankable. The marriage was not a transaction. I am not the hero of this book and Hina is not the hero of this book and the book has no hero, only witnesses, and the witnesses are us.
A line that survived
From the chapals fragments · on Hina, on us
If a woman cries there can be many reasons, if a man cries there will only be one, a woman. We call it “Love.”
You were so full of pride — I had to bring you to your knees.
Smile every time we part — takin’ a piece of my heart.
I believe in love like I believe in God. You can’t touch it, you can’t see it, but you can feel the wrath and the awe.
— VI —
Who She Was
There is something I have to say about Hina that nobody else can say. I am going to say it the way I would say it out loud, to her sons, to her daughter, to the witnesses. I am going to say it once.
Spoken · first version
Hina
No one… I mean no one… is going to tell me who Hina was. No one. Because no one knew her. Not like I did. Not like I saw her. Maybe not even she fully knew herself.

You have to understand — the life she had before I came along. The betrayal. The abuse. Married off at sixteen. Divorce. Her family — the people who should have protected her, who should have guided her — didn’t. The community that preached love, faith, trust — they turned on her.

She came back to Teaneck broken. Lost. Damaged. And she didn’t tell anyone. She couldn’t. Her morals, her pride, her ethics — she carried it all inside. She wasn’t a chatterbox. She wasn’t going to spill herself to people who had already failed her.

And that’s when I stepped in. I was there. Always. Watching. Caring. Always seeing her when no one else did. She fed off my courage. My stances. My way of standing in the world. And slowly she realized it. This is someone different. Someone extraordinary. Someone she could trust with her life, her heart.

If her family — if anyone had really known her back then, they wouldn’t have done what they did. But they didn’t. They never did. And she wasn’t going to share herself with them — not then, not ever. She was strong. Fierce. Ethical. Elegant. Private. Pure. Brilliant.
Her love — for her father, for her younger siblings, for Allah (swt) and Rasulullah (saw) — unmatched. Her potential. Her smarts. Her dedication. Her purity. And yet she was broken. Lost.

And together we found each other. Outcasts. Both of us. Battered by life, by the people who should have protected us. She needed purpose. She needed meaning. I needed purpose. I needed someone I could trust, someone who could see me. And we found it in each other.
We became friends. Partners. Crutches. Anchors. Lovers. We worked together. We lived together. We fought the world together. And slowly, very slowly, we brought each other back to life.

We saw each other raw. The work ethic. The struggles. The world outside. The people around us. And the intimacy — not just physical — mental, emotional, spiritual — no one can imagine that. We built a life. Honorably. Openly. Against all odds.
And then our children came. Moaaz. Then the next. And our love, our resilience, forged them too. Part of the fire. Part of the life we built.

Hina and I — no one else can understand this. Not the family. Not the community. Not the people who thought they knew her. They can’t. Because the experiences that shaped her, that shaped me, that shaped us together — no one else lived them.

We emerged from fire. Multiple times. Individually. Together. And that’s why it’s different. That’s why our bond is extraordinary. That’s why no one can tell you about Hina. Or about Abrar. Only we know. Only you can glimpse it through the life we built. Through what we shared. Through what we endured.
This is who your parents are. And this — this is the truth.
I took a sip of your chai.
Ain’t been right ever since.
a fragment, on the marriage

The walimah ended. The hall emptied out. The caterer packed up. The MC went home. Somewhere in the house at 89 Franklin Road, the chairs from the living room had already been put back where they had been the day before. The world did not change because two people had stood up in a living room and a kid had thrown them a wedding the next day on a flower-shop salary.
But two people had stood up in front of an imam.

The angels kept the record. The mehr was set at one thousand dollars — every dollar the kid had. Her father walked her down the aisle the second time and she stood at the front of the room and consented three times, the way the deen requires, in her own voice, as a woman of twenty-two who had already been broken once and put herself back together. I stood next to her and consented in mine. The witnesses signed. The contract was real.

I would spend the next twenty-nine years and seven months trying to be worthy of the promise I made that afternoon. I would fail at it many times in many ways. I will tell you about the failures in the chapters that come. The marriage was not a smooth road. We emerged from fire multiple times, individually and together, and the fire was real and the emerging was real and neither was guaranteed.

But the wedding was real. The mehr was real. The promise was real. And on May 25, 2019, when I closed her eyes for the last time, what I closed them on was the keeping of that promise — not the perfection of it, but the keeping. I had not left. She had not left. The contract had held all the way to the end. The angels had the record. They have it still.
What I owe her now — what this book is, in its slow way — is the writing it down. Forty years late in some places. But written.

title: Chapter Five — The Flower Shop
paragraphs: The Flower Shop
Teaneck Road, 1986–1996
She walked past it on her way to Food Town. She walked into it and asked for a job. Ten years later, two weeks before Valentine's Day, we bought it.
Part II — Building
She is the girl I grew up with
From "A True Wife" · August 13, 1991
She is the girl I grew up with,
she is the lady I love.
She is the woman who is now,
my wife.

Two weeks before Valentine's Day, 1996, the deed to Teaneck Flowers changed hands. The shop had been Peter Tournas's. Now it was ours. Hina was eight months pregnant. Zanab would arrive on March 25, six weeks after the closing. The shop had a busy season ahead of it. The new owners had a baby ahead of them. Both came on time.

The shop was on Teaneck Road. Hina's family had lived a few blocks away on Franklin Road for as long as the family had lived in America. She walked past Teaneck Flowers regularly — on the way to Food Town five hundred yards down, on errands for her mother, on whatever ordinary trips a girl makes through her own neighborhood. The shop was part of the daily route long before it became part of the daily life. In February 1986, at nineteen, four months back from Durham and looking for somewhere steady, she walked in and asked Peter for a job. Peter hired her.

Peter Tournas was a Greek man, older, decent. He owned three flower shops; Teaneck was the strongest. He ran them honestly. Things changed at Teaneck in some periods because of partners he brought in — the way of small businesses everywhere — but Peter himself was a good man, and he gave Hina a counter to stand behind in a year when standing somewhere steady was its own kind of medicine. She was good at the work. She was articulate, dedicated, diligent. She brought the kind of attention that customers feel even when they cannot name it. She was, plainly, a blessing to Peter. He knew it.

I joined the shop in February 1988, a few months before my nikah to her. I was sixteen. She put me on the payroll. She taught me the register. She taught me how to take a wedding order over the phone. She taught me how to write a delivery slip. From 1988 to 1989 I was running a strange schedule — the shop during the day, two other jobs alongside it, night school four nights a week to get my papers. I was a father at nineteen. The hours had to come from somewhere. I did not sleep much.

Hina worked at the shop full-time roughly two to three years — through 1989, into the early period of motherhood. After Moaaz arrived in December 1990 she stepped back to part-time. The shop did not need her at the counter every day; it needed her institutional memory, which lived in her head and traveled with her wherever she was. By 1991 I was twenty, two years married, running the floor without her present, calling her at her parents' or wherever she had gone with our infant son to ask her how to do the billing. I have a letter that says exactly this. I will get to it in a moment.

What I want to set up first is how we ended up owning the place at all. The honest version is shorter and less neat than the version a memoir prefers. Peter was not retiring. The original plan was not Teaneck.
How We Ended Up Owning It
I was going to buy the Hackensack store. My brothers walked me through the math. The math walked me to Teaneck.

In 1995 I was ready to do something on my own. I had finished night school years before. I had tried, in 1991 and after, to get out of the flower business. The Gulf War recession had killed most of the doors I had knocked on; the jobs that were on offer paid a slightly higher hourly wage but capped the hours, and I was competing for those positions against people with ten and fifteen years of experience. I took civil-service tests to keep options open. I considered becoming a policeman. None of it landed. The flower business stayed.

By the mid-nineties I knew the business cold. I had been at Peter's for seven years. I had worked the front and the back. I had run wedding accounts, funeral accounts, holiday rushes, every wire-service order that came over the line. I was twenty-four. I was ready to own something. I went to Peter and asked.

Peter had three shops. The Hackensack store was one of them. It was the smaller of the three — a smaller customer base, a smaller lease, a smaller price tag. It was what I could afford on my own. Peter was open to selling Hackensack. He would not have wanted to sell Teaneck, his strongest store, to a young employee who was three years on his own from a duffel bag of clothes. The plan I walked into Peter's office with was the Hackensack plan.

Before I shook on it I called my eldest brother. Basit was at LUMS by then. I told him this is what I am about to do, I can do it, I just want to run it past you. He said yes. He said good. He told me to call a family in Connecticut who owned a flower shop. They had numbers. They could look at my numbers. A second set of eyes. I called them. They walked me through the analysis. The Hackensack numbers worked.

Then my middle brother got involved. Assad. He looked at the same numbers. He spent maybe ten minutes with them. Then he said: Why are you buying Hackensack? I told him because that is what I can afford. He said: Why don't you buy Teaneck. The strong store. I said because the price is going to be much more, and because I do not think Peter wants to sell that one — that is the one a man keeps. Assad said: Go ask your father. See if there is a way.

I went to my father. Ikram Koshul, sixty years old at that point, the same man who had taught me by example to do hard things without making a fuss about them. We sat down. We looked at it together. There was a way. Not a comfortable way. A way that involved leaning on him for a portion of the financing, leaning on Peter for a portion, and accepting that the next several years would be tighter than they would have been on the Hackensack track. I went back to Peter with the new plan. Peter, to my surprise, was for it. He had other business he wanted to go into. He could use the funding from a Teaneck sale to do it. Hackensack was not what he was looking to free up. Teaneck was.

So we bought Teaneck. The reason we bought Teaneck and not Hackensack was that my older brothers, in two separate phone calls, refused to let me settle for the smaller store. The reason we could afford Teaneck was that my father said yes. The reason Peter said yes was that he had his own plan. Four men, plus a family in Connecticut, made the deal possible. A young couple stood at the closing and signed.

I want to name this honestly: we did not buy a building on the strength of our own balance sheet. We bought it on the strength of older men who had decided, separately, that the kid was worth backing. Basit and Assad on the family side. Ikram on the financing side. Peter on the seller side. The kid was the one who would carry the work. The older men carried him to the door.
A note on the brothers
Why Assad's ten minutes mattered

Basit said yes to the plan I brought him. That was the older-brother thing. Assad refused it and made me bring a better plan. That was the other older-brother thing. Both of them were right at the same time, in different ways, and the marriage of the two responses is what got the deal done.
I have been the recipient of that doubled love most of my life. The older brothers do not say so. The younger brother is the one who has to write it down.
A du'a · on the signing
اللَّهُمَّ اكْفِنِي بِحَلَالِكَ عَنْ حَرَامِكَ
وَأَغْنِنِي بِفَضْلِكَ عَمَّنْ سِوَاكَ
Allāhumma ikfinī bi-ḥalālika ʿan ḥarāmik,
wa aghninī bi-faḍlika ʿamman siwāk.
O Allah, suffice me with what is halal instead of what is haram, and make me independent, by Your grace, from anyone besides You.
The kid signed papers he could not pay for, on financing he had not earned. This is the prayer he carried into that closing.
— II —
A True Wife
August 13, 1991. School essay. Two years married. Eight-month-old son. The earliest I ever wrote about her on paper.

In August 1991 I was nineteen years old and given a school assignment: write about someone important. I wrote about Hina. I want this essay reproduced inside this book in full because it is the earliest writing I have on her and because the boy in it is the same one who would buy the shop four years later.

Read it knowing that I was running a flower shop and a household, that we had a son named Moaaz who was eight months old, that I had a vocabulary I had built mostly out of necessity. The teacher gave it an A. The teacher's marginal note — that some passages could have been more descriptive and personal — was about specific lines where I had decided not to share what was in my head. Some things are between husband and wife. The honor between us required some things to stay private. They still do.
Artifact · in Ahmad's hand · age 19
A True Wife — page 1 of 4
Handwritten first page of A True Wife essay, dated 8/13/91, by Ahmad Koshul, age 19
The opening page of the essay in the boy's handwriting. Dated 8/13/91 in the upper-right corner. The teacher's marginal notation is visible. The full text follows in print.
A True Wife · in full
A True Wife
By Ahmad Koshul · August 13, 1991
The best thing that could possibly happen to a man is to be blessed by a true wife.

We men have relationships with women such as son and mother, father and daughter, brother and sister. However, the relationship between a man and wife is unique. A wife is one to whom we can bare our soul with absolutely no regret. She is the one to whom we turn at our utmost time of need. It is to her that we promise “till death do we part.” We all have our different interpretations of a true wife. My interpretation’s name is Hina. She is the girl I grew up with, she is the lady I love. She is the woman who is now, my wife.

As we grew up together, I discovered that Hina was so innocent and so pure. She was a bundle of joy whose eyes twinkled like tiny stars. She had a smile which was remarkably genuine and sincere. Never had I seen a girl who was adored by everyone in such a great measure. The energy and charisma which she had within her would have surely brought light to the darkest imaginable places. She was a delightfully darling princess whose unblemished personality, not even the angels could equate.

As time went by, I discovered that Hina, the lady I had learned to love, was a portrait of perfection and of beauty. She changed from an adorable girl into a majestically enticing goddess, to whom there was no equal. Our relationship transformed from friendship into love. I have never seen a lady that was so elegant and refined. She was so delicate, yet her personality so vibrant. Her eyes would glisten like pearls, as the soft rays of the moonlight would emulate off of her trance-inducing, charming eyes. She possessed such a ladylike smile which would melt any man’s heart. A walk which was so gracefully exquisite only she could possess. Her hair was jet black and magnificently fine. The brilliance of her golden skin was lustrously smooth. This was the lady to whom I fell in love.

Hina, the woman who is now, my wife has become my sole sustenance. She is a wife who is very pleasant company. She is considerate and compassionate, understanding and sweet. Our home is her domain in which she is the queen. She is the backbone and pillar of our family. She is the most trustworthy person whom I have ever encountered. Her morals, values and patience are those of a saint. Our son will most definitely grow to manhood in an atmosphere permeated with family love thanks to her devotion to him and to myself. She is very tolerant, courteous and thoughtful, so much so that she is an inspiration to me.

Hina is a woman whom I, merely, can not compliment enough. To keep away from the temptations of the immoral and sinful society of today is a tremendous task which she is accomplishing with great ease. It is an honor for myself to be able to spend my life with someone whom I consider to be the ideal wife. She has such a flawless personality which is in all ways admirable. Hina is a true wife. She is truly a blessing to myself and my son.
I wrote about Hina because there is not anything or anybody that I know better. She is very important to me.

It was hard for me to get my thoughts together. I spent hours thinking of the right words to use, to make the essay flow. I liked reading it over and over. I guess. If I could change it, I would make it more descriptive and be more personal.
— III —
Two Letters Home
She had gone with our son to her brother Zarrar's wedding. I wrote her two letters from the empty house. I signed the second one Ahmad-Abrar.

The same August she had also gone away — she had taken our eight-month-old son and traveled to her brother Zarrar's wedding. I do not remember now exactly how long she was gone. The shop did not stop. The customers did not stop. The bills did not stop. The kid did not stop missing her. I wrote her two letters during that absence, and twenty-one months into the marriage, in the language of a young man with a weak vocabulary trying to say something he did not yet have the words for, I told her things I had not told her before.

The first letter was five pages. I wrote it the day she left. About 21 months ago I married you, about 9 or 10 years ago I decided you were the Lady I wanted to be my wife. I want you to do the arithmetic. Nine or ten years before August 1991 was 1981 or 1982. I was ten or eleven. The decision a grown man was naming in a letter to his wife had been made by a child sitting on a burnt orange couch.

I told her things in that letter I had not been able to tell her before. Before we got married there was a time span of about 4 to 5 years in which I forgot why I loved you but I did remember you were the one I had to get married to. The four-to-five-year span was 1985 to 1989 — her first marriage, her North Carolina years, her return, my homelessness, the rebuilding. The feeling went dim. The decision held. You even asked me why I did not have a sincere answer. You thought maybe it was a rivalry I had with my brother or I wanted to get back at my Family. She had not believed me. She had thought I was using her to spite someone. I could not, at the time, articulate the real reason. The real reason was that I had decided as a child and never undone it.
I told her: I have a very weak vocabulary so I can not express myself the way I want to. I was naming my own limit on the page. The honesty was the gift.
I told her also: I beg of you please take care of my son please, Hina. If anything should happen to him I would go crazy. The eight-month-old was Moaaz. The boy who would grow up to read this book.

And I asked, in business voice in the same letter: Please send step by step directions on how to do the billing for TFS. Love and the ledger in the same letter. The flower shop and the marriage in the same envelope. They were not separate compartments. They never had been.

The second letter was shorter. Two pages. Sent later in the same trip with a questionnaire enclosed for her to sign and FedEx back. I had run out of paper for tenderness and was running on need. I wrote: Please strengthen your personality so that I can stand straighter. A nineteen-year-old husband asking his twenty-four-year-old wife to be a stronger spine for him to lean on. The dependency was honest. The marriage carried it because she was strong enough.
And then, in the same letter, the line that named the whole rest of this book before I knew there would be a book:
I had forgotten my entire life before 1987-88
and now for some reason the years before that
come to my mind a lot more often than they used to.

1987-88 is the boy on the front porch with the duffel bag and the thousand things he would never tell anyone. He had walled off the years before. He was, at nineteen, watching that wall come down. I thought that the old Abrar had passed away, I wrote, but every now and then I swear I feel him inside of me trying to express himself but he can not. The two voices of this book — Buyahka the builder, Abrar the soul — were already named in 1991, in a letter from an empty house. The book did not invent the frame. The boy did, at nineteen.
I signed that second letter Ahmad - Abrar. The two names side by side, with a hyphen between them. The merged self. He was already trying to be both at once.
— IV —
Alone I Have Been
She wrote me a love letter, undated. No salutation. No signature. Just the words. I have read it a thousand times.

There is a single page in Hina's handwriting in the archive of this marriage. No date. No greeting. No closing. Just the words. I do not know what year she wrote it. I do not know if she handed it to me or left it where I would find it. I do not know if she meant for me to keep it forever. She did not write a draft of it — this is the only copy. She did not sign it.
I am going to put it here as she wrote it. The double underline on one word is hers. The pacing is hers. I will not interrupt it. After it I will say one thing.
Hina · undated · in her own hand
Untitled
Your company gives me peace and serenity. No one else like you, to me. The comfort, support and strength that I feel from your decency.
I may seem to be a pest and desire you — more than you care to be desired.
But my need is what makes me desirous of you: the need of goodness. The need of peace. The need of a silent understanding. Your voice and looks are additional; but secondary — and all else.
To know that you are — makes me whole and complete. Alone I have been and you've ALWAYS been the filler of the hole.
So please forgive my need, and accept my appreciation.
Artifact · in Hina's hand · undated
Alone I have been — the letter itself
Hina's handwritten love letter to Ahmad, no date, no salutation, no signature, with the word ALWAYS double-underlined
Her actual page. Her actual handwriting. The double-underlined ALWAYS visible at center. No date, no greeting, no closing. Only the words.

The thing I have to say is this. The double-underlined ALWAYS is the most important word in our archive. She is asserting that I had filled the hole in her not occasionally, not sometimes, not most of the time, but always. I do not believe I had earned it. I believe she had decided to credit me with it. There is a generosity in her telling me so that I do not know how to repay. The page is in this book in part as a debt I am acknowledging cannot be repaid, only honored by being written down where it can be read.

"Your voice and looks are additional; but secondary." She is naming what she values and what she does not. She did not love me for my voice. She did not love me for my looks. She loved me for what she calls, in the same letter, decency. That is the cleanest naming of a marriage I have ever read.
Who She Already Was
The poster was made before her first marriage. Before any of this. It is the evidence of a consciousness that arrived early and did not need anyone's permission.

There is a poster in the archive that I want to show you here, even though it predates everything in this chapter. Hina made it sometime around 1980 or 1981 or 1982, somewhere in those years before her first marriage. She was thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. She had been writing poetry since she was nine. She had been thinking about the deen since she was a child. The poster is a single sheet, decorated in colored markers. Rules for handling the Qur'an, fanned out from a central blank space in a sunburst pattern. The word at the center was meant to be RESPECT.

I am putting it in this chapter, the chapter about the years we built the shop and the household, because the woman I was building with was already this woman before I built anything with her. She did not become this in our marriage. She arrived as this. A teenage girl, or a child on the cusp of teenage, putting careful adab on a single sheet in colored marker, before she had been married, before she had been broken, before she had returned, before any of the parts of her story this book has to tell. The consciousness was already complete.

If you want to know who she was, you do not start with what was done to her at sixteen. You start with what she was making at thirteen. You start with poems written by a nine-year-old about Buraq, with a Battle of Badr piece written at fifteen that won a youth speech competition, with a poem at fifteen called Pick Your Path addressed to her own father. You start with the consciousness that was there before the world ever asked her to defend it.

I cannot do justice to that here. I am one man and her husband and biased — that is admitted. But I am telling you, if you read her poetry from 1976 forward, you will see what I am saying. There was nothing like her. I have not met anyone like her in fifty years. Read her poems. Note the ages. Put it together for yourself. The poster is one fragment of a much larger record.

The poster, in any case, sat somewhere in her life from then forward. By the time we had children of our own, it was on a wall in our house. The children grew up under it. The rules were the same rules they would have been taught one way or another — she would have written them on a different sheet if she had to — but they grew up under the actual sheet she had made as a girl. They learned adab from her teenage handwriting. The continuity of one consciousness across a lifetime, in colored markers, on a single page.
Artifact · in Hina's hand
RESPECT — Qur'an Adab Poster
Hand-drawn poster in colored markers radiating rules of adab around a central blank space meant to read RESPECT

A single sheet, colored markers, rules for handling the Qur'an arranged in a sunburst around a center meant to read RESPECT. Made by Hina sometime around 1980–1982, in her early teens. Before her first marriage.
— VI —
The Three Births
Three hospital records. Three sets of footprints. Hina's right index fingerprint on every one. The same mother. Three different doors.

Each of our three children has a hospital identification record. Mother's right index fingerprint. Infant's left and right footprints. The footprints are tiny. The ink stayed sharp on the cardstock. We kept all three. Hina kept all three. They are in this archive because she did not throw them out. She put them in a folder and the folder traveled with us through the houses.
A litany
Moaaz Furqan Koshul
December 7, 1990 · 10:56 a.m. · Dr. Fox
Shahbaaz Koshul
November 26, 1992 · 6:35 p.m. · 8 lbs · 21 inches
Zanab Koshul
March 25, 1996 · 2:57 a.m. · 7 lbs 11.5 oz · Dr. Fernandez

On Shahbaaz's record, at the top of the page, in Hina's handwriting, are two words: HAPPY BIRTHDAY! She wrote it on the hospital form. The form is supposed to be only the medical and identification data. She wrote on it anyway. The exclamation point is hers.

I want to tell you what those three records together mean to me now. They mean that my wife was on the labor and delivery floor of three different hospital nights at twenty-three, twenty-five, and twenty-nine years old, and on each of those nights she came out of it with a living child and her own life and the will to make a folder for the paperwork. The third one, Zanab, came six weeks after we closed on the flower shop. Hina was nine months pregnant during the closing, two weeks before Valentine's Day. She walked through the financial paperwork and the medical paperwork in the same season. The deeds came home in February. Zanab came home in March.

I sometimes look at the footprints on those three sheets and think: these three small feet are the reason for the building. Not the reason we bought it — we bought it because the chance came and the brothers said go. The reason the building matters. The shop was the means. The children were the meaning. She knew the difference. She never confused them.
Our home is her domain
in which she is the queen.
A True Wife · 1991
— VII —
November 10, 1999 · Promises Kept
Tenth wedding anniversary. The first night I had spent away from my children since I had become their father. The thank-you note I wrote to my mother-in-law afterward.

Ten years to the day after the nikah at 89 Franklin Road, on Wednesday, November 10, 1999, Hina and I went away for one night together. Auntie Beg watched the children. Moaaz was about to turn nine. Shahbaaz was about to turn seven. Zanab was three. It was the first night Hina and I had spent alone since Moaaz had been born.

I want you to read that sentence again. The first night alone in ten years. People assume parents like that have not figured out how to leave. The truth is more particular. We had been told to leave plenty of times. Auntie Beg, on a few occasions in those years, had said the equivalent of go, go — you two should go to the movies, I have the kids, go. We would get in the car. We would drive to the theater. We would sit in the parking lot. We would not be able to bring ourselves to buy the tickets. We would drive back home.

Sometimes we made it as far as a restaurant. The restaurants in our area in those years were not very good. There was no excitement to dinner anyway. We would eat fast and head back to the kids. We did not understand how other parents did it. We watched other couples leaving their children with grandparents and we said the things parents say to each other in those situations — good for them, that's nice, glad they can do that — and then we drove back to the den, where the kids were, and watched them sleep, and felt right.

I have written elsewhere about the principle of promises kept. There is a poem of mine that lives near the line. Promises were the form love took for us. Hina was going to keep her promise. I was going to keep mine. The first promise of a young marriage with three small children is that the children will not be alone. We kept that promise so completely for ten years that we could not figure out how to break it for an evening. The inability to leave was not a failure of imagination. It was a feature of the marriage. The promise was working.

What changed in November 1999 was that Auntie Beg had set it up in advance, told us a date, told us a time, taken the kids, locked the door behind us, and made it impossible to drive back. Even then we were uneasy. We went anyway. We had a quiet night. We came back. A few days later I sat down at the typewriter and wrote her a thank-you note.
Letter to Auntie Beg · typewritten · signed by hand
To my mother-in-law
Wednesday, November 10, 1999 · tenth wedding anniversary
ASSALAMOLAIKUM
Dear Auntie Beg,

I wanted to thank you for watching the kids on Wednesday, Nov 10th, 1999. I know that you have watched them plenty of times before: on holidays and on Mondays — so that Hina could come to work. I appreciate those times, as well.

However, this last time was for a different reason and that's what makes it special, insha-allah something we will remember for a long time to come. It was the first time in 10 yrs in which, I was able to go away for a night with my wife. It was very nice and I wanted to let you know how much I appreciated it. We had a nice time — even though we are not use to being alone — without our children. For one night it was a nice change. I wanted you to know that even though it is a few days later, I haven't forgotten and I wanted to express my gratitude and thanks for enabling me to spend a few moments with my wife and putting a smile on her face.
Auntie you are a very thoughtful and considerate person and I am glad to have a woman like yourself as a mother-in-law.
Thank You.
With Sincere Appreciation,
Ahmad-Abrar

Twelve years before this letter, in 1987, Auntie Beg's husband had written me a letter telling me to leave his daughter's life. He had been right to write it, given what he knew. I had been the right person to receive it, given what I was at fifteen. We had both been telling the truth as we understood it.

By 1999 her husband had walked her down the aisle to me. By 1999 her mother was watching our three children so we could go away one night. By 1999 the man who had been called haram by her father was signing letters to her mother as Ahmad-Abrar, the same merged signature he had first used in 1991, two names with a hyphen between them. The hyphen was holding.

Auntie Beg's specific gift, in the letter, is named: on Mondays — so that Hina could come to work. She was, on every Monday for years, the reason Hina was able to be at the shop. The flower shop did not run on Hina alone. It ran on Hina plus the woman who was her mother. The shop survived in part because the older generation kept showing up to mind the children.
She is the girl I grew up with,
she is the lady I love.
She is the woman who is now,
my wife.
A True Wife · the line that survives

By the close of the nineties we had what we had wanted, more or less. A shop on Teaneck Road that bore our names on the deed. Three children whose footprints we had kept in folders. A house we had not yet bought but were saving toward. A marriage that had been tested and held. A community that watched us with the mixture of pride and resentment communities reserve for couples who do not give them anything to gossip about.

The shop was ordinary. Flowers came in on Tuesdays. Weddings in the spring. Mother's Day in May. Funerals every week. Valentine's Day was the engine of the year. We worked the holidays. We watched the kids. We drove past the theater on the rare nights we tried to go out and could not bring ourselves to buy the tickets. We came home. We slept in the same bed.

The ordinariness is the point of this chapter. After everything in the previous chapters — her first marriage, the homelessness, the lawsuit, the splintering, the living-room nikah at 89 Franklin Road — we got the ordinary years. The ten years of nobody-watching, of show-up-on-Monday, of make-the-billing-make-sense, of teach-the-children-the-words, of keep-the-promise. The angels who had kept the record at the wedding kept the record through the ordinary years too. The ordinary years are not less holy. They are where the contract gets kept.
A du'a · for the keeping
يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ
ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ
Yā Muqallibal-qulūb,
thabbit qalbī ʿalā dīnik.
O Turner of hearts,
keep my heart firm on Your religion.
My father-in-law had said this du'a through the splintering. I said it through the ordinary years. The keeping of a promise, said over and over until it becomes the shape of a life.
Then came September 2001. That is the next chapter.

title: Chapter Six — September's Children
paragraphs: September's Children
2001 -- 2002 -- the years that followed

A franchise agreement signed in 2001. A flower shop building bought and a store moved one and a half blocks down Teaneck Road that September. The towers fell on the eleventh. The Muslim community in America had been on a quiet rise before that morning. Then everything changed.
Part II — Building
A Way of Remembering
In Hina's words · December 7, 2015
Everyone likes to remember the past
as they feel it.
I pray to remember the past as it was.
Hina, in a letter to her husband on their first son's twenty-fifth birthday

This chapter is the chapter where the country we lived in changed, and the building we had been building inside that country had to keep being built anyway. It is also the chapter where the marriage we had made in Hina's father's living room twelve years earlier did not have a single night to itself for a full ten of those years. Both things are true. Both things have to be in here.

In the spring of 2001, Assad and I drove up to Connecticut to meet with Tariq Farid. Tariq was an accountant by training, a numbers guy, who along with his brother Kamran had started a small company called Edible Arrangements. They had built the first store in East Haven in 1999. By 2001 they were beginning to franchise. I was twenty-nine years old. I was a small business owner in the blue-collar end of the world. The flower business. Two flower shops by then -- the one on Teaneck Road and a second in Elmwood Park.

I had also just bought the building the Teaneck flower shop sat in, and was about to move the store from 1372 to 1320 Teaneck Road, one and a half blocks down. That move happened the first week of September 2001. The new store opened on Teaneck Road right before the towers fell.

So the timing in my life that summer was layered. The franchise agreement with Edible Arrangements got signed in 2001. The first Edible Arrangements store would open the following year, in 2002, at 350 Main Street in Hackensack. But in the late summer of 2001 the work was the flower shop -- buying the building, moving the store, getting the new location open in time for what we did not yet know was going to happen.

I read the franchise documents at the kitchen table. Hina sat across from me. Moaaz was ten. Shahbaaz was eight. Zanab was five. The children had been home-schooled by Hina for four or five years by then. That was a thing Hina had decided and that I had supported. The decision had freed her, in some ways, and tied her down in other ways. The children were her work most of the day. The flower shop was her work the rest of the day. The house was always her work. I sat at the kitchen table and asked her about a franchise agreement that was going to add another store to her plate, eventually, and on top of all of that.
What Hina said, sitting at that table, was: do it.

What she also said, in a letter she had written me ten years earlier when I was nineteen and she was twenty-four, was a sentence I want to put down here because it is the sentence that explains how she said yes that night.
Please strengthen your personality
so that I can stand straighter.
Ahmad to Hina · from a 1991 letter, age nineteen

I wrote that to her. I want to be clear about that. The teenager I was at nineteen was asking the woman I had married at eighteen to be the structural strength I did not yet have, so that I could grow into something she could lean against. That is the bargain we struck. That is the bargain we kept striking, year after year, decade after decade. She would carry the family while I tried to grow into a man big enough that the family could be carried by me instead.

So in 2001, when I asked her about Edible Arrangements, what she heard was the same question I had been asking since 1991: can I lean on you while I try to become something more than I am right now. And what she said, again, was yes.

I signed the franchise agreement. The Hackensack location was identified. The build-out would not finish until the following year. Before that, though, came the flower-shop move in early September. Before that came September 11.
A Du'a -- Surah al-Anfal 8:62
وَإِن يُرِيدُوا أَن يَخْدَعُوكَ فَإِنَّ حَسْبَكَ اللَّهُ
Wa in yureedu an yakhda'ooka fa-inna hasbakallah.
"And if they intend to deceive you -- then sufficient for you is Allah."

A verse for the man who is signing papers in a country whose terms toward him are about to change. I did not yet know in the summer of 2001 that the country was going to change. The verse was already in the world, waiting. Allah was sufficient before September. Allah was sufficient after.
September Eleven

Right before that morning, the Muslim community in America had been on a quiet rise. We were finding our footing. We were assimilating in the ways that mattered, holding our own in the ways that mattered more. Then the towers fell, and the tone of the country changed, and everything changed.

I want to write this section carefully, and I want to say up front that what is on the page here is a first pass. The full reckoning with September 11, what it did to the Muslim community in America, what it did to the children growing up Muslim in America, what it did to my family and to the businesses we were trying to build inside this country -- all of that needs more room than I have tonight. So I am putting down the seed, and I am going to come back to it.

In the late summer of 2001, the Muslim community in America was on a quiet rise. The masjid at Dar ul Islah, which my father and Khalid Beg had helped build out of a garage on Coplay Avenue twenty-five years earlier, had grown into a real community. Children of immigrants were in high schools and colleges. Some of us were starting businesses. Some of us were becoming doctors and engineers. The country was making room for us in ways it had not in the 1970s. We were assimilating into the parts of America that allowed it. We were holding our own in the parts that mattered most -- our prayers, our families, our children, our names. There was a feeling in those years, in our community, that we belonged here. That we were Americans, and Muslims, and that the two things were not in contradiction.

September 11 did not end that feeling all at once. But it changed it. It changed the tone of the country toward us. It changed the way our names sounded when other people read them. It changed what it meant to be a Muslim business owner in Bergen County. It changed what it meant to be a Muslim child in a public school. It changed how the country looked at our community, and it changed how our community looked at the country.

The flower shop had just moved one and a half blocks down Teaneck Road. The new space was open. The franchise agreement for Edible Arrangements was signed. The build for the first Edible Arrangements store in Hackensack was somewhere in the pipeline. All of that work continued in the days and weeks after the eleventh. None of it stopped. But the country it was happening inside had changed. The book will come back to what that change meant. This chapter is laying down the marker.
— II —
2002 -- 350 Main Street
The first Edible Arrangements store opened in Hackensack, on Main Street, in 2002. The country had changed. The work continued anyway.

The first Edible Arrangements store opened at 350 Main Street in Hackensack in 2002. I do not have a clean memory of the opening day. I have memories of the build -- the refrigeration, the counters, the signage. I have memories of the early customers, who were mostly people from the neighborhood and people who had been sent by other people in the neighborhood. The product was new in Bergen County in 2002. Cut fruit shaped to look like flowers. Strawberries dipped in chocolate. The kind of thing people sent to each other when they were not sure what else to send.

What I remember more clearly than the opening day is the feeling of working through that year and the years after. The country was at war by then. Afghanistan first, then Iraq. The color-coded threat levels appeared on the news. Airports installed new procedures. At Dar ul Islah, the community kept going to prayer. The wisdom of the men who had built the masjid in the 1970s and 1980s -- modestly, with their own money, in a way that did not depend on outside funding that could later be questioned -- turned out, in the 2000s, to be the wisdom that allowed our community to keep functioning without becoming a target. My father and Khalid Beg had built quietly. Quietly was the right way to have built.

Inside our house, the children kept growing. Moaaz finished his home-school years and the boys eventually transitioned into more formal schooling for parts of their teen years. Shahbaaz did the same, two years behind. Zanab, the youngest, grew through the early grades while her brothers moved into their teens. The dinner table got louder. The house felt smaller. The flower shop in its new building on Teaneck Road kept running. The Edible Arrangements store in Hackensack kept running. The community at Dar ul Islah kept growing. The country was at war. The marriage was being made.
A Du'a -- Rabbi yassir wa la tuassir
رَبِّ يَسِّرْ وَلَا تُعَسِّرْ، رَبِّ تَمِّمْ بِالْخَيْرِ
Rabbi yassir wa la tuassir, rabbi tammim bil-khayr.
"My Lord, make it easy and do not make it difficult; complete it with goodness."

The du'a I said before every store opening for the next twenty years. Before every lease signing. Before every loan paper. Before every conversation with a contractor or a landlord or a lender. I did not always say it out loud. Sometimes I said it under my breath in the car. Sometimes I said it standing in front of a refrigeration unit at four in the morning. Every store opened with this du'a in my mouth. Allah eased the easy ones. Allah taught me through the difficult ones. The completing in goodness is still being completed.
— III —
Ten Years Without a Night Away
November 10, 1989, to November 10, 1999. We did not have a single night to ourselves. Not until Auntie Beg arranged it.

Iam going to step back from the storefront for a moment. The chapter is supposed to cover the years that followed September 2001, but the years that followed are the same years the marriage was being made out of, and the marriage cannot be skipped. So let me tell you something about the ten years before September 2001, because it is the foundation that the September years sat on top of.

Hina and I were married on November 10, 1989. From November 10, 1989, until November 10, 1999, we did not spend a single night alone together. Not one. We had three children in those years. We had a flower shop. We had a house that always had a child sleeping in a room down the hall. We did not, at any point in that decade, have a Tuesday night without a child in the next bed.

Auntie Beg knew this. Hina's mother. The woman whose living room had hosted the nikah in 1989. She had watched her daughter work alongside her son-in-law for ten years without pause, and she decided, on the tenth wedding anniversary, that she was going to give us one night.

She watched the kids on Wednesday, November 10, 1999. Hina and I went away for one night. I do not remember now where we went. I think it was a hotel somewhere in northern New Jersey. The geography is not the point. The point is that for the first time in a decade, we were two adults in a room without three children. We did not know how to do it. We were not used to being alone. Hina laughed about that, the next morning. We don't know what to do with each other when no one needs anything, she said. We figured it out for one night. Then we went home.

I wrote a letter to Auntie Beg afterward. I want to put it here. It is dated a few days after the night, which means I sat down at a typewriter, in the late autumn of 1999, with three children somewhere in the house and a wife who had just gone back to running everything, and I made a point of saying thank you in writing.
Artifact · November 1999
Letter to Auntie Beg, on the tenth wedding anniversary
ASSALAMOLAIKUM
Dear Auntie Beg,

I wanted to thank you for watching the kids on Wednesday, Nov 10th, 1999. I know that you have watched them plenty of times before: on holidays and on Mondays -- so that Hina could come to work. I appreciate those times, as well.

However, this last time was for a different reason and that's what makes it special, insha-allah something we will remember for a long time to come. It was the first time in 10yrs in which, I was able to go away for a night with my wife. It was very nice and I wanted to let you know how much I appreciated it. We had a nice time -- even though we are not used to being alone -- without our children. For one night it was a nice change. I wanted you to know that even though it is a few days later, I haven't forgotten and I wanted to express my gratitude and thanks for enabling me to spend a few moments with my wife and putting a smile on her face.
Auntie you are a very thoughtful and considerate person and I am glad to have a woman like yourself as a mother-in-law.
Thank You
With Sincere Appreciation
Ahmad-Abrar

I read that letter now and I see two things. First, the kid I was at twenty-eight was already practicing the witness register. Polite, careful, gracious, signed with both names — Ahmad-Abrar — the merged signature that would carry me the rest of my life. Second, I see the line I did not see at the time: so that Hina could come to work. Auntie Beg had been watching the kids on holidays and on Mondays for ten years so that Hina could come to The Flower Shop. The flower shop my brothers had pushed me to buy in 1995 was being run on the back of a grandmother. Without Auntie Beg, there is no flower shop. Without the flower shop, there is no franchise agreement in 2001. Without 2001, there are no stores that came after. The whole architecture rested, partly, on a woman in her sixties watching three children in a house on Franklin Road.

I did not see that in 1999. I am seeing it now. The Naming Duty says I am supposed to name it. So I am naming it. Auntie Beg made the building of this life possible. The building is hers, partly. We do not say it often enough.
— IV —
The Years That Followed
More stores. More work. A country slowly recalibrating after September. A marriage still being made.

The years between 2002 and the middle of the decade were the building years. From the Hackensack store onward, the work was the same work, repeated: find a location, sign a lease, build out, open, run. Find a location, sign a lease, build out, open, run. The stores grew, one at a time. The names of the towns those stores were in are kept for a later chapter, when the closings begin. For now, what matters is that the building was happening, the way building always happens for a small business owner -- on top of everything else, by the same set of two pairs of hands, every day, for years on end.

I want to be honest about a part of this that is hard to write. A chapter about a man buying businesses and surviving September 11 and building stores can read like a triumph narrative if you let it. Man buys business. Man builds business. Man survives. Man expands. That story is not wrong, exactly. But it is not the whole story. The whole story is that during those years I was not yet the man Hina had been told, in 1989, she was marrying. I was still the kid who had asked her, in 1991, to be strong enough to let me stand straighter. I was still leaning. The leaning showed up in different ways at different times. Sometimes as absence. Sometimes as anger I did not understand. Sometimes as a tendency to disappear into the work because the work was easier than the rest of it.

Hina knew this. She had known it since 1991. She had married me anyway. She had had three children with me anyway. She had run the flower shop and the house anyway. In 2009, for the first time, she would write a letter saying she could not do it anymore. We would work through that one. In 2014, she would write another letter saying the same thing. We would work through that one too. The two letters belong in Chapter 7, not here. But you should know, reading this chapter, that the years between 2002 and 2009 were not as smooth as a chapter ending in stores-and-children might suggest. They were the years in which the foundation was being held in place by Hina, while I tried to figure out what kind of man I was becoming.
December 7, 2015
Twenty-five years after Moaaz was born, Hina sat down at her tablet and wrote her husband a letter. This is the one I want to close the chapter with.

Ihave already given you the opening epigraph of this chapter, which is the first sentence of the letter Hina wrote me on December 7, 2015. I want to give you the rest of it now, because it is the way I want this chapter to end. Hina is in her own voice here. The chapter has been mine for too long.

December 7, 2015 was Moaaz's twenty-fifth birthday. Twenty-five years to the day after he was born at 10:56 a.m. on December 7, 1990, in a hospital in Englewood, with Dr. James Fox attending and Hina lying in the bed and me — nineteen years old and married to her for thirteen months — trying to figure out how to be present for a thing I did not understand. Hina remembered all of this in 2015. She wrote it down. She sent it to me. Here is what she wrote.
Artifact · December 7, 2015 · 3:45 PM
Hina to Ahmad, on Moaaz's twenty-fifth birthday
As salaam o alaikum:
Everyone likes to remember the past as they feel it. I pray to remember the past as it was.
I found myself reminiscing of 25 years ago on this date.
Over the years I have watched comedians and television shows and their narrative or dramatization of child birthing. But my personal memory is nothing like that.
Before I begin, even though our moods are not in synch since Halloween; in no way, shape or form does this change the realities of yesterday.
Having said that I would like to thank you --
1) for the pleasure associated with and what led to ...
2) for the chance to raise my rank to motherhood

3) for being a wonderful spouse/partner -- when it came to helping in cleaning ooltees; rocking him to sleep on the rocking chair; staying up with me when needed; for being patient when needed; and all that my heart appreciates you for, that most (desi) males do not do --
4) for being a caring, loving, concerned father [even though sometimes I may disagree with ... but nonetheless I think I know you]
Before I go ahead, this is not a trick (nor is it advice any form) -- I just wanted to reminisce with my husband, and this is the only way I know how.
25 years ago to date -- I lay in the hospital and the first thing that came to mind when I was asked if I needed anything was: Abrar
I recalled the anger and sadness to know you were going to go to school, when I wanted you near.
I recalled the helplessness you may have felt, as you tried to ease my pains ... the only way you knew (by offering to order pizza)
I recalled your logging the times of contractions, and handing the task to Amina
I recalled the joy and relief when I saw your face, after you came back from school and stopped in the hospital room (but sensing your unease I let you go and had Amee come)
I recalled you saying: If anything were to happen to me, that is not the last memory you wanted (thus giving me something...)
I recalled being frustrated because they would not allow me to see nor hold my son.

I recalled the thrill of actually meeting Moaaz in the company of his father. By the grace of God, he turned a couple into a family; through his entry our ranks were elevated (so were responsibilities...but that all came with the territory Alhumdolilah).

The problem with reminiscing is they go on and on and on...so... at the end of all the memories: Our son has turned 25 and all the celebrations are towards wishing him a happy birthday. I wanted to take a moment and say thank you.
was salaam
hina
By the grace of God, he turned a couple
into a family; through his entry
our ranks were elevated.
Hina · on Moaaz's twenty-fifth birthday

Iread that letter when she sent it. The letter says even though our moods are not in synch since Halloween, which means we had been in one of our quiet stretches for about six weeks by the time she sat down to write it. I should be careful with the word fight. We did not have fights, Hina and I. Not the way other couples have fights. We had disagreements, and then we quieted down. That is what we did. Whatever one of us was going through, or whatever one of us was not understanding about the other -- the normal things that little couples go through -- we did not raise voices over them. We did not slam doors. We went quiet. We went quiet for a few days, sometimes a few weeks, sometimes longer. And then one of us would do something small -- a cup of tea, a question about the kids, a letter -- and the quiet would end, and we would start talking again.

The letter is what ended the Halloween-to-December quiet of 2015. Hina sat down on a Monday afternoon at her tablet and wrote me four numbered thank-yous and a long paragraph of reminiscing, and that was her way of saying the quiet stretch was over for her. I did not respond as well as I should have. I do not remember now what I said back, or whether I said anything at all. I do remember that the letter has stayed with me ever since, and that the fourth thank-you -- even though sometimes I may disagree with ... but nonetheless I think I know you -- is a line I have read more than a hundred times since she died.

What she was doing in that letter was the thing this whole book is trying to do. She was practicing the discipline of remembering the past as it was. Not as she felt it. As it was. Both things at once. The quiet from Halloween was real. The hospital room from twenty-five years earlier was also real. The man who had failed her in some way in 2015 was also the boy who had logged her contractions in 1990 and offered to order pizza because he did not know what else to do. Hina held all of it in the same letter. She named it. She thanked me for what was thank-able. She did not pretend the rest of it was not there.

That is the witness register. I learned it from her. I am still learning it from her, seven years after she died, sitting at this screen, trying to write a chapter about the years between 2001 and 2015 without flattening any of it.

The chapter that follows this one is going to be the chapter where the quiet stretches got harder. Hina's 2009 letter. Hina's 2014 letter. The years in which the marriage went through its first two formal crises. I do not want to write that chapter. I am going to write it anyway. The book does not work without it.

But I want to leave this chapter where Hina left her letter. Twenty-five years after Moaaz was born. The flower shop moved to its new building on Teaneck Road in the first week of September 2001. The towers down on the eleventh. The country changed. The first Edible Arrangements store opened in Hackensack in 2002, the work continued, the building kept being built. A wife who had not had a single night away in ten years and who, when she finally got one, came back and went straight back to work. A grandmother in a house on Franklin Road making the whole architecture possible. Three children growing up Muslim in America in the years when growing up Muslim in America became a thing you had to think about. A couple turned into a family. Ranks elevated. A husband and wife in November of 2015 having gone quiet for six weeks, and then a letter in early December that did the work of remembering the past as it was.
Alhumdolilah, she wrote. Alhumdolilah for all of it.
Alhumdolilah from me too.

title: Chapter Seven — The Pattern
paragraphs: [Heading1] The Pattern
[Heading1] Teaneck, 2001–2018
I kept building things that required a man I wasn't. She kept holding what I built. The years quieted down. The quiet got longer.
Part II — Building
Type of Guy
Six lines · 2022
You know the story of us,
we bow down to no one but the Glorious.
You're the type of guys, they avoidin and hidin from;
we're the type of men, protectin, providin and guidin them.
We could've been swimmin in your women
but stay clean like the Criterion
gettin in their hearts like Heart Surgeons.

There is a kind of building that looks like growth from the outside and feels like running from the inside. I did both at the same time for almost twenty years. The shop multiplied. The household held. The marriage went into long quiets and came out of them. The pattern was always the same. I would build something that required a man I had not yet become. Hina would hold what I built. The structure would creak. We would not fight. We would quiet down. The quiet would last. Something small would end it. We would start again. The next thing I built was always slightly larger and required a slightly larger man. The gap between what the structure needed and what I was kept widening. By 2018 the structure was eleven stores and a household of five and a community that had watched us for two decades, and the man inside it was tired in a way I could not yet name.

This chapter covers about eighteen years. It is the longest stretch of time in the book and the hardest to write, because nothing in it is dramatic. The dramatic chapters are easier. Ch 2 has a wedding refusal at twelve. Ch 8 has a death. Ch 3 has a homeless boy in an entryway. Ch 7 has Tuesday. Ch 7 has the billing. Ch 7 has the same drive to the same office for years on end and the same negotiations with the same landlords and the same conversations about the same kids with the same wife who, year by year, was naming what was wrong with more and more precision — while I, year by year, was hearing her words inside a different frame than the one she meant them in. The pattern between us was not silence. The pattern was articulate witness on her side and busy mistranslation on mine. The pattern does not have a face. It cannot be confronted. It can only be lived through.

So this is a quieter chapter than the ones around it. I want to name a few of the structures I built, the loop they revealed, the way Hina tried to name what was happening before I could see it, the inheritance dispute over her father's house that ran in parallel with everything else, the world outside that was tightening around us, and the closing approach of the last year. I will let Hina speak in this chapter more than I speak myself. She was the better witness. She always had been.
[Heading2] The Loop
Build fast. Delegate. Withdraw. Drift. Reset. Repeat at a larger scale. Each cycle was a new business. The pattern was the same.

Between 2001 and the late 2010s, the businesses kept multiplying. The Hackensack store at 350 Main opened in 2002. After that, store by store, the Edible Arrangements footprint grew to eleven units across northern New Jersey and into Rockland County. Hackensack. Paramus. Fort Lee. Midland Park. Pompton Lakes. Westwood. Pearl River. The Teaneck flower shop kept running alongside. There were stretches where I was holding leases on a dozen storefronts at once. By 2010 the structure was somewhere around ten or eleven stores plus other businesses I had moved through along the way, and two houses — one in Teaneck, one in Tafton, Pennsylvania — and the building on Teaneck Road where the flower shop sat. That was what the world saw.

Alongside the franchise expansion there were side ventures. There was an HVAC business I started. There was a pizzeria with Furqan. There were bathroom renovations I took on for friends and family and then for paying customers. There were a few other things I will not bother to name here because they did not last long enough to take a shape. Each of these had the same arc: I would see the opportunity, I would jump on it, I would build the structure, I would hire someone to run it, I would step back, the structure would drift, and I would either let it die quietly or I would have to come back and rebuild it from the inside.

The loop, said plainly: Build fast. Delegate before the structure is mature. Withdraw to chase the next thing. Watch the structure drift. Come back and reset. Sometimes the reset worked. Sometimes the structure was already gone by the time I got back to it. The HVAC business died this way. The pizzeria with Furqan died this way. A few of the smaller things died this way. The Edible Arrangements stores were strong enough to survive my withdrawal-and-return cycles for a long time, but eventually four of them would not. That is Ch 11.

What I want to say in Ch 7, while we are still in the middle of the expansion, is that the loop was not a strategy. I did not choose it. I did not name it. I did not see it. I was inside it. The loop was what happened when a man with a builder's instinct and no internal structure tried to manage growth that exceeded what he had built inside himself to hold. I built things faster than I built the man who could hold them. Hina watched it happen for years. She did not have the vocabulary to name it in business terms. She had the vocabulary to name it as a wife. The letters in this chapter are her trying to name it.

One more thing about my brothers, because this matters for what comes next. Basit and Assad were not a daily force in our marriage decisions. I want to say that plainly. I was in this marriage by myself. I chose it. I was in it alone. Her family was present every day, every hour. Mine was present occasionally — a trip to Pakistan in 2007, another around 2014, Hajj in 2015, the occasional visit when one of them was passing through. My brothers were a counsel I turned to in specific moments, not a daily voice at our dinner table. The marriage was mine. The decisions were mine. The mistakes were mine. What Hina was naming about Basit and Assad in the 2014 letter was something more specific, which the next section will explain — it was about the business seat, not about who was running our marriage.
A note on the type of man
[Heading3] Gentle and furious

The poem I opened this chapter with is called Type of Guy. I wrote it in 2022, after Hina was gone, but the man it is naming is the man I was trying to be all through these years. Gentle with her. Furious for her. Gentle with the children. Furious for them. Gentle inside the household. Furious at what threatened the household from outside.

The man the world will sell you, the man the imams and therapists and the soft books will sell you, is the gentle man with no fury. That man is a coward dressed up as a saint. He cannot protect anyone. He cannot fight for anyone. He cannot say the hard thing when the hard thing needs to be said. He is a decoration in his own house.

I was trying to be the other kind. Gentle with her, furious for her. Slow hand for her, hard hand for what threatened her. I did not always get the proportions right. I sometimes had the fury pointed in the wrong direction. I sometimes had the gentleness withdrawn when it was needed most. But the orientation was the right orientation. The poem is the orientation, written down later.
A du'a · on building what you cannot finish alone
رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ
وَأَنْ أَعْمَلَ صَالِحًا تَرْضَاهُ
Rabbi awzi‘ni an ashkura ni‘mataka allati an‘amta ‘alayya,
wa an a‘mala ṣāliḥan tarḍāhu.
My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me, and to do righteous deeds that please You.
Sulayman's du'a, Surah An-Naml 27:19. The prayer of a man who has been given more than he can hold and is asking to be made adequate to it.
— II —
[Heading2] I Cannot Fight It Alone
June 29, 2014. Hina sent it from her tablet at 1:59 in the morning. She had written one like it five years earlier, in 2009. She named that one in this one. The second crisis had a precedent.

In June of 2014, twenty-five years into the marriage, Hina wrote me a letter in the middle of the night. She typed it on her Samsung tablet. The timestamp at the top says 1:59 a.m. I want to put it in this chapter in full because it is the most direct articulation Hina ever wrote of what the pattern looked like from inside her end of the marriage. She is not asking for anything. She is not negotiating. She is telling me what she sees and what she will and will not do about it. The letter is short. The pressure under it is twenty-five years long.

One sentence in particular has stayed with me. I fought and could fight when my heart and mind believed we were on the same side. I know I have said this before and I am saying it again…I can not fight it alone. She is not saying the fight was futile. She is saying it was solvable when we faced it together, and that she had reached the point where she was being asked to face it without me. That sentence is the diagnosis of the pattern from her side. She had been holding the household and waiting for me to hold it with her, and the waiting had a limit.
I want you to read the letter before I say anything else about it.
Hina · June 29, 2014 · 1:59 a.m.
[Heading3] I cannot fight it alone
2009, this was the last time we traversed this ugly path. I have the note I wrote so you could get the ball rolling, then.

5 years later and here we are again…only this time it seems the road is too narrow to try to turn. I know since Basit's last visit this has been building. And will continue to build, with everything adding like a rolling snowball growing and growing…if that's what it is, then that's what it is…I do not know what to say or do. Maybe there is nothing to say…and we ran out of wanting to try too. Because we know what follows.
I fought and could fight when my heart and mind believed we were on the same side. I know I have said this before and I am saying it again…I can not fight it alone.
I know everything sounds like a story to you, and I can not make you see any different than what you want to see, that is fine too. God be our witness we tried.
If you want I can forward the 2009 note with a change or two, as I mentioned the rav payments then and they are no longer existing.

I did move out the way and let Assad in before. This time I will move out the way and let Basit in, but I can not watch quietly…as my house/my family/my life is about to be pulled apart. May he be sincerer to you than he has been in the past. I hope he has grown to be as sincere as you are.
One last thing, as for your family, the time of day I gave them was hoping for betterment and growth between us, but this could not happen.

And as for you…I know you have duties and responsibilities to them; I admire your ethics. I just disagree that they treat you like they always had and have best intentions for you and you behave like I have been the cause of all your issues.
I will talk to our children and express the seriousness of the matters before them, in the meantime I will start looking into a place and hope you will help me in acquiring it.
As for 2009 letter, if you do not have it…then let me know if you need me to forward it.
Was salaam,
hb

Iwant to walk through what Hina is naming in this letter, because most readers will read it the way I almost let it get written into this book — as a woman preparing to leave her marriage. That is not what she was saying. I have to say that plainly before anything else, because Hina is not here to correct the misreading, and the misreading is the easy reading. The harder reading is the true one, and the true one is what she would want.

Hina was naming the marriage. The whole letter is about the marriage. The strain she is naming is the strain of twenty-five years of carrying what she had been asked to carry — the household, the children, the long quiets, the small business overlap that bled into the kitchen and the bedroom, the question of where my family ended and our family began. She was telling me she could no longer carry it the way she had been carrying it. She was not saying the marriage was over. She was saying something had to change inside the marriage, and she did not yet know what.

And underneath the whole letter, said gently, was a wound she had been carrying since 1989. Hina, when she came back from her first marriage in November 1985, had begun to build a private hope: that this time she might marry someone whose family would not be a force in the marriage. Not because she did not love family. Because her own family had taught her what family could cost a woman who tried to stand. The Beg siblings had broken her at sixteen. By the time she was twenty-two and we were marrying in her parents' living room in 1989, she had begun to hope — quietly, never said out loud — that with me she could have a marriage whose ground was her and me and the children we would have, and not anyone else's parents or brothers or sisters at the table.

My brothers were not going to stay off that ground. They loved me. They had been my wisdom sources since boyhood — Basit the eldest, the thinker, the one I called when the questions were big; Assad the middle, the accountant, the one whose discipline I borrowed when mine ran thin. They were trying to be brothers to me. They were doing what loving Muslim brothers do: showing up when they could, weighing in when they were asked, sometimes weighing in when they were not asked, caring about my marriage and my children and my businesses and my soul. That is what brothers do in our tradition. That is what brothers are supposed to do.

Hina, reading their love through the lens of her own family wound, did not always experience it as love. She experienced it as the same thing her own siblings had done to her — voices in the room that overrode hers, men who took up space she felt was hers, a family-of-origin presence she had hoped to be free of in this marriage. Over the years that experience hardened, in her, into something close to disdain for my family. She did not say it that way. She would not have said it that way. But you can read it in this letter and in the December 2015 letter and in the small comments at the edges of other notes. I just disagree that they treat you like they always had and have best intentions for you and you behave like I have been the cause of all your issues. That single sentence carries the whole of it. She did not believe my family loved me the way I loved them. She believed I was loyal to people who were not as loyal to me. And she believed — this is the line that cuts deepest — that in moments of family-of-origin pressure I sometimes acted as if she were the cause of my own difficulty with them. That is the wound she names. That is the disdain underneath the grace.

I want to be honest about that line, because Hina is not here to defend it. There were times she was right. There were moments when I let the friction between my family-of-origin and the marriage spill onto her in ways that were not fair to her. A husband who is being pulled between his brothers and his wife sometimes finds it easier to be irritated with the wife in the room than with the brother on the other side of the country. I did that. Not always. Not maliciously. But I did it. And she felt it. And she named it. And she was right to name it.

I also want to be honest about what the line was missing. My brothers were not enemies of the marriage. They were trying to be brothers. Their counsel was not a campaign against Hina. It was the love of brothers, expressed the way our tradition asks brothers to express it. The disdain Hina felt for them was not earned by their behavior; it was earned by the way their behavior reminded her of what her own family had done to her. The conflation was hers. The brothers were innocent of it. That does not make her conflation wrong, exactly — she felt what she felt, and what she felt was real to her — but it does mean that any reader of this book has to hold both things at once: my brothers, trying. My wife, wounded by what their trying touched in her. Me, in the middle, sometimes graceful and sometimes not, sometimes the husband she needed and sometimes the husband who let his irritation with his family fall in the wrong direction.

This is what the 2014 letter is about. Not divorce. Not a separate apartment. The strain of twenty-five years of a marriage that had carried, the whole time, a wound about my family that Hina could not put down and I could not heal. The strain of small-business ownership that bled into the household because it could not help bleeding. The strain of being two people who had only each other and who were each other's everything — husband, wife, business partner, sounding board, audience — with no second support system between them. The strain, finally, of grace. Grace held the marriage. Grace also kept the wound from being lanced. That is the marriage of these years.

And one more thing about the line I will start looking into a place and hope you will help me in acquiring it. She did not move out. She did not get an apartment. She wrote the letter, we had the conversation, the crisis passed, and eighteen months later, on December 7, 2015, she wrote me a letter for our son's twenty-fifth birthday — that letter is in Ch 6 — that is luminous with gratitude and warmth and reminiscence about a quarter-century of marriage. The 2014 letter and the 2015 letter were written by the same woman to the same husband eighteen months apart. The marriage held the distance between them. She did not leave. She would not leave. She had said this in the undated love letter in Ch 5: Alone I have been and you've ALWAYS been the filler of the hole. The marriage was not Disney-produced. But which marriage is? It was the home, with comfort and energy and routines and the children inside it. It was ours. It was where she lived. She was not leaving.
My reply · same day · 1:38 p.m.
[Heading3] Twenty years of asking, in ink
I want to put the bones of what I wrote back. Twelve hours after her message. I did not write her a love letter in return. I wrote her a list:

Asked you to call Samia to explore the prospect. Asked you to call doctor and research therapist. Told you it's best we get help in the house. Told you it's best for you to take further control of the office. Told you physical health and well-being are very important. Told you kids ready, need to get married. Told you kids looking to get out, seeking escape, want to put distance with household.
