I closed with: My suggestions, directions above were not that deranged, out of bounds, or crazy. My observations or take on things can not be and are not that off.

I want the sons reading this to look at the list. Not as an argument I was throwing at her. Not as a husband missing his wife's emotional cry by handing her a to-do. Look at what is in the list. Every single line is about you. About her. About us.
Call my sister Samia about a marriage prospect for one of you. The boys were in their early twenties. They were ready.
Call a doctor. Find a therapist. Get help for what you have been carrying since you were fifteen and nobody named what was being done to you.
Get help in the house. Stop carrying the whole thing on your own. Stop disappearing behind a load you do not have to lift alone.
Step fully into the office seat that is already yours. Own the work you are already doing. You are capable of more than the corner of it you are letting yourself occupy.
Take care of your physical health. Please. Take care of your body. We need you in this body.
The boys are ready to be married. Let us help them. Let us be the parents who set them up well.
The kids are pulling away from the household. They are seeking escape. Let us look at why, together, while there is still time.

That is the list. Every item is about her, the children, the marriage, the nuclear family we had built. Not one item is about the stores. Not one item is about Edible Arrangements. Not one item is about an expansion. The list is a husband, twenty years in, writing down what he had been asking for the entire time.

Because the list was not a list. The list was twenty to twenty-five years of asking, gently, quietly, in the kitchen, in the car, on a walk, after a phone call about one of the kids. The list at 1:38 p.m. on June 29, 2014 was the moment I wrote down what I had been asking for two decades, in ink, because finally, after another two a.m. letter from my wife, I needed it not to get lost again. The list was not the opening of an argument. The list was a record. I have been here, asking, for half our marriage. Please look.
And four to five years later she was dead.

The husband who had been asking his wife for twenty years to see a doctor about her health would bury her on May 26, 2019. The husband who had been asking his wife to find a therapist for what she carried from 1983 and 1984 and Lima and Durham and Franklin Road would never get to hear her tell a therapist what she could not tell him. The husband who had been asking his wife to get help in the house would, in the years after, watch the household run without her and understand, only then, what she had been carrying. The husband who had been asking his wife to take care of her body would lose her in her body before her body was sixty. The husband who had been asking his wife to help him marry off their sons would marry off Moaaz in November 2018 with Hina in the hospital and not get to marry off Shahbaaz with her at all.

I want every husband and every wife who reads this book to look at that list and understand. I am not writing it down to win an old argument. Hina is not here to argue with. I am writing it down because some things, asked for twenty years, need to be on paper so that the asking is not lost. The sons need to see it. Their wives need to see it. The grandchildren who will read this in 2030 and 2050 need to see it. A husband can love his wife with everything he has and ask her, for twenty years, to take care of herself, and she can be too wounded to receive the asking, and four years later she can be gone, and the asking will not have saved her. That is the truth of this marriage. Both halves of it are true. The asking was real. The wounds that kept it from landing were real. The love through all of it was real.

We were blessed with more than most marriages get. Three children. A household that held. A community that watched us for forty years. A faith we both believed in. A business that lifted a whole family out of where we started. We were blessed. The book has to honor that. The book cannot be small. Sitting on these years to defend an old position would be a small life. The life we had was not small. The marriage was not small. Hina was not small. I do not want to make her, or us, smaller in retrospect than we were while she was here.

I write this still as a contribution to the conversation taking place in barzakh. Still fighting. Still trying. Still pushing forward with what I have left. Even though my audience of one is no longer here, I am still trying to get into that conversation in barzakh, where I may, perhaps, finally be heard. Maybe now. Like only Hina could say: time flies like an arrow, fruit flies like bananas. I miss those ridiculous idioms only she could fathom.
Sometimes the frustration, the tension, the quietness, the anger —
it actually is the devotion in love.
Ahmad · on the 2014 letter, looking back
— III —
[Heading2] Franklin Road

Eighty-nine Franklin Road, Teaneck. Her parents' house. Her mother passed in 2006. The dispute over what to do with the house lingered for twelve years and resolved two months before our son's wedding. Hina was put in the middle.

There is a piece of property at 89 Franklin Road in Teaneck that has to be part of this chapter, because of how heavily it weighed on Hina from 2006 onward. It is the house where she grew up. It is the house her father bought when the Beg family arrived in New Jersey. It is the living room where my nikah to her took place in 1989. It is the house her mother, Auntie Beg, lived in until she passed away in 2006. After Auntie Beg died, the house and what would happen to it became a matter that the five Beg children had to settle among themselves. They did not settle it cleanly. The unsettling lasted twelve years.
I want to start before 2006, because the dispute did not begin where it surfaced. It began earlier, in trust.

Uncle Beg — Khalid Beg, Hina's father, my father-in-law, the man who co-founded our masjid — passed away in 2003. Three years later, around 2004 or 2005, Auntie Beg came to me. She said: Abrar, the uncle has passed, the house is here, the kids are here, I want to set things up before I go. She was older. She knew she would not be here forever. She wanted a framework. She wanted a will. She wanted to clean things up so that after she went, the house and its disposition would be settled and her children would not have to fight about it.

She came to me. I want you to hold that. She had two daughters in their thirties — Naila, very intelligent, and Hina, her own daughter who was my wife. She had a son, Karrar. She had a youngest daughter, Amina, whom Hina had largely raised. She had her own brothers in the wider family — Mamoo Akamoo and others. She was not without people. And out of all those people, she came to her son-in-law. Why? Because she trusted me. Because she had known me since I was six years old. Because she had watched me for thirty years and decided I was an honest person and a trustworthy one, and that when she wanted help setting up her affairs so they would not become a fight, the person to ask was me.

I put her in touch with my accountant. The accountant met with Auntie Beg. The conversation about what she wanted done was open. Nothing in the corners. Nothing in the shadows. Nothing horse-traded. She told me what she wanted done with the house. She told me what her purpose was. I shared that with the family at the time. There was nothing hidden in it. There was nothing tilted in my direction. I had, alhamdulillah, no horse in the race. I was not looking for a larger share of the inheritance to come into our household. My only horse was honesty, transparency, and her parents' wishes. That was all I wanted held.
Then in 2006 Auntie Beg passed.

The five Beg children — Naila (Apa), Zarrar, Hina, Karrar, and Amina — began having conversations about the house and the inheritance. They held those conversations at our house, in our finished attic on Park Avenue. They would come over and sit upstairs and talk. There was no mature voice in the room. There was no one with real authority. The dynamics among the siblings were what they had always been. The four with louder voices — Naila, Zarrar, Karrar, Amina — spoke. Hina, the quiet one, the middle child, the one who had spent her childhood raising the youngest two, sat in the room. She had been ground down inside that family dynamic for thirty-five years already. She was the one all four siblings respected, in their way, more than they respected each other — so she became the person put in charge. She was made the pseudo-mediator. But the authority she was given was not real authority. The other four followed her only when she was agreeing with what they already wanted. When she tried to take a stand — that is not what your mother wanted — she was answered with listen, I don't know, don't worry about it. She would say it again. They would brush it aside again. The role she was put into looked like authority and functioned as exposure. She had to deal with the disagreement every day. The decisions were never closed out. The conversation never ended.

Hina had a hard time taking stands. She had had a hard time taking stands for thirty-five, forty years — ever since she was made the dealing-person for that one particular incident at sixteen, and the family had refused to back the authority they had handed her. What that incident did to her, what the lack of backing did to her, was the wound she carried into every role she was put into after. Including this one. Being made the pseudo-mediator of a property dispute she had no real authority over — with siblings who were her equals now but had once been her charges — was a re-enactment of the original wound at a new scale. Nobody saw it. I saw it. Nobody cared. I cared. And I will say, plainly, that some of what Hina was attributing to the marriage in her 2014 letter and elsewhere had Franklin Road embedded inside it. The strain of being the carrier with no power, of being shut down every time she tried to stand, of having to deal with it every day while no one else even noticed — that strain bled into how she experienced everything else, including us. The marriage took some of the weight of Franklin Road. That is the honest accounting.

I tried to broker resolution. I tried for years. The emails are there. I begged. I pleaded. I offered to put money in to close whatever gap was between the two sides — whatever the difference was, I said, I will pay it. Let it be done. The hearts on the other side of the table did not turn. They could not. They were not ready. Some things take time that no amount of money can shorten.

Through 2007, 2008, 2009, into 2010 — Amina was living in the Franklin Road house, single. She was supposed to clean it up. To take care of what needed to be taken care of. To act on what the family had agreed she would act on. It did not get done. It just lingered. There was chit-chatter. There was friction. There was tension. Around 2010, after three or four years of that, Amina moved out and got her own apartment. She was on her own then. Advice was not taken. Things were not dealt with.

In 2015 Amina got married. That is its own long story, with its own questions about who was looking out for her well-being, her mental stability, her comfort, her protection. I will not write it here. It belongs to her. What I will say is that before her marriage I told the family, plainly: this matter needs to be resolved before she gets married, otherwise it is going to be a problem. No one wanted to name it. Hina did not want to name it. The matter was brushed under the door again. Buried again. Forty years of patterns inside that family that nobody wanted to surface.
Then 2018 came.

Early 2018, the engagement discussions for Moaaz began. Our oldest. Twenty-eight years old. About to start his own household with Qurat-ul-ain. At the exact same time, the 89 Franklin Road matter rose back up. By 2018 the dispute had narrowed to its real shape: Karrar on one side, Amina on the other. The two youngest siblings, the two Hina had once raised, now at each other's throats over their parents' house. Karrar — gentle, joking, a ray of sunshine in most rooms. Amina — warm, vibrant, the youngest. Two beautiful people. Two siblings who had grown up in the same house. Now opposed.

The two events ran in parallel. Week by week. Month by month. On one side of the calendar, Moaaz's engagement. The walima planning. The guest lists. The questions a father and mother ask each other when their eldest son is about to get married. On the other side, the property dispute coming back up after twelve years, and Hina sitting in the middle of it, pseudo-mediator again, with no authority again, watching her two younger siblings dig in against each other. Nobody noticed the two things were running parallel. Nobody saw they were the same nervous system being asked to hold two opposite weights at once. The wedding was supposed to be our moment — for once in thirty years, Hina's and mine. My father, may God have mercy on him, was watching his eldest son's eldest son get married. I was watching my son. I was looking at Hina. I was trying to help with the engagement, with the wedding, with everything. And underneath all of that, Hina was carrying Franklin Road.

The dispute finally resolved in September or October of 2018. Two months before the wedding. By the grace of God it did get resolved in Hina's lifetime. But the lingering effects did not resolve with it. Karrar and Amina did not speak to each other at the wedding. I watched my wife at the gatherings, at the dinners with Amina and her husband Ahmet and with Karrar and his family, and I watched her trying to hold the air in the room together while the two siblings did not look at each other. That was the November of our son's wedding. That was the gift the Beg family inheritance gave its middle child.

In the first days of November 2018, Hina was in the hospital. Her heart again. Her body had been giving warnings for years. This time the warning was loud. The wedding was November 26. There were moments when we thought it might have to be called off. I had to make decisions and choices between my son and my wife — not in the dramatic sense, but in the daily sense, the hour-by-hour sense, the where-do-I-stand-right-now sense. My son was getting married. My wife was in a hospital bed. Both things were true. Both things mattered.

The wedding happened. Hina was there. She held it together. She always held it together. The half of the heart pendant on her chest that had broken earlier that year was sitting next to the half that had stayed. I have written elsewhere that I believe some objects in a marriage carry information the people in the marriage do not yet have access to. The heart was carrying information. I would not be able to read it until later.

Hina did not live to see the working-through of Franklin Road. The resolution was on paper. The repair between the siblings would come slowly, over years, and she would not be here for it. She lived only the strain. That is the cost of being the middle child in a family where the youngers were once your charges and now they are your equals and now they are on the other side of the table from each other about the house you were all raised in. There is no clean way out of that. There is only the working through. Hina did not get to see the working through.

I am putting this here, in the chapter about the pattern, because the Franklin Road weight ran in parallel with everything else she was carrying. The pattern at home was not the only pattern. The pattern in her family of origin was running alongside. The two patterns met inside her. She held both. She held the household and the shop and our children and the property dispute and her father's legacy and her mother's absence and the cumulative effect of the marriage's quiet years, all of it inside one body, and that body was not invincible.
A du'a · on hearts that will not turn
يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ
Yā muqallibal-qulūb, thabbit qalbi ‘alā dīnik.
O Turner of Hearts, keep my heart firm upon Your faith.

A du'a of the Prophet (ṣallallāhu ‘alayhi wa sallam). The hearts that need turning are not always other people's. Sometimes the heart that needs turning is the one inside your own chest, that has been begging and pleading at a closed door for twelve years and is starting to harden.
— IV —
[Heading2] What the World Was Doing

Two thousand one through twenty eighteen. America after 9/11. The community at Dar ul Islah. A semester of Bergen Community College, two sisters at the same desks, ended by what came down the avenue from Manhattan.

Iwant to note, briefly, that the years 2001 to 2018 in America were not neutral background for a Muslim immigrant family in northern New Jersey. They were the years after the towers came down. They were the years of the wars. They were the years of the airport lines and the watch lists and the FBI visits that happened to people we knew. They were the years of the surveillance program in New York that targeted mosques and Muslim student associations. They were the years of community members being deported on technicalities. They were the years when every business success my family had was shadowed by the question of how it would be read by people who were already suspicious of us.

I am not going to do a full reckoning with that period here. The book will come back to it more thoroughly in a later draft. I want to name it now, so that the reader understands the household we were building, the marriage we were holding, the stores we were opening, were all happening inside an America that had recently decided we were the enemy. The community at Dar ul Islah grew from twenty families when my father and father-in-law founded it to several hundred families by the 2010s. We were rising as a community while the country was tightening around us. That tension is part of the pattern too.
I want to tell one small piece of it now, because it belongs to Hina and to her youngest sister and to what could have been.

In the spring or summer of 2001, before the towers came down, Hina and Amina were taking classes together at Bergen Community College. I do not remember exactly what subject. I remember the energy. Hina loved going. She was on a positive trajectory. It was one of the first times she had stepped out of the house into something that was hers, alongside Amina, the sister she had largely raised. The two of them at the same desks. Both of them adults now, women now. Older sister and younger sister, side by side. Hina would come home and tell me about the classes. About the teacher. About who was the teacher's pet. About what was discussed. I remember those evenings. Those were some of the most beautiful evenings of our marriage. To watch a wife who had been a girl in a basement at sixteen, now a woman in her thirties, going to college with her sister, animated by it, lit up by it — that was something I did not know I was watching the end of.

Then September 11 happened. The classes did not stop immediately. The environment got bad. Two months later, three months later, the sisters dropped the classes. The environment was just bad. That was the phrase Hina used. The environment was just bad. She did not go back. Amina did not go back. A door had opened in Hina's life and then closed on her, and the thing that closed it was not anything inside our marriage. It was the geopolitical weather of post-9/11 America deciding that two Muslim women going to community college together were targets in some way she could feel even when nobody had laid a hand on her.

I want the reader of this book in 2030 or 2050 to know that. Hina lost a future in 2001 because of what came down out of the sky into Manhattan. She would never go back to school. She would put the books down and pick the household back up and never set the household back down again. The cost is invisible from the outside. From the inside, in our kitchen, on the nights she had been coming home telling me about her teacher — the cost was the lit-up version of her going dark again.

I will let this part of the chapter be brief for now and come back to it. There is a fuller treatment of the post-9/11 generational arc that belongs in this book, and I do not yet have the words for it. The seed is here. The fruit will come.
A du'a · for the household under strain
رَبَّنَا هَبْ لَنَا مِنْ أَزْوَاجِنَا وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ
وَاجْعَلْنَا لِلْمُتَّقِينَ إِمَامًا
Rabbanā hab lanā min azwājinā wa dhurriyyātinā qurrata a‘yunin,
waj‘alnā lil-muttaqīna imāmā.
Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and children comfort to our eyes, and make us a guide for the righteous.
Surah Al-Furqan 25:74. The du'a of the servants of the Most Merciful. Hina would have said this one in the long quiets. So would I, sometimes, without knowing she was saying it too.
[Heading2] We Did Not Fight
I want to be exact about how the marriage moved during these years. Because if you have read the 2014 letter and you imagine us yelling at each other, you have the marriage wrong.

Hina and I did not fight. I want to state that plainly, because the 2014 letter could give the impression of a marriage in open conflict, and it was not. The marriage's conflict pattern was not fights. It was slight withdrawals that lasted.

I want to describe what slight withdrawal looked like, because the phrase is too small for what it actually was. It was not coldness. The marriage did not go cold. It went bland. Functional. A staying-away from the touchy topics on both sides, and the staying-away itself was the wound — because warmth that has to step around things is warmth that has been pulled out of the room. The smiles weakened. The radiance dimmed. We were still kind to each other. We were still careful with each other. We still slept in the same bed and ate at the same table and prayed in the same rooms. But the air had less of itself in it. A zombieish quality settled in. The household ran. The marriage operated. The radiance was elsewhere or not there.

Hina had too much grace to lash out. She had too much goodness to fight on the surface. She was not capable of the kind of cruelty that ends a marriage in a single hour. Neither was I, by the standards of how the world fights. Our ethics, our etiquette, our manners were beyond the surface-level fight. We were the people who had been raised in the houses our parents built — Ikram's house, Khalid Beg's house — where you did not raise a voice, you did not slam a door, you did not say the thing you would regret. We had absorbed that. We held that. Even at our worst, we held that.

But here is the thing about holding the higher etiquette while small cracks are spreading underneath. The cracks do not stop spreading because you are graceful about them. Grace is not a sealant. The cracks spread anyway. They spread silently. They metastasize. By the second decade of the marriage there were small unhealed places — topics we had stopped circling, questions we had stopped asking, kinds of touch that had become rare, kinds of laughter we did not have together as often — and the unhealed places were getting larger because no surface fight ever lanced them. We were too graceful to fight. The grace cost us the fight. The fight is what would have lanced the cracks. The cracks kept spreading because we kept being graceful.

I have to name one more thing here, and it is the hardest thing in this chapter for me to say. When Hina came back from her first marriage in November of 1985, I was the angel in the room. I was the one untouched by the world. I had been a boy at fifteen and a boy at sixteen and a boy at seventeen, and the world had not yet sanded me down. I had grace I had inherited from my father and from the masjid and from the Bahishti Zewar on the shelf and from a Surah Al-Asr I had written out at twelve. I was the higher etiquette in the room when she came home in 1985. She had been ground down by what had been done to her at fifteen and sixteen. She needed an angel. She got one.

Twenty years later the pendulum had swung. I had been out in the world. Twenty years of landlords and lawyers and contractors and customers and banks and the daily grind of running stores and pulling a family up through American capitalism while America was tightening around us after 9/11 had done what twenty years of the world does to a man. I had been tainted. Touched. Some of the higher human values I had carried so cleanly at sixteen had been sanded down in me. Not destroyed. Sanded. The grace was still there. There was less of it. Hina, meanwhile, had spent two decades inside a household that held her. She had recovered some of what had been taken from her at sixteen. By the end of the second decade of our marriage, she held more grace than I did. She was the angel in the room now, and I was the one with the sanded edges. Neither of us said this out loud. We both knew it. I think she knew it more clearly than I did, because she was the better witness, as I keep saying. She watched the pendulum swing and she did not name it because naming it would have been one more topic the marriage had to step around.

We were both trying to hold. That is the line I want the children and grandchildren to read carefully. We were both trying to hold. The trying was the love. The trying was real. The trying held the marriage through stretches that would have broken other marriages. But the trying did not stop the cracks from spreading, because the cracks were not the kind of thing trying fixes. The cracks were the slow result of two people carrying weights that neither of them could share with the other, and a world outside that was sanding both of them at different rates, and a grace differential between them that neither of them named, and the choice to be graceful instead of loud. The grace was the love and the grace was also the cost. That is the marriage of Ch 7.

One more thing. There were moments, sometimes, when the surface broke for a minute. A sharper word than usual. A withdrawal that lasted a beat longer. A silence that was not the usual silence. They were rare. They were small. They were what happens when two people are each other's everything and have been each other's everything for twenty-five years and are tired in places they cannot name to each other. Neither of us ever lashed out. Neither of us ever broke the etiquette. But the surface broke for a minute, sometimes, in micro-moments. The moments would close back over. The bland would return. The radiance would not.

By 2018, twenty-nine years into the marriage, the cracks had reached tissue the marriage could not regenerate. The heart pendant broke in 2018, a year before her death. That is in Ch 8. I am not yet ready to say what the breaking meant. But part of what it meant was that the spread had reached the place it could not go past. The structure was straining under the metastasis. The grace was still in the room. The radiance was almost gone. We were both still trying to hold. The thing we were trying to hold was thinning.
A note on the man inside the pattern
[Heading3] The structure I had not built inside myself
The line that gets at this chapter most clearly is one I have to say plainly, because Hina would have wanted me to say it plainly: the structure I had not built inside myself — yes, this is true.

The anchor under everything, behind all of this, was God's qadr. That was what allowed me to move at all. That was what gave me the courage to do what I did. What I was built upon was my family — my father, my brothers, in their ways — and then Hina. Those were my pillars. But the two would not always reconcile well. And the friction between them, year after year, ground me down. It did not let me build or keep what I had begun to build inside myself. Somewhere in those years it started coming apart. The patience began wearing thin, thinner, thinner. The container started eroding. The scaffolding loosened. The screws got loose.

Life forces you to slow down eventually. It uses tragic events to do it. Some of those events look tragic from the outside and are blessings from the inside, depending on the lens. They make you absorb what is around you. They make you read books and listen to people and watch a stranger you walk past in a hospital corridor. They train you to live with awareness. But the awareness gets clouded. You lose yourself in your head instead of falling back to the heart — the brain of the heart, the core — because we all know it, we just need to dust it off and clean it up a little.

And by God, I tried. Especially regarding Franklin Road from 2006 onward, I tried. You try. Sometimes it is not even noticed. But it is okay. At least you can put your head on the pillow and know that you tried. That is what I say to my sons now. The stuff going on in the world — you cannot do much about it. But at least your heart can feel some turbulence about it. That is the victory. That your heart feels turbulence about it — that is the achievement. Not the summer home. Not the diamonds on a finger. Not the necklace your wife is wearing now. The necklace from when you were nine years old, the one she kept her whole life, that is still here — that is the victory.
And you are still striving to be worthy. By God I am still striving to be worthy. Whether it is seen or not does not matter. Some things you do not need an audience for.

And for me, she was my audience. An audience of one. It is nice to have that audience — it gives you courage. My audience is gone. Now it comes down to what you do even when the one single person who was your audience is not there. When there is absolutely no audience. By God I pray and I ask that I do.
A du'a · for the carrier no one names
اللَّهُمَّ بَارِكْ لَنَا فِيمَا رَزَقْتَنَا
وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
Allāhumma bārik lanā fīmā razaqtanā,
wa qinā ‘adhāban-nār.
O Allah, bless us in what You have provided for us, and save us from the punishment of the Fire.
A sunnah du'a after meals. Said quietly at our table for thirty years. The wife who set the food on the table was the larger part of the rizq itself. I did not know it at the time. I know it now.
— VI —
[Heading2] The Approach of the Last Year

By late 2018 the pattern had been running for almost thirty years. The heart on her chest had broken. Half of it. The 2014 letter had not been answered the way it asked to be answered. The quiet was getting longer. Then the last year began.

Iam going to close this chapter without resolution because the years it covers had no resolution. The pattern ran. The businesses grew. The marriage held. The quiets lengthened. The 2014 letter was written and answered and absorbed. The 2015 letter, in Ch 6, was written and received and felt. The Franklin Road dispute resolved on paper in September or October of 2018, two months before our son's wedding, and the lingering between the siblings stayed unresolved through that wedding and beyond Hina's lifetime. Her heart palpitations, which had begun in 2006, continued. The children grew. Moaaz married Qurat-ul-ain on November 26, 2018. Shahbaaz was working alongside me. Zanab was in her twenties. The household kept running. The shop kept running. The eleven stores kept running. The man inside the structures was, by 2018, deeply tired without being able to say where the tiredness lived.

In 2018 the heart pendant Hina wore daily — the one I had given her in Ramadan of 1981 when I was nine and she was fourteen, the one she had carried with her through her first marriage to South Carolina in 1984 and back to New Jersey in 1986, the one she had worn every day for the thirty-three years since — broke. Not all of it. Half of it. One half of the heart broke clean off. The other half stayed on the chain. There was no jewelry-trauma. There was no fall. There was nothing that should have broken it. It broke anyway. One year before she died.

I have written elsewhere that I believe some objects in a marriage carry information the people in the marriage do not yet have access to. The half that broke was carrying information. The half that stayed was carrying different information. The breaking and the staying were both messages. I would not be able to read either message until later. Half of the heart broke. Half of the heart is still here. It has not broken further. It will not. The information the staying half is carrying is the information that the audience can leave the room and the worship can continue.

The chapter ends here. The next chapter is the year that begins when the heart breaks and ends on May 25, 2019. I am going to need a different voice for Ch 8. I am going to open it with a poem I wrote after she was gone called I Adore Her, which is the strongest piece in the entire archive, and I am going to use the rest of the chapter to walk through her last year and that last Saturday. The pattern in this chapter does not continue into Ch 8. The pattern is interrupted by something larger. The interruption is the rupture. The rupture is what the rest of the book is, in one way or another, the working through of.

For now: the pattern. The loop. The 2014 letter. The Franklin Road weight. The semester of community college that 9/11 ended. The quiet that kept growing. The husband who wrote a reply that read more like a memo than a marriage. The wife who absorbed all of it and went on holding the household until the household had to let her go. That is Ch 7. That is the eighteen quiet years.

And underneath all of it — this I want to say one more time before the chapter ends — the anger was the love. The frustration was the devotion. The begging was the infatuation. The pleading came from a deep, deep affection for someone. The list I wrote her in 1:38 p.m. on June 29, 2014 was not the opposite of love. It was love that had not yet learned how to listen. I learned later. I am still learning. Hina is the teacher. The lesson is the rest of this book.

title: Chapter Eight — The Last Year and May 25, 2019
paragraphs: The Last Year
May 25, 2019 · Ramadan 20, 1440
The glass heart broke in 2018. She had a year left. I did not know that. I think it knew.
Part III — Rupture & Collapse
I Adore Her
A love forged in fire · raw, after
I adore her
A love forged in fire
Every time i walked by her
She called me her
Rock of Gibraltar
We never figured out who was whose anchor
Like Abu Bakr
We did everything first

Still flow through my soul
I’m trying to leave because you wouldn’t stay
You are getting on my last nerve
To hell with these people — How could they understand
Everyday the wind keeps whispering your name
Won’t let me live nor can i die
I’ve been tryin to leave because you wouldn’t stay
A love that ran that deep
How do i fight God over you — But i try
Why does this pain feel so good, its the only thing that lets me know that i am still alive
Like a shell like a cocoon I have this butterfly living inside of me
Did you really have to die in order to save my life
Did you really have to die in order to save our lives?
I cant make sense of any of it..
I dont understand why the birds still sing
You touch my skin like ocean rain
You came and went like the tide
Only you and I knew we were meant to be
I had you and you had me..
When the world turned its back on you — God sent me.
When the world turned its back on me.. You became my deen. My peace.
We never had to speak — glances and mental telepathy
I didn’t realize that you had to die
In order to save my life

And leave me in solitude
So i could see the truth
So i could begin to remake myself and become worthy of you
Once again pure and clean like my youth

Our Joys and Pain — I cherish them so dearly — I cherish them the same.

35 years together but it seems you came and went like the tide
The Glass Heart
Ramadan 1402 AH. June or July of 1982. I was ten. She was fifteen. I gave her a glass heart. She wore it through every worst time of her life. It broke in 2018. Half is still here.

The glass heart I gave Hina in Ramadan of 1982 broke in 2018. The same one. The one in Chapter One. The one she wore through her first marriage and her return and her second marriage and every year that followed. Glass that age does not just break. Not that kind of glass, not that kind of crystal, not the way it happened. Hina told me it had broken. I did not see it happen. She just told me. The half I still have is on my dresser. The other half is gone. I do not know where it ended up.

Iwant to say plainly what the glass heart was, because it is the evidence the rest of this book stands on. Without it the whole story sounds like a man exaggerating after the fact. It is not believable, what I am writing. In Ramadan of 1982 a boy of ten gives a glass heart to a girl of fifteen. The girl carries it her entire life. Thirty-seven years later it breaks, one year before she does. If I had read it in someone else's book I would have thought they were embellishing. The glass heart is the proof. The half on my dresser is the proof. I am writing this with it in front of me.

I want to be precise about the date and the ages, because they matter. Ramadan 1402 in the Hijri calendar fell in June and July of 1982. Hina was born January 1, 1967. I was born November 8, 1971. The gap between us was always four years, ten months, seven days — the same gap at every moment of our lives, never five years, never less. In Ramadan of 1982 I was ten years old. Hina was fifteen. I would turn eleven that November. She would turn sixteen the following January. By the end of that same year, 1982, the adults around her were already moving toward what would become her engagement at fifteen and her wedding in August of 1983. The boy giving the glass heart in Ramadan was ten years old, fasting his first fasts, holding a small thing in his hand for a teenager who, in the same calendar window the boy was giving her the heart, was on the edge of being given away to a man twice her age.

The heart was not about dating. It was not about boyfriend and girlfriend. It was not about anything that the world would later make it into. It was about innocence. The purity of a gesture made by a child of ten who saw something in a store and saw a teenager he had been put on the earth to know and bought the heart because the heart was what he had to give and what she was worth receiving. She kept it because she understood what it was. She wore it through her worst times — the August 1983 wedding, Lima in 1984, the forced abortion that November, the years in Durham, the return in November 1985, the rebuilding that began in 1986 — because the gesture had been pure and she was holding onto something pure in a world that had stopped being pure to her in the same months and the same years the boy of ten had been giving it to her in.
The heart carried her. That is the only way to say it. The heart carried her through what nobody else could carry her through. It did the work the adults around her would not do.

It broke in 2018. Not from a fall. Not from being struck. Glass like that, in a setting like that, does not break from ordinary wear. It broke anyway. The half stayed with her. The other half disappeared. She brought it to me and showed me. We did not say much about it. I think we both knew what we were not saying. I held the half in my palm and looked at her and she looked at me and we kept going. There was nothing to say that would have helped.
One year later she was gone.
The half is here.
The glass heart is the proof.
Without it the whole story sounds like a man exaggerating after the fact.
Abrar · on the half that remains
— II —
The Last Year

2018 into early 2019. The Karrar and Amina fight bled through everything. Underneath it, the year I spent with my eldest son preparing for his wedding. Trips to Indiana. Eleven hours in the car alone with Hina. Some of the best time we had together.

The last year of Hina's life was dominated by the Karrar and Amina fight. I have written about that fight in Chapter Seven. The fight had been between those two from the beginning — it did not narrow to them in 2018; it had always been them. By 2018 it was still them, with Hina sitting in the middle of it as the pseudo-mediator she had been made into for twelve years. The fight took a heavy toll on her. The selfishness of the two of them deciding to surface, in 2018, what they had not dealt with for fifteen years — this was the doorway through which the big wound surfaced again. The Beg-family wound. The one she had been carrying since she was sixteen. It had reopened at the worst possible time.

And underneath that, alongside it, around it, was the other half of 2018, which I want to say plainly because it was beautiful. Most of 2018 was the year of my eldest son's wedding. Moaaz and Qurat-ul-ain had been introduced, had spoken, had decided there was real compatibility between them. The engagement took place in April of 2018. The wedding was set for November. From April through November there were trips back and forth to Indiana, where Qurat-ul-ain's family is. Wedding planning. Wedding stuff. The kind of months that are wonderful for a father and a mother in a way that is hard to describe to anyone who has not been in them.

Hina and I drove together. Eleven hours each way. Just the two of us in the car. I want to say that again because I want the sons reading this to hear it. Eleven hours alone in the car with their mother, sometimes twice in a week. Some of the best times we ever spent together were in 2018 in that car going to and from Indiana. The warmth was coming back into our marriage. Not back to the early years — you do not get back to the early years — but a different warmth, a warmth that thirty years of marriage builds when both people are aging into it together. We were going to come together as a family again. The eldest was getting married. The focus was returning to the household. The business expansion phase was ending. I was scaling back. We were about to enter the phase we had been waiting for since 1989.

I put more into Moaaz's wedding than I had put into my own when I was eighteen. By God, I did. Alhamdulillah. I gave that wedding everything. Hina did the same. It was, for both of us, a magical year on that side of the calendar.

On the other side of the calendar, Karrar and Amina were tearing into each other over Franklin Road, and the friction was bleeding into us, and the Beg-family wound was reopening, and Hina was being asked to hold both sides at once — the magical side of preparing her eldest son's wedding, and the worst side of being made the carrier for a fight her two younger siblings should have settled twelve years earlier. She held both. Nobody else could see her holding both. I could see her holding both. I could not take either weight off her. I tried. The trying did not lift it.

This is the year. Magical on one side. Cracking on the other. Hina in the middle holding both. The glass heart breaks in the middle of it, sometime in 2018, and neither of us says what we know we both know.
A note · on a line I had written years before that came true in 2018
I would be your dreams — if I could be
Years before 2018, I had written Hina a Valentine. Inside the card was a typed poem. One of the lines went: When you aspire, I want to feel your desires — I would be your dreams — if I could be.

I had written that line maybe a decade earlier. I did not know, when I wrote it, what year it would come true in. By God, in 2018 it came true. When Hina aspired in 2018, I felt her desires. I was trying to be her dream. I was doing my absolute best for her, for our eldest son, for the marriage we were carrying into its next phase. The magical year and the cracking year were happening inside the same body and inside the same marriage and inside the same eleven-hour car ride, and I was trying to be everything I had promised in that old Valentine to be.
I was still trying. The trying was real. The trying did not save her. The trying mattered anyway.
A du'a · on the year I did not know was the last year
رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ
Rabbi awzi‘nī an ashkura ni‘mataka allatī an‘amta ‘alayya.
My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me.

Surah An-Naml 27:19. The du'a of a man who has been given more than he can hold and is asking to be made adequate to it. I did not know in 2018 that the year was the year. I should have been more grateful. I am asking for the inspiration to have been.
— III —
Her Notes

Pieces of paper in her handwriting that I found later. Some say All Attacks. One says Flashback. One says God Protect Us. The chronology of when she wrote them is not yet sorted — some may belong to the Franklin Road years and not the last year. They sit here as I found them.

Hina wrote things down. She had written things down her whole life — the NC letters in 1984, the forced-abortion poem in November of that year, the love letters of the late 1980s, the 2009 leaving-note she walked back, the 2014 letter that is in Chapter Seven, the December 2015 birthday-of-Moaaz letter in Chapter Six. She wrote at three in the morning. She wrote on whatever paper was nearby. She wrote when no one was looking.

After she passed, going through her things over the months and years that followed, I came across pages in her handwriting that I had not seen before. Some had titles. All Attacks. Flashback. God Protect Us. Others did not have titles. They are her voice without an audience. They are what was happening inside the body that was holding the household.

I want to put what I have here, in this chapter, with the honest acknowledgment that I am still sorting which of these belong to her last year and which belong earlier — the 2006-onward Franklin Road years, when her parents were both gone and the dispute was eating at her. The placement chronology comes later. The notes are here because they are her hand and her voice and they belong wherever in the book they go.

A du'a · in her own words, in her own hand
حَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ
Hasbunā Allāhu wa ni‘ma'l-wakīl.
Allah is sufficient for us, and the best Disposer of affairs.
Surah Āli ‘Imrān 3:173. The verse said by the believers when the world tightened around them. Hina wrote God Protect Us in her own hand. It is the same prayer in two languages.
— IV —
The Last Week
Thursday she found out about the valve. Friday Azmath came in the afternoon, and that night she said things. Saturday she went.

There was something about that week. There was something about that day and the day before and the day before that. They were not normal days. I am going to walk through them the way they happened, the way I remember them, because the sons and the grandchildren and whoever else reads this will want to know what the last days looked like from inside.
Thursday, May 23, 2019

Thursday Hina found out that the surgeon had made a grave error. The valve that had been put into her heart in her surgery was the wrong material. The surgeons had been specifically instructed to use the bovine valve — the cow material. She found out, that Thursday, that they had used porcine instead. The pig material. Not what had been asked for. Not what had been agreed.

This caused her grief and pain like I had not seen in her in her life. Hina was not one to cry. She was not one to sniffle. She was freaking strong. In the years I had known her, including the worst of the worst years, she did not break that way in front of me. All Thursday she cried. All that Thursday did she cry. It broke me to watch it. There was nothing I could say. There was nothing anyone could say.

She called the people she called. She called her older sister Naila. She called her younger sister Amina. She called her brothers. She called the kids. The phones were going all day. It was a bad bad day. It was a not good day. The whole family knew by sundown that something had been done to her body that should not have been done, and the something could not be undone.

If anyone said anything she would not have heard it. It did not matter what was said. The best thing was to stay quiet. You do not come between Hina and her love for Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. You do not come between Hina and her faith. You do not come between Hina and her relationship with her Lord. I do not care who you are — husband, brother, surgeon, doctor, lawyer, billionaire — you do not put yourself between Hina and God. That is what made Hina Hina.
I stayed quiet. The room held the quiet. The day ended.
Friday, May 24, 2019

Friday afternoon, Azmath Qureshi stopped by. Around three. He had been supposed to come a week and a half earlier and had finally made it. He came with his wife. They sat with Hina for an hour and a half, maybe a couple of hours, until five or five-thirty in the afternoon. Azmath is a wonderful person. Younger-brother personality. Very warm, very caring — the kind of person you call when there is no business reason to call. His wife is the same. A sweetheart. The two of them sat with Hina, and the room held them for those two hours.
Then they left. The afternoon turned into evening. The evening was a tough evening.

Hina was on the sofa in the TV room. She was agitated — understandably agitated, because she had found out about the valve the day before and her body was still her body and her body knew what she knew. She was not comfortable. She was not right. Hina was not one to complain about being uncomfortable. Even after surgery, even with the things her body had been through, she did not say I am uncomfortable. But that night she was visibly uncomfortable. It was hard to see. It was hard to be in the presence of. There was nothing to do.

She was making comments. Around nine, around ten at night, sitting with me on the sofa, she said it repeatedly. She said: there's something in the house. There's something in the house. I don't know what's happening. There's something in the house. She kept saying it. I did not know what to say back. I did not say anything.

Then she said: why didn't anyone from my family help me? Why didn't anyone from my family help me? She said it more than once. The lifetime she had been carrying since she was sixteen was surfacing through the body and through the agitation and through the night.
Then she said: Abrar, what did we do? What did we do?

I said to her: Hina, I know. I know. We fell, we got up, we pushed, we did some things we're not crazy about. But there's a lot of things we have to be proud of. And in the end there's Allah's mercy. That is what I said. That is what I had. It was not much. It was what was true.

She was in another place that evening. Not unconscious — she was not going under. She was between two places. Somewhere in between here and not here. I have been in that place a couple of times in my own life. You are not here and you are not somewhere else — you are between. That is where she was for those couple of hours. From thirty years of marriage and forty years of knowing her, from the fragments she was saying, I understood enough to know where she was. I am not an expert on these things. This was my first experience of someone close to me being in that place. It will be my only experience of it with the one who was closest.

Then the night ended. She slept. The next morning she woke up and she was back to normal. Which was nice. Which was the thing about Hina — she would come back. She would always come back. The morning after a bad night, she was Hina again.
Saturday, May 25, 2019
Ramadan 20, 1440. One day after the Hijri birthday she and I shared. The day she went.
Icould go minute by minute through Saturday. Every minute of it matters to me. But for the book the short of it is enough. The short of it is the truth, and the truth does not need decoration.

Saturday morning I was with her. Late morning, an hour and a half, in the bedroom. Just the two of us. We talked. I do not remember what we talked about. I remember being there. Then around one-thirty or two in the afternoon I went to the office. I was going to be there a couple of hours and come back.

While I was at the office she texted me. She was hungry. Could I bring her something to eat. I texted back: sure, what would you like. She told me okra and something from Toros — the restaurant in New Milford. I told her okay, I would pick it up, I would be home in half an hour or forty minutes. She said okay great.

She was not fasting. She could not fast because of the surgery and the recovery. Ramadan was on, but Hina was on medical leave from it. So I picked up the food from Toros and got home around five o'clock. I came in and went upstairs to the master bedroom.

She was on the bed. She was on her back. Her legs were off the side of the bed. The position was weird. She was lying back with her legs off the side. Her eyes were closed. I took two steps forward to look more closely. I thought she was sleeping. The position was weird but I thought, let her rest. So I went back downstairs.

Around six, six-fifteen, six-thirty, Amina and Ahmet came over for iftar. They were coming to see Hina, to sit with her, to spend the iftar with her sister. I went and sat at the table downstairs with Ahmet. We were chit-chatting, getting ready for iftar, preparing the food.

Zanab came downstairs. I asked her: how's your mother? What's she doing? Zanab said: she's still sleeping. I asked her: in that weird position? Zanab said: yes. Okay. We continued waiting for iftar time, preparing the meal.

A few minutes later I called Moaaz. Moaaz came down. I said: Moaaz, please go check on your mother — is she still sleeping? Moaaz went up. Moaaz came back down. He said: yes, she's still sleeping. I asked him: in that weird position? Moaaz said: yes.
I got up from the chair to go check for myself. Slow. Heavy. I started up the stairs.

On the walk upstairs is when I knew. Not at the table. Not when Zanab said yes. Not when Moaaz said yes. On the walk — one step, then another step, then another — I knew. The position had been wrong at five. The position was still wrong now. Hina did not hold that position. Hina did not sleep that way for fifteen minutes. The body was telling me on the walk up what the body had been telling me all along, and on the walk up I finally heard it. I did not think about it. I knew it. The two are not the same thing. Thinking comes later. Knowing comes when the knowing comes, and the knowing came on the stairs.
I reached the master bedroom door. The threshold. Her.

She was still in the same position. Both of her hands were up by her ears, palms facing out — the way you say Allahu Akbar. Her hands were small and dainty. Her fingers were semi-bent. Her pinkies especially — her pinkies were always bent, that was how her hands held themselves. The little cups of her hands. She had on her qameez. She did not have on her shalwar. Just the qameez, which on her went down to her shins, and her hands up by her ears in the takbeer position, and her legs off the side of the bed, and her face turned, and her eyes closed.
I got closer. I touched her hand. She was gone.

I yelled down: call 911. Call 911. I'm going to call 911. Ahmet, Amina, and Zanab came running upstairs. Moaaz had stepped out for a minute after iftar — he was not in the house when I yelled. Ahmet picked Hina up with Zanab and put her on the floor. Picked her up, put her on the floor. Zanab started doing CPR. Amina was on the phone, panicking, dialing 911. Ahmet took over the chest compressions.
I did not stop anyone from doing anything. What else was there to do. Stay busy as much as you can. Do not second-guess. The knowing did not leave room for thinking. The thinking came later.

The thinking came later that night. After the ambulance. After the hospital. After they pronounced. Sitting somewhere quiet, the way the mind goes back over a day when the worst thing has happened, the timeline put itself together for me. She had texted me at four-fifteen. She had wanted okra and something from Toros. I had told her I would be home in half an hour, forty minutes. I had walked in at five with the food. The position had already been the position by then. In the window between four-fifteen, when she texted me, and five, when I came in with the food, was when she went. I had been at the office. I had been on the way home with the okra she had asked for. She had texted me hungry and then her body had finished while I was driving with her okra in the car, and by the time I reached the bedroom she was already gone, and I had read the gone-ness as sleep and left her there for two and a half more hours.

That is the timeline as I understood it later. On the stairs I had only known she was gone. I had not yet known the window. The window I figured out that night, with the day in my head, and the okra in the trash, and Hina at the hospital.

The ambulance arrived. I was discombobulated. I did not know anything. I was seeing things. My brain was here and there. From the outside I was not visibly going under. From the outside I was Abrar. Inside there were hurricanes and tornadoes and volcanoes and monsoons and tsunamis. All of it. That was Hina — outside calm, inside everything. And that was me. I was hers in that way too.
We followed the ambulance to the hospital. Half an hour, forty-five minutes later, they pronounced. She had passed.

From that moment on I was lost. That was my anchor. I lost my anchor. It is not the way it was supposed to be. It is never the way it was supposed to be. When I was eighteen I did not think I was going to make it to thirty-five — the life I was living, the way I was — but God had other plans, and I made it past thirty-five and past forty and past forty-seven and Hina was supposed to be next to me for all of it. The husband goes first. The husband goes first and the wife remains. That is how I thought it was supposed to go down. That is not how it went.
Her hands were up by her ears,
palms facing out,
the way you say Allahu Akbar.
May 25, 2019 · the master bedroom
A du'a · for the one we return to Him
إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ
Innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rāji‘ūn.
Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return.
Surah Al-Baqarah 2:156. The verse you say when you hear of a death. We had said it about other people for decades before we had to say it about her. I have said it every day since.
— VI —
The Night and Sunday

One call to Azmath. Maybe one to siblings later, I do not recall. Quran recitation through the night. Burial by noon on Sunday, May 26. Ramadan. Memorial Day weekend. She would not have wanted anyone to be a bother for her.

Idid not make many calls that night. Maybe one to siblings later in the evening — I do not recall. The one call I clearly remember making was to Azmath Qureshi. I called him and said: Azmath, Hina passed. Please come. Bring the Quran. Bring your cousins. When Azmath's father had passed some years before, I had seen what he and his cousins did — they sat in the room with the body and recited Quran through the night. That was what I knew to do for Hina. So I asked Azmath to come.

From there, Yasmin Hammeeduddin and Zarrar took over. They handled what needed to be handled. It was nine, ten at night by then. Everything from that point forward is a fog to me. I was there but I was not there. I was Abrar on the outside doing what had to be done. Inside I was somewhere I do not have words for.
By noon or one o'clock the next day, Sunday May 26, 2019, she was buried.

It was Memorial Day weekend. It was Ramadan. It was a Sunday. Nobody had to take off work. Nobody had to call in. Nobody had to rearrange anything. Hina would have wanted it exactly that way. She would not be a bother to anybody. She would not be a burden on her way out. Before her surgery and after her surgery she had been making the du'a: do not let me be a bother or a burden on anyone. Her du'as were answered.

The ghusl — the washing of her body — was done by Zanab, my daughter, and by Amina, Hina's youngest sister. Aisha, Karrar's wife, who is also Hina's cousin, was there. Tayyaba, Zarrar's wife, was there. I believe there was an older auntie there with them for instruction. The ghusl was done at Nida ul Islam — the second community masjid — because Hina had been adamant that her ghusl be done there. The janazah prayer was also at Nida ul Islam.

Then we drove her up to the cemetery. The cemetery is in upstate New York, near Woodbury Commons, about forty-five minutes to an hour from Teaneck. It is the same cemetery where Hina's mother — Auntie Beg — is buried. When Auntie Beg passed in 2006, Hina and I had taken on organizing the family. We had said: let us buy plots while we have the chance. We asked who else wanted to be in on it. We bought three. Zarrar bought plots too. Karrar and Amina joined in. Altogether the family bought somewhere around ten or twelve plots. By the time Hina was buried, five of them were used — Auntie Beg, Zarrar's daughters, and now Hina.
Shahbaaz rode in the hearse with the body. I do not remember who else was in the hearse. I drove by myself. I do not remember where everyone else was. I remember the road.

The body is washed and wrapped in three pieces of white sheet. Because of the cemetery policies in America, the wrapped body is placed in a plain pine box. We did all of that. The hole was already dug. We lowered the box into the grave. We tilted the body toward the east. The face facing east, toward the qibla. I did that with my own hands.

The first shovels of dirt fall to the husband. That is how it is done. I started shoveling. I wanted to shovel all of it myself. I would have shoveled the whole grave closed if Mufti Abdul Muqtadir — the imam of Nida ul Islam — had let me. He did not let me. I wanted to argue. I wanted to fight. I wanted to fight everybody that day, because I did not know what to do with what I was feeling, and fighting is love, and I did not know where else to put it. But I had to be respectful. So I shoveled what I shoveled and then the rest of the men took over — friends, family, brothers, sons, nephews. Everyone took a turn. The grave was filled.

Afterwards, the way it is done, we walked away from the grave a hundred yards. We all did that. Then I walked back. I sat at the grave for a couple of hours. I sat there just absorbing what I had just done. What had just been done. What was now done.
I wanted to shovel the whole grave closed.
I would have, if he had let me.
May 26, 2019 · at the grave
A note · on the people who came
People I had not seen in fifteen, twenty years

I do not know how everyone found out so quickly. Twelve hours between her passing and the burial. People I had not seen in fifteen years, twenty years, showed up at Nida ul Islam for the janazah. I do not know how the word traveled.

There are three reasons for it. The first is the barakah of Hina herself. She was a quiet person but she was not the kind of person you meet and forget. Her high school years, the people who lived through them with her, her co-workers, her bosses, anyone who had spent ten minutes in a room with her — you did not forget her. Her style, her radiance, her dignity, her presence. That is reason one.

The second is that she is Khalid Beg's daughter. Uncle Beg meant everything to everyone in our community. Father figure, big brother, imam, the one who taught us suras and knowledge that had nowhere else to come from in those years. Not just to the younger generation — even the uncles in our parents' generation went to Uncle Beg. So when his daughter was being buried, it was not just Hina's funeral. It was Uncle Beg's daughter's funeral. People came for him as much as for her.
The third is the Beg family itself. The siblings, the wider family — well-known, well-placed in the community over decades.

Some of the people who came probably did not even know I was the husband. There is a whole faction — people who came to Teaneck in the mid-nineties or the two-thousands — who would have no idea who the husband was. I was the low-key one. I am the low-key one. That is fine. The community came for Hina. The community came for Uncle Beg's daughter. That is what the community should have come for. I was there. I was the husband. I knew where I stood.
A note · on the count
The fifth most important man in her life
I have said this elsewhere in the book and I want to be precise about it here. In Hina's life there was a count, and the count went like this:
First, Rasulullah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.
Second, Abu Bakr radiyallahu anhu, the first Caliph.
Third, Umar radiyallahu anhu, the second Caliph.
Then a flip-flop between her father, Khalid Beg, and me. Some days he was fourth and I was fifth. Some days the order swapped.

I never minded. I never resented the count. Alhamdulillah, after the Prophet and the first two Caliphs and her father in any order — that is a beautiful standing. I knew where I stood. I was where I wanted to be. To be in any rank in Hina's life that had those four names ahead of me was an honor. The honor is the placement, not the number.

The husband is fifth, sometimes fourth. He is grateful for that placement. He would not have wanted to be anywhere else in the order. He understood the order the woman he loved was holding herself to, and he was proud of her for holding it, even when it meant he stood behind four other men in her count.
A du'a · from the janazah prayer
اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لَهَا وَارْحَمْهَا وَعَافِهَا وَاعْفُ عَنْهَا
وَأَكْرِمْ نُزُلَهَا وَوَسِّعْ مُدْخَلَهَا
Allāhumma'ghfir lahā wa'rhamhā wa ‘āfihā wa ‘fu ‘anhā,
wa akrim nuzulahā wa wassi‘ mudkhalahā.
O Allah, forgive her, have mercy on her, give her peace, and absolve her. Receive her with honor and make her resting place spacious.

From the janazah prayer over a woman. I said this over Hina at Nida ul Islam. I have said it every day since. I will say it every day for the rest of my life. It is the only thing left to do for her in this world.

For two weeks after the burial I went to the cemetery every day. Every single day. Sometimes for hours. Sometimes I just sat at the grave and did not speak. Sometimes I read Quran. Sometimes I said her name. Sometimes I said nothing.

I went the next day. And the next day. And the next day. And the next day. And the next. Two weeks of going to be close to her. That was all I could do. The household was full of people but the house was empty of her. The cemetery was empty of people but full of her. So I went where she was.

That is how the first two weeks passed. The phone calls had their own life. The community had its own life. The kids had their own grief. I went to the grave. I did the only thing I could do for her. I sat there. I asked Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to forgive her, to be merciful to her, to give her peace.
A note · on the spreadsheet I opened that week
The should-have document

Within the first week after Hina passed, I sat down and opened a Google Sheet. I wrote down what I called the should-have document — between myself and her. What I could have done. What I should have done. Where I fell short. What I had been expecting from her. What I had been pissed off about. Where I should have been gentler and warmer.

I had thought we had more time. Not because we were young — I was forty-seven, she was fifty-two, the eldest was getting married, the household was about to enter the next phase. I had thought the focus would shift back to the family. The building of the businesses was the work we had been doing for two decades; that time was ending. I was scaling back. We had been waiting for this phase. We were about to enter it.

That was not what happened. What was to be was what was to be. So I sat down and wrote the should-have document. I do not know if it belongs in this chapter or somewhere else in the book. I am putting a note here that it exists, and that I wrote it that first week, because the reader should know that the husband's first reflex, in the week after his wife of thirty years passed, was to sit down and itemize where he had fallen short. That is the kind of husband he was trying to be. That was the worship the writing had become.

The glass heart from 1981 or 1982 broke in 2018. The woman who had worn it broke in 2019. The half of the glass heart that remained stayed on the dresser. The husband who had given the heart sat at the grave for two weeks. The household reorganized itself slowly around an absence it could not get used to. The community remembered Uncle Beg's daughter. The eldest son's marriage held. The middle son would marry three years later. The daughter would walk her own path. The husband would do what husbands without their wives do — he would keep going, and the keeping-going would itself be the worship.

This chapter ends here. The chapters that follow are about what came next. The six months. The office month. The second marriage and the third. The stores closing. The return. The naming duty. The husband who survived past the wife learning, in the years he was not supposed to have, what the marriage had been carrying for thirty years and what the next thirty years would have to be carrying for her now that she was no longer the one carrying.
The book has further to go. I keep walking. She would have wanted me to.

title: Chapter Nine — Six Months Later
paragraphs: [Heading1] The Moon Gone
[Heading1] May 25, 2019 · December 25, 2019 · and after

She had been the undercurrent since I was ten. When she went, the gravity went. The six months that followed had no container. The decisions made inside the no-container shaped the years that came after.
Part III — Rupture & Collapse

The problem is, how do you begin to try and explain anything to anyone? Language is limiting. Life is limiting. I think what we are doing in life is trying to be understood. To be understood — that is what success looks like. I think that is what we are all after, even when we cannot say so.

You want to be understood. If you find a woman who gets you, bonds form. She becomes your wife. And the trying to be understood goes on inside the marriage, and around it, and the limitations of language are met by another person who has agreed to listen past them. That is what a wife is. That is, in part, what a wife is.

If you were to ask men who are seventy, eighty, ninety what they learned, I think they would tell you the same thing: that they had spent a life trying to be understood, and at some point they hit the limits of language and the limits of life and the limits of every other person they had been trying to be understood by, and they quieted down. They stopped trying. They stopped talking as much. They stopped caring about other people's opinion. Some did it with less of a filter. Some with more grace. That is where the term grumpy old man comes from — the man is not interested anymore. The values have shifted. He is not running for a popularity contest.

I want to begin this chapter there because the six months I am about to write about are the six months in which a man who had spent his whole life being understood by one woman discovered he was now trying to be understood by no one, and that the trying-to-be-understood reflex did not turn off when the audience went away. It only got louder. The chapter is about what a husband does when the only person who ever understood him without his having to explain stops being on the earth, and he keeps trying to be understood anyway, and the trying-to-be-understood ends up in places it should not have ended up. Some of those places I will describe. Some are too private. The whole of it is the chapter.
[Heading2] The Undercurrent

From the time I was ten she had been the undercurrent of my life. The source of peace, of serenity, of sakina — whether I was with her or not, whether she was writing back or not. The mind would travel to her. The travel was the peace.

From the time I was ten Hina had been the undercurrent of my life. I want to say that plainly because it is the load-bearing fact of everything that follows. She was the source of peace and serenity and sakina, whether I was with her or not, whether she was writing back or not. My mind would travel to her. The travel was itself the peace. Eternal thoughts of her, time spent thinking about her — that was my serenity. That was my sakina. She was the undercurrent of my life no matter what was happening, even when she was off married to someone else, even when there was no contact, even when there was no reason at all for her to be in my mind and she was in my mind anyway.

It sounds like hyperbole. It is not hyperbole. It is what it was. The presence was always there, within my heart and soul, in my conscious and unconscious mind. The one positive radiance — the one source of light — in a world that was otherwise dim. Not because the world was dark, but because the world I grew up in was the world I grew up in — the times, the baggage, the community, the parents, the minority culture, all of it, the rest of it. And inside that dimness was this one piece of radiant light. It was always there. Brighter and more vibrant in the early years, of course. But nonetheless that was what she was for me.

I hope — not that I hope — I think those who knew her in the small inner circle understood the same thing about her. Not the same thing about my relationship to her; that was mine and hers. But the radiance. The radiance was not only for me. It was who she was. As a sister, as a mother, as a friend, you saw it. There are plenty of examples in life that prove it.

One example I want to put on the page, because it has nothing to do with me, and because of that it is evidence in its purest form. After she passed, a man from the eighties stopped by the flower shop. His name is Kenny Lauzon — L-A-U-Z-O-N. He came to the flower shop and saw Ali behind the counter. He said: I have this strange feeling I don't understand. I keep seeing Hina in my dreams. Something has happened. Ali told him she had passed. Kenny was a coworker, a holiday helper — he came in on the holidays to help out at the flower shop. His family owned the building I would later purchase and move the flower shop into. He saw her maybe three or four times a year, on holidays, for a few hours each time. And after she was gone, his sleep brought her back to him before he had been told. That was Hina. That is the radiance I am talking about. Even a man who saw her a few hours a year, twenty years before, dreamed her into his sleep and came to the shop because his body was telling him something his ears had not yet heard.

That radiance was the undercurrent. It took different shapes and forms through the years — sometimes it was the sun, sometimes the moon — but it was always there. The gravity of my life was made of it. The whole orbit of my life, since I was ten, had been set by it.
Then it was gone.
— II —
[Heading2] The Moon Gone

You do not realize the moon is doing the work until the moon is not there. Then the tides stop. The gravity stops. The things that had been in orbit begin to drift, then collide. That is what the six months were.

There is no visual tie between the moon and the things on the earth. The moon is up there. The tides are down here. The ships float, the water moves, the rhythm holds. From the deck of a ship you do not see anything connecting the moon to the water. There appears to be no connection. So when the moon is doing its work you might think the moon has nothing to do with anything — the ship is just floating, the tide is just doing what tides do.

Then the moon is gone. And the tide stops. And the ship begins to drift, and the gravity is no longer organizing anything, and the things that were in orbit around the moon begin to float free and run into each other. The friction starts. The collisions start. Where there used to be an undercurrent holding everything in balance, now there is nothing — just floating, just running into other things. Chaos. Anarchy. Things hurting themselves because the undercurrent is no longer there.

That is what the following six months were like. No structure. No container. No gravity. Nothing steadfast. That is what was ripped from within the orbit of our family on May 25, 2019. Everyone felt it. The husband more than anyone, but the children, the in-laws, the community, the friends — everyone in the orbit felt the moon was gone, even the ones who did not realize the moon had been doing the work.

I am going to walk through what happened in that no-container in roughly the order it happened, because the order matters. Each thing that happened was a consequence of the no-container. None of it would have happened if the moon had still been doing its work. That does not make the decisions inside the no-container any less mine. It only locates them. The decisions were made by a man whose gravity had gone. The man is responsible for the decisions. The chapter is honest about the gravity.
— III —
[Heading2] What Was Left in the House

Within the first month I lost the daughter too. Within the first two weeks I was in bed with hives, my whole body burning. The nuclear family Hina had built started coming apart almost immediately, because she had been the thing holding it together.

The household Hina had built was a strictly nuclear one. The small social circle was Moaaz, Shahbaaz, Zanab, Hina, myself, and her own siblings — and the children's friendships within the wider community. Beyond that, not much. Hina was a quiet person and she had drawn the line of the family close around herself and her children. That was her right and that was her gift; she had built a tight, warm, small world.

Within the first month after she passed, that small world began to come apart. Within the first month Zanab chose to exit the home. I want to say that on the page and let it sit. She left without saying very much. I am still, in 2026, sorting through what that month was for her and what the years before had been — things had been moving for her in the year or two before Hina's passing that Hina did not see, that the brothers were partly aware of and I was not. I do not want to characterize my daughter's reasons in this book because I do not have her words for them and because the book is not the place to argue with my own daughter. The fact for the chapter is: I lost the wife in May, and within a month I had lost the daughter too. The nuclear family was now three people in the house. The wife and the daughter were not in it.

The three people left were Moaaz, Shahbaaz, and me — plus Moaaz's wife Qurat-ul-ain, newly married into the home, and Shahbaaz, who had moved back home upon his mother's death. That was the household. A widowed father, a newly married eldest son, a newly returned middle son, and a new daughter-in-law trying to be the woman of a house she had only just entered, in a house where the woman of the house had just died.

I want to acknowledge what Qurat-ul-ain walked into. She had been married seven months. She had been part of our family seven months. She had not had the years with Hina that the rest of us had. And now she was being asked, by life and by the circumstance, to step into a house that had just lost its center, with a husband who had just lost his mother, with a father-in-law who was a widower of three weeks, and a brother-in-law moving back home in grief, and a sister-in-law gone.
