She did what she could. The household held the shape it could hold. None of it was her fault. None of it was even her job, in any honest reading. But she was there and she was the only adult woman in the house, and the gravity of that fell on her in ways she had not signed up for.

Within the first two weeks, my own body broke. I came down with hives. Across the whole body, excruciating, the kind of pain that does not let you function. I could not get out of bed. Two weeks in bed with the skin on fire. The body keeps the score. The body had been keeping the score of thirty years of marriage and forty years of knowing her, and the day she went, the body did its math, and the math came out in hives. I lay there. I rode it out. I do not remember much else from those two weeks. I remember the burning.

Amina, Hina's youngest sister, stayed about three weeks. She was grieving her sister and she wanted to be around her nephews and her niece and the home, processing what she had lost. I was grateful she was there. We did not say much to each other — what was there to say — but the presence was a presence. The other siblings — Zarrar, Karrar, Naila — I did not see much in those two, three, four months. I am not going to assign motive. I will say what I think is true: people did not know what to say. There had been tension before. The sister had passed. Everyone was carrying their own grief and their own pieces of the Franklin Road wound that Chapter Eight describes. I do not blame anyone for being scarce. I notice it. I name it. The chapter requires me to.

The in-laws kept their distance. The only ones who brought anything to the house in those months — food, something warm to eat — were Mr. Mohammed and his wife. Salt-of-the-earth people. The kind of people who show up because showing up is who they are. I will not name the rest of them; this chapter is not a settling of accounts. The chapter is a record. The record is: Mr. Mohammed and his wife brought food. The rest mostly did not.

That is what was left in the house. Three of us, one daughter-in-law, no wife, no daughter, hives, an aunt-sister for three weeks, and a quiet house with a kitchen that was not being run by the woman who had run it.
A du'a · for the one who is left
رَبِّ لَا تَذَرْنِي فَرْدًا وَأَنْتَ خَيْرُ الْوَارِثِينَ
Rabbi lā tadharnī fardan wa anta khayru'l-wārithīn.
My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors.

Surah Al-Anbiya 21:89. The du'a of Zakariya alayhi'l-salam, made in old age when he feared he would be left without continuation. I made it many times in those weeks. Not from fear of being childless — alhamdulillah I have three. From the simpler thing: I had been left.
— IV —
[Heading2] Shahbaaz Says No
Two or three months in, I asked Shahbaaz: let's start the search for your marriage. The family needs something. We need a kickstart, a movement, anything. He said no. I asked again. He said no.

About two or three months in, I came to Shahbaaz. He had moved back home after his mother's death. He was twenty-six, going on twenty-seven. He had been born in November of 1992. I said to him: Shahbaaz, listen. The family needs something. We should start to search for your marriage. We need something to try to kickstart us up out of this. It is time. Going on the search for a spouse, for yourself, is what we need to do.
He said no.
I touched on it again, a few weeks later. He said no.
I touched on it a third time. He said no.

I want to be careful here because Shahbaaz was right and Shahbaaz was wrong at the same time, and the chapter has to hold both. He was right that two or three months after your mother passes is not the time to be looking for a wife for yourself. The grief was real. He needed time. He was twenty-six years old; there was no clock on him. The clock I felt was not his clock. He was right to say no.

He was wrong — if wrong is even the word — in the sense that without his marriage search to anchor the household, there was no other movement on the horizon. Moaaz was newly married, in his first eight months. Qurat-ul-ain was newly arrived. Shahbaaz was grieving, sleeping in until noon, twelve, one in the afternoon. Zanab was gone. Hina was gone. And I was the only adult in the house with the energy — or the curse — of needing to move.

My nature is to move. I have said this before in the book. It is the shark image: the shark cannot breathe if it does not continue moving through the water. That is what allowed me to do what I did with Hina at the age of ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen. That is what allowed me to stand and refuse the 1983 wedding when I was twelve. That is what allowed me to be homeless at fifteen and find work and food and a foothold. The seeing-what-is-right, the standing, the moving — those were the qualities that had carried me. The same qualities that had served me in life and in work and on the athletic field and in business.

Now, in that quiet, full-of-grief, no-gravity household, those same qualities became a curse. I could not sit and wait for things to fall into my lap. I could not lie in bed past noon. I could not pretend nothing needed to be done. I could not be Shahbaaz, however right Shahbaaz was. I was who I was. The shark could not breathe.

So when Shahbaaz said no a third time, I sat with what was left. The household needed something. No one was going to start it but me. The men around me were doing the best they could in their own grief. My friends and family who could see what was going on from the outside — my brother, my sister-in-law, Mr. Mohammed — saw what they saw, and they said what they said, and you hear what you want to hear in those conversations. Ultimately the decisions were mine. The mistakes are mine. The choices were made within the context of what was going on, and that is all I can say in defense of them.

I will say one more thing in defense. When I looked for guidance — when I asked, what does a man do in this situation — I looked at the seerah. The Prophet sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, after Khadija radiyallahu anha passed, married within two weeks of her death. Two weeks. I was three months in and still looking for permission to move. The seerah gave me the permission. The framework I had been raised in said: a man should marry. A man should not be alone. I had been alone three months and the loneliness was breaking me, and the seerah told me the Prophet did not wait that long. So I moved.
A note · from the should-have document
[Heading3] June 29, 2019 — one month and four days after she passed

I have already mentioned in Chapter Eight that in the first week after Hina passed I sat down and opened a Google Sheet. I called it the should-have document. Between myself and her. What I could have done. Where I had fallen short. The Sheet's first save is dated June 29, 2019.

I am putting the existence of it here, in this chapter too, because I want the reader to see that the writing started before the moving did. Before I asked Shahbaaz about his marriage. Before I joined any app. Before any of what comes next in this chapter, I was already writing into the silence she had left. The writing was, by then, the worship. The writing is, by 2026, the book.
[Heading2] The App
I joined a Muslim matchmaking app. Communication. Get-to-know-someone. A way to keep yourself busy, or to pretend you are. I came across Zahira there.

Ijoined a Muslim matchmaking app. I will not name the brand — the brand is not the point. The point is that a forty-seven-year-old widower, three or four months out from his wife of thirty years, sat down with his phone in 2019 and joined an app for Muslims looking for spouses. That is a sentence I never thought I would write. It is a sentence that, written, has the kind of small flat ugliness that the truth often has.

It was not casual. It was not exploratory. It was the search. I was looking for a wife. I did not know how else to begin. I had been a husband since I was eighteen. I had asked for Hina's hand at fifteen and been refused, asked again at eighteen and been granted. I had never courted anyone. I had never been on what English-speakers call a date. The framework of my life had not given me a path for finding a wife outside the family-and-community process — and the family-and-community process, in 2019, was not delivering. Mr. Mohammed and my brother saw I needed something; they did what they could. The community was busy with its own. The app was a place where the search could happen without my having to ask everyone around me, all the time, do you know anyone.

I came across Zahira on the app. We began to communicate — messages, then conversation, then meeting. Just getting-to-know-someone. To keep yourself busy. To put one foot in front of the other. To do something with the wreckage.
— VI —
[Heading2] Zahira

She was one year older than me, had three sons, was coming out of a bad marriage, lived in Philadelphia, wanted out. Two broken homes trying to help each other. No Romeo and Juliet. A stake in the ground.

Zahira was a year older than me. She had three sons — eldest about twenty-nine, youngest about twenty-two, twenty-three. She was coming out of a marriage that had been hard on her. She was distraught. She was looking for a husband.

I want to be honest about what I was and was not looking for. I was not looking for what I had had with Hina. I was not foolish enough to think that was on offer. I was not even looking for what English-speakers call chemistry or synergy. I had had the chemistry. I had had the synergy. I had had the marriage. What I was looking for, at three months out, was a stake in the ground. Something to give the household a routine. Some presence. A little structure. That was the whole of it. There was no Romeo-and-Juliet pretense. I was a widower of three or four months. She was a divorced woman with three sons and a difficult past. The proposition between us was modest: two broken homes, can we help each other, can we make a decent thing out of two damaged ones.

She had a home in the Philadelphia area, and a second home, and a job. The plan she proposed was that she would rent out the first home, quit the job, collect unemployment, and move up to Teaneck with her middle son, whose name is Junaid — J-U-N-A-I-D. The house in Teaneck was plenty big enough for all of us. Financially she was set. She wanted out of where she was. I wanted someone in the house. The arithmetic seemed to work.

For the first month it was wonderful. I want to put that on the page too. The wedding had been done, the household had a woman in it again, Junaid had moved in, the new chapter was starting. I will describe the wedding day itself in a moment. The first month after the wedding was a good month. I am not going to pretend otherwise. Whatever came later, the first month was hopeful.

Then COVID hit, January or February 2020, and the world closed in around the marriage, and the inside of the marriage was where the trouble lived, and the closing-in of COVID made the inside visible faster than it would have been visible otherwise.
— VII —
[Heading2] The Nikah, December 25, 2019

Her first marriage had not been what it should have been. I tried to give the second one everything. About a hundred people. A hall. Food. Music. Clothes. Done as right as I could do it. She was very happy. My feelings were mixed.

The day itself was December 25, 2019. I do not remember the date in the way I remember May 25 — so much has gone on since — but the date is documented. I could slow it down and find the details. For the chapter, what matters is what the day was.

Zahira's first marriage had not been the swept-off-the-feet thing a woman often wants a marriage to be. She had not had the celebration. She had not had the function and the hall and the clothes and the food and the music. At her age, going into a second marriage, she wanted those things this time. I understood why. I did what I could to give them to her.

We did the wedding. About a hundred people. There are videos. There was a hall, there was food, there was music, there were clothes and makeup. I did the best that could be done for her on a day like that. She was very happy. I want the record to show that. She was happy.

For me the day was a mixed one. I was torn. My family — the sons, the daughter-in-law — were doing the best they could to be present, to be supportive, but no one in my family was looking at this day as a celebration in the simple sense. It was not, for us, a party. It was a foundation. It was a routine. It was the stake in the ground I had been talking about. The sons saw it that way. I saw it that way. Zahira and her side saw it differently, and that was fair — this was her wedding too, and for her it was the wedding she had not had the first time, and the difference in how the two sides were experiencing the same day was probably visible to anyone who knew where to look.

What I can say about the day itself is what I have said: we did it. We did it as well as it could be done. She was happy. I tried to keep everyone's feelings and thoughts in mind. When you are trying to do that for many people at once, some things get missed. Some things get overstepped or unknowingly forgotten. And in my case — this is the pattern that ran underneath the whole marriage — the person who got missed first was always me. I was raised to put other people's wants first. The sons were raised the same way. I do not regret that as a principle. I do regret that the principle, applied without limit, caused a problem when the other person did not share it. But that part comes later in this chapter and is the chapter's hardest piece. I am noting it here. I am not yet unpacking it.

The nikah was conducted. The mehr was paid. The witnesses witnessed. The community heard the announcement. The husband heard the words of the marriage du'a a second time in his life, thirty years and forty-five days after the first time he had heard them. The dua is the same dua. The marriages are not the same marriages. The man hearing them was not the same man.
A du'a · said over the new spouse
بَارَكَ اللَّهُ لَكَ وَبَارَكَ عَلَيْكَ وَجَمَعَ بَيْنَكُمَا فِي خَيْرٍ
Bāraka'llāhu laka wa bāraka ‘alayka wa jama‘a baynakumā fī khayr.
May Allah bless you, and shower His blessings upon you, and join you both together in goodness.

It had been said over me once in November 1989 in Khalid Beg's living room. It was said over me a second time on December 25, 2019. Same words. Different marriage. The husband heard them both times and tried, with what he had, to be worthy of them. The second time he had less than the first time. He was working with what was left.
— VIII —
[Heading2] Broken Wings

One month after the nikah I sat down and wrote. I borrowed the opening line from a Mr. Mister song from 1985. What walked through the borrowed door was mine. The wife the piece is addressed to is not the wife I was married to. The mission, as I named it, remained the same.
Broken Wings
January 2020 · seven months in · one month married
Let's take these broken wings
and learn to fly again.
I can. We can —
with the added burdens,
with you by my side,
and the strength of the memories
and moments lived.
Mission remains the same.
May the love be true.
May we honor those that have passed.
It's the same —
one and only God
that takes and gives.
Love and death —
ask someone that's been there.
My life says one thing:
a wife is everything.
Without a wife a man is not much.
Since I was fifteen — since I was ten.
At least I am not much without a wife.
A wife is the guardian.
Her husband's champion.
A wife is everything.
Life is not life without a wife.
A wife is the backbone.
A wife is gateway to faith.
Gateway to virtue.
A wife is a man's reason to be.
Allah (swt) gives.
Allah (swt) takes.
Allah (swt) gives.
Allah (swt) made the world
and constructed its laws
of the march of time.

Mr. Mister released Broken Wings in 1985. The chorus says: Take these broken wings and learn to fly again. I was fourteen when the song was on the radio. I remembered it. In January of 2020, a month into the new marriage, the chorus came back to me, and I borrowed the opening line as a doorway.
What walked through the doorway was mine. I can. We can — with the added burdens, with you by my side, and the strength of the memories and moments lived. Mission remains the same.

The you in those lines is not Zahira. The new marriage was already a month old when I wrote them. The you is Hina. I want to be honest about that on the page. Even married to someone else, even a month into a second nikah, when I sat down to write about getting up and learning to fly again, the wife I was addressing was the wife who had passed. The first wife was the wife. The second wife was a wife. The two are not the same word in the same mouth.

The piece then turned to the marriage thesis. My life says one thing — a wife is everything. Without a wife a man is not much. Since I was fifteen — since I was ten. Ten is the necklace. Fifteen is the homelessness, the year Hina caught the homeless boy and gave him work and food and a foothold. The piece was dated January 2020 and the content of it was 1981 and 1986. The marriage I was inside, in January 2020, was three weeks old. The marriage the piece was about was the one that had ended seven months earlier.

That is what the Broken Wings piece was. A husband who had remarried a month before, writing into the silence again. The silence was still Hina. The new marriage was on the calendar. The audience-of-one had not changed. The audience-of-one was not going to change.
Mission remains the same.
The audience of one did not change.
January 2020 · one month after the second nikah
— IX —
[Heading2] What Went Wrong, in Order

COVID hit. The questions began. The houses started piling up. The sakina I had been looking for in the new marriage went somewhere else, and what arrived instead was constant talk — about other people, about other choices, about the past.

COVID hit in January or February of 2020. The first month of the marriage had been the wonderful month. By the second and third month the chatter had started. I am going to use that word, chatter, because it is the right word for what it was. Chitter-chatter. Constant. About this person. About that person. About what someone in the community had done. About what someone's friend had said. About what someone else's friend was doing. About who in the community was being judged for what, and who was being praised for what, and who you should be like and who you should not be like.

The peace and the sakina I had been looking for in the new marriage was not landing. What was landing was talk — small talk, gossip-talk, getting-into-people's-business talk. I am a quiet person. Hina had been a quiet person. We had built a quiet marriage out of two quiet people who did not need to fill silence with talk. The new marriage was not quiet. The new marriage filled every silence.

Then came the questions. The questions that, in retrospect, were the first signs of what the marriage was actually about. Why didn't you marry this one? Why didn't you marry that one? Why didn't you marry someone younger? Why didn't you marry there? Why didn't you do this? Why didn't you do that? I did not know how to answer them. I had married her. I was in front of her. I had said yes. The questions were not really questions; they were a register. They were the language of a person who needed to know she was not the consolation prize. I understood that, looking back. In the moment I just heard the questions and did not know what to say to them.

And then the houses. Within sixteen or eighteen months of the marriage, Zahira had bought three houses in Binghamton. Three. I helped. I supported. I drove. I went up there. I did what a husband does. But the constant motion — driving back and forth from Binghamton to Teaneck, going to the closings, dealing with the paperwork, the renovations, the tenants — the constant motion was not the structure I had been looking for in the second marriage. It was the opposite of structure. It was movement on top of movement on top of movement. My own sakina did not survive it. I had remarried for a stake in the ground. What I had instead was a marriage that could not stop moving.

And then she started complaining. Not just to me — that would have been fine, that is what a wife and husband do, you talk it out. She started complaining to my brother. To my sister-in-law. To others. That is a different thing. That is the family-pressure move. That is the trying-to-put-the-husband-on-the-defensive-with-his-own-people move. In the framework I come from, you handle your own things with your own spouse. You do not bring third parties into the marriage unless something egregious has happened. When you start going outside the marriage with complaints that are not egregious — that is usually, in my experience, the beginning of the end. A fifty-year-old woman knows that. I knew it. I was not the smartest person in the room, but that I knew.
[Heading2] The Garage

She came down from Binghamton to pick something up, meant to go back the same night. Slept over. In the morning she wanted to fight. I asked her to let it cool. She would not. I went to the garage and sat there seven, eight hours. I called the sons. They were busy. The fear that kept me there was not the fear most people would assume.

There was a particular incident. I do not want to relive the specific argument that triggered it — the specifics do not matter for the chapter, and rehearsing them is not the work the chapter is trying to do. What matters is the shape of the day, and what I did inside it, and what the doing inside it told me about what I was now in.

She had been up in Binghamton. She came down to Teaneck to pick something up. The plan was that she would go right back the same night. It got late. She stayed over. In the morning she wanted to argue. About what is not the point; about something she had decided overnight was worth pushing on. I said: please, let it cool off. Give it time. We will talk again later. Nobody wants to fight. She would not let it cool. She wanted to raise her voice. She wanted to push it. She started making threats.

I said: please, do not push further. Please. I want the boys reading this to hear that word. Please. I said it more than once. I said it the way a man says it when he has already made a decision inside himself that he is not going to escalate, and he is asking the other person to meet him at the de-escalation. I said it the way a man says it when he knows what is on the other side of his patience and does not want to find out.
She kept pushing.

So I left the room. I went to the garage. I sat in the garage. Seven hours. Eight hours. I do not remember exactly. Long enough that the day passed through me. Long enough that whatever was rising in me could fall back. Long enough that nothing was going to come out of my hands or out of my mouth that I could not take back.

I called her sons. Not my sons — hers. Her three sons from her first marriage. I called them and said: please, you need to come. Speak with your mom. She is not being sensible. She needs you to come and be with her. They said they were busy. I called again. They said they were busy. I do not blame them. They were grown men with their own lives, and I was not their father, and what they were being asked to walk into was their own mother in a state I could not pull her out of. I said: listen, this is not good. Please come. They did not come.

I want the chapter to record that. The husband, in his garage, called the sons of the wife he was trying to step away from for a few hours, and asked them to come help their mother. Those sons did not come. That fact is part of the picture. A wife whose own sons will not come, when the husband calls them in good faith, is a wife whose marriage has already been telling something that the husband has been refusing to hear. I had been refusing to hear it. The garage day was when the hearing started.
So I stayed in the garage. Eight hours. The day ended. The pushing did not stop. The threats did not stop. I made a decision.

I want to name what the decision was about, because the easy reading of it is wrong. The easy reading is: a man's pride could not take being yelled at, a man's reputation could not take being threatened, a man wanted to teach a wife a lesson, a man wanted out. None of those were the operating fear. The operating fear was simpler and harder to talk about.

I am not Bahishti Zewar culture. I want to put that on the page. The Bahishti Zewar is the book that has run, for over a century, as the operating manual for what a Muslim woman of the Indian subcontinent is and what she is for. It is also, by extension, the operating manual for what a Muslim man of the Indian subcontinent is allowed to fear. Bahishti Zewar man fears what people will say. He fears the embarrassment. He fears the loss of face. He stays in the marriage, he stays in the room, he stays in the situation, because his motivation is the gaze of the community.

That is not where I come from. That is what I have been fighting since I was twelve years old refusing to attend the 1983 wedding. The fear of what people will say has never been a thing in me that can be used as leverage. The community has been a community I have served and loved, but it has never been the master of my decisions. Hina knew that about me. It was one of the things she had loved about me. It was one of the things her father had refused to give her hand to at fifteen because of, and granted it at eighteen in spite of. The not-being-Bahishti-Zewar in me has been a constant.

What I do fear is this: losing my senses. Doing something without my wit. Acting before I have thought. Saying something I cannot take back. Letting the worst part of me speak before the better part of me has had a chance to. That is the fear. That is the failure I will not allow. That is what eight hours in a garage was for — to make absolutely sure that whatever came next was decided by the man I am at my most awake, not the man I might become at the bottom of an argument I had not chosen to be in.

At the end of those eight hours, with the pushing not stopping, with the sons not coming, with the wife not relenting, I made the decision that the marriage could not continue in proximity. I filed a restraining order. I am not going to walk through the legal mechanics of that here. The mechanics are in their own folder; they will be in the appendix or in Chapter Ten when the timeline calls for them. What I want this chapter to record is: the husband sat in his garage for eight hours to be sure he was making the decision from the right place. He called for help and the help did not come. He made the decision alone. The decision was not made out of fear of what people would say. The decision was made out of the older, deeper fear of what he might do if he stayed in the room.

I want one more thing on the page about that day. I had never thought, in my life, that I would have to file a restraining order on a wife. I had not grown up knowing such a thing was possible. I had not been raised to handle it. I had been raised to handle a wife like Hina, who would not have made the day end this way because she was Hina. When the day did end this way, with a different woman, I was a man in my late forties filing a paper I had not, at any prior point in my life, known I might need to file. The paper got filed. The marriage proceeded into its later stages. The talaq came in July of 2021. That timeline belongs to Chapter Ten.
The fear was not what people would say.
The fear was what I might do if I stayed in the room.
A garage in Teaneck · eight hours
— XI —
[Heading2] The Pattern Underneath
I do not put myself first. I raised the sons not to put themselves first. With the right partner, that is a marriage. With the wrong partner, that becomes the trap.

Iwant to name the pattern that ran underneath the second marriage, because it is also the pattern that ran underneath the first marriage and underneath the third one and underneath the way I have lived. The naming is not exculpation. The naming is the work of the book.

I am not the type of person who puts himself first. I have raised the sons the same way. Always put the other people's wants and needs first. Sacrifice your own. That is the Buyahka in me — it is the value system Ammi and Abbu raised me with, and it is the value system Hina shared with me, and it is the value system the marriage with Hina ran on, beautifully, because she also did not put herself first. Two people each putting the other first, for thirty years, is what made the first marriage what it was. It is the whole structure of Buyahka love. It is the whole point.
It is a beautiful pattern when the partner shares it. It is a trap when the partner does not.

With Zahira, the pattern became the trap. I kept putting her wants first. Her wedding day. Her three houses in Binghamton. Her family pressures. Her complaints. Her plans. The husband putting the wife first is what a husband does. But when the wife is not also putting the husband first — when the dynamic is one-way — the pattern becomes a slow draining. The husband does not notice the draining until something breaks. In my case the breaking was the garage day. In other men's cases the breaking comes earlier or later. The shape is the same.

I want to say plainly: that was a mistake on my part. The mistake was not loving her. The mistake was not marrying. The mistake was not putting myself first when the other person was not putting me first. The mistake was the pattern, applied without limit, into a marriage that could not absorb it. I should have protected myself and my family more than I did. I should have come first more than I did. I do not know how to find the perfect balance — I have not, in 2026, figured it out. I am still working on it.

I can see how the same pattern, watched from the outside, would teach the sons something I did not mean to teach them. They were raised in a home where their father did not put himself first. They watched that man, in his second marriage, continue not putting himself first, and the marriage failed anyway, and the sons saw the failure. I do not know what each of them took from watching. I hope they took: at some point, enough is enough. I hope they took: your father did not know how to draw the line and that cost him. I hope they took it as a warning more than a model.

The chapter ends here, with the failure named and the pattern named and the responsibility taken. It does not end with the marriage; the marriage limps on into 2020 and 2021 in ways Chapter Ten will describe. It ends with a man in his late forties, in 2020, in 2021, having to admit to himself that the moon was gone, that the gravity had not come back, that the new marriage had not provided the gravity he was looking for, and that the only honest framing of the whole episode was the one he would write down later in plain words: it is failure. It is a mistake. It is regretful. If I had been better structured, had more gravity, was more steadfast, and had my prayers established at that time, the mistakes would be less.
If I had been better structured,
had more gravity,
was more steadfast,
and had my prayers established at that time,
the mistakes would be less.
A widower, looking back, in his own words
A du'a · for the one asking to be steadied
رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا وَثَبِّتْ أَقْدَامَنَا
Rabbanā afrigh ‘alaynā ṣabran wa thabbit aqdāmanā.
Our Lord, pour upon us patience, and make our feet firm.

Surah Al-Baqarah 2:250. The du'a of the believers who went out with Talut against Jalut. The believers who were outnumbered and asked for two things: patience, and steadiness of foot. I had neither in 2019 and 2020. I am asking, now, for both. The asking is itself the beginning.

The chapter closes on the moon. The moon was gone. The gravity was gone. The man whose orbit had been set by her since he was ten, who had been her husband for thirty years since the age of eighteen, lost the wife at forty-seven, lost the daughter the same month, lay sick in bed two weeks, asked the son to begin a search, was told no, joined an app, found Zahira, signed a nikah-nama seven months after the funeral, gave her the wedding she had not had the first time, watched the first month be wonderful, watched COVID close in, watched the houses pile up, watched the questions begin, watched the complaints go outside the marriage, sat in a garage for eight hours so he would not become the man he refused to be, called her sons and they were busy, filed the paper he had never thought he would file, and looked at all of it later and said: I was without gravity. The decisions were mine. The pattern was the pattern. The mistakes were the mistakes. If I had been more steadfast and had my prayers established, the mistakes would be less.

That is the chapter. That is the seven months of moon-gone and the year of moon-gone-still that followed. The next chapter is about the years after that — 2020, 2021, 2022. The talaq. The third marriage on the anniversary of Hina's first one. The naming duty. The slow return of structure to a life that had been without structure for the longest stretch since 1986.
I am still walking. She would have wanted me to. The walking is not what I thought it would be. The walking is what it is.
Held space · one name to confirm

Mr. Mohammed's wife's name in the voice notes came through as “sister Neha” or similar — the dictation was unclear. The chapter currently refers to her only as “Mr. Mohammed and his wife.” When the correct spelling is confirmed, the line in Section III will be updated.

title: Chapter Ten — 2020–2022 / Talaq / The Third Marriage
paragraphs: The Bridge
A man who does for others, then is punished for the doing. Three keys of the same pattern: a wife lifted, a son ruptured, a stranger paid for.
Part III — Rupture & Collapse

There is a kind of man who, when he sees someone drowning, does not stop to ask whether the water belongs to him. He gets in. He pulls. He gets out. He goes home. If the person he pulled later says the water was fine and he had no business in it, he does not argue. He had not been doing it for thanks.

Ihad been that kind of man my whole life. I did not know any other way to be. This chapter is about the years when being that kind of man cost me the most. Not because the doing was wrong. Because the doing, without limit, without protection, without a partner who shared the same orientation, ran me out. The bridge that I was kept building got walked across. The walking across, in most cases, was the right outcome. The cost of the building was always paid by me, and in this chapter the cost compounded faster than the building could replenish.

The chapter has three keys. The first is Zahira and the bridge I built for her, which she walked across, mostly after I was no longer standing on it. The second is Moaaz and the cleaning of three empty rooms, which became the rupture that lasted eighteen months and longer. The third is Kaltoum, whom I met on the same app I had met Zahira on, whose hotel bill I paid before I had ever met her, whom I married seven and a half years after Hina passed, in September of 2022. Three keys, one pattern.
The Bridge

Zahira had been drowning in Philadelphia. The marriage was the rope. The fourteen months were the foundation. She walked the rest after the marriage ended — that was always the deepest design of it, even when I did not see it that way at the time.

Zahira had been drowning in Philadelphia. A bad marriage behind her. Three sons trying to find their footing. A house she could not stay in. A job she was tired of. She came up to New Jersey and we married seven months after Hina was buried — December 25, 2019, about a hundred people in the hall, food, music, clothes, makeup, videos that still exist. She was very happy. My own feelings were mixed. I have written about that in Chapter Nine.
What came next was that I did what I do. I built the bridge.

She rented out the Philadelphia house. Her middle son Junaid moved up. Quiet boy. Reserved. The kind of young man who did not yet know what he had inside him. I took him in at Edible. Walked him through the work — first the floor, then the staff, then the books, then the hire-and-fire. The Ready Aim Fire approach. Read the numbers. Trust the antennas. Work hard first, then work smart. Leave a piece of yourself in the place you build.

He absorbed it the way a young man absorbs things — ten percent in the first week, twenty in the first month, then one day a moment lands and he hears something I had said six months earlier and didn't catch the first time, and now it is his. That is how a person becomes their own. The shyness melts. The way they walk changes. The way they talk changes. I had watched it happen to me at fifteen and sixteen, when Hina had given me shelter and a job and the first chance to feel like a man instead of a boy with no roof. Now I was on the other side of it, doing for Junaid what Hina had done for me.

Within those fourteen months Junaid was a young man. Zahira said so herself. He had come in quiet and reserved and walked out with the antennas, with the numbers, with the way of standing in a room that says I belong here. That much had landed by the time we divorced.

Inside our marriage she bought two houses in Binghamton. A third came soon after, just after we divorced. She bought them. Not me. What I did was different and less visible. I made the ground beneath her stop shaking. I gave her the freedom to use her own money, her own judgment, her own time. I gave her the strength that comes from not having to fight for every step on your own. I set her free to do the things she could not do while she was holding her old life together alone in Philadelphia.

That was the bridge. Freedom enabled. Strength enabled. Set free. The houses, the moves, the new starts — those were hers. I did not lift her family up to Binghamton. She did. I made it possible for her to do it. There is a difference, and the difference matters.

Most of the bridge she walked across after I was no longer standing on it. Her two other sons followed her up. The wives came. Junaid got married. The family she had been carrying alone became a family standing on its own ground.

I am not going to pretend I did not know what I was doing. I knew. I had done it before. For Hina at sixteen when she came back from Durham. For my own brothers and my own family. For employees over thirty years. This is what I am. The third world gets work done by sheer effort, longer and harder than anyone else, and then if it is lucky it learns to read the numbers and use its antennas and begins to compete. That is how a person gets pulled up. That is how a family gets pulled up. That is how an ummah gets pulled up. You take the small steps. No one fifty years from now will remember Abrar and Junaid. That is not the point. The point is that the steps get taken.
So the conditions got built. And then —
— II —
The Chatter

COVID hit. The chatter started. The complaints went out of the house and into the family. What the family heard was that nothing was egregious. The complaint that did not land became its own grievance. That is when I knew.
The marriage began to go wrong the way most marriages go wrong: not in one place, but in a hundred small places at once.

COVID hit in January or February of 2020, six weeks after the wedding. The world locked down. The hall full of a hundred people in December became a memory of the last big gathering before everything closed. Whatever Zahira and I were going to learn about each other, we were going to have to learn it inside the house, with the doors shut, with the world reduced to four walls and a screen.
This is where the chatter started.

There is a kind of talking that is not communication. It is filler. It is the sound a person makes to fill the space they cannot stand to leave silent. So-and-so did this. So-and-so said that. What is going on in this person's house. What is going on in that person's house. Who in the community is being judged for what. Who is being praised for what. Who you should be like and who you should not be like. Hours of it. Days of it. The evenings filled with discussion of people who were not in the room.

I had spent thirty years married to a woman who could sit with me in silence and the silence would mean something. Hina and I could be in a car for eleven hours driving to Indiana for Moaaz's wedding meetings in 2018 and the silence between us was full. Now I was in a house with a woman who could not bear silence for ten minutes, and what filled the silence was the assessment of people who had nothing to do with us.

The picnic trips happened. The barbecues happened. The pickleball with the friends. The karaoke. The weekend trips. I was doing all of it. A second wife who had not had any of that in her first marriage was going to have it now. I was doing it for her. I was doing it past the point of my own depletion. I was doing it because that is what I do.

It was not enough. There was always another person to bring into the conversation. Another household to assess. Another piece of news to repeat. The chatter did not slow down because the trips were happening. The chatter ran on its own engine.
And then the chatter began to leave the house. Complaints to my brother. Complaints to my sister-in-law. The family-pressure move.

What my brother and sister-in-law heard, when she came to them, was not what she had hoped they would hear. They listened. They asked questions. They asked the question that a person who has been married a long time learns to ask: What is egregious here? What is the actual harm? And the answer they came back with — quietly, between themselves and to me — was that there was nothing egregious. There was friction. There was adjustment. There was a husband and a wife in the first year of a second marriage learning each other while a virus had locked the world inside the same four walls. That is not a crisis. That is the normal weight of two people who did not grow up together trying to grow into each other late.

My brother and sister-in-law did not take a side. They did not enable anything. They did what mature people do when a younger family member comes to them with a complaint: they listened with care, and then they told the truth as they understood it. The truth was that nothing they were hearing rose to the level Zahira seemed to need it to rise to.

This should have been a relief. In a healthy marriage, when the elders say this is just the work, keep doing the work, the couple goes back to the work. What happened instead was that the absence of validation became its own grievance. The complaint that did not land became proof that no one understood. The marriage was now being measured against a standard no one inside it had set and no one outside it would confirm.
That is when I knew. Not when she said the words she could not take back. Not when the restraining order was filed. Earlier. When the complaint had no substance and the complaining did not stop.
— III —
The Words That Cannot Be Taken Back

She said it in Urdu, in the middle of an argument that should have been about nothing. Once such words leave the tongue they do not return. They are out there in the cosmos. The marriage had crossed a line.
There is a thing that happens between two people who are no longer building. They stop trying to find each other. They start trying to be right.

I do not remember exactly when the back-and-forth tipped over into the place where the words came out. I remember that it had been building for weeks. The chatter, the trips to my brother, the small accusations that grew into bigger ones. I remember that Zahira spent more and more time in Binghamton, with her son Junaid, in the houses she had bought. I remember asking myself, sometimes out loud and sometimes only to myself, What am I doing here. What am I trying to get out of this. Peace. Routine. A little Sakina. Some forward motion. That was the whole list. I was not trying to take anything from anyone. I had not taken a penny. I had not taken a nickel. I had spent and built and run and driven and hosted and gone to the pickleball and the karaoke and the camping trips. I was trying to be alive enough to keep the household upright.
The morning the words came was the morning of the garage day I wrote about in Chapter Nine.

She had come down from Binghamton the day before to pick something up, meant to go back the same night. It got late. She stayed over. In the morning she wanted to argue. I said: please, let it cool off. Give it time. We will talk again later. Nobody wants to fight. She would not let it cool. She wanted to raise her voice. She wanted to push it.
And then, in Urdu, she said it:
Main tumhari aulaad ko maar daloongi.
I will kill your progeny.

A person who is in extremity says things that the person they actually are would never say. I know that. I have lived long enough to know that. But the thing about words is that once they have left the tongue, they do not return. They are out there in the cosmos. They cannot be unsaid. The person who said them can apologize. The person who heard them can forgive. But the words remain where they have been spoken. And once a curse against your children has been spoken into your hearing by the woman who is supposed to be their stepmother, the marriage has crossed a line that nothing — not love, not patience, not the most generous reading possible — can pull it back across.

That was the sentence that put me in the garage for eight hours. The waiting in the garage, the calling of her sons who did not come, the sitting on a concrete floor through a whole afternoon — I described all of that in the chapter before this one. The Bahishti Zewar refusal that the chapter before this one names as the moral hinge of those eight hours: that is also where it belongs. It is the spine that ties this whole period back to the twelve-year-old boy who refused the 1983 wedding. I do not need to retell it here.

What I do need to record in this chapter is what came at the end of those eight hours. At the end of those eight hours, with no one coming, with the words still hanging in the air upstairs, I made the decision. I filed a restraining order. That day.

The fence I had wanted, in filing, was a fence around the words. Not a fence around my body. I had not been physically threatened. I was a man twice her size. I knew, in the part of my mind that calculates such things, that I was not in danger of being struck. What I was in danger of was a curse against my children, spoken aloud, sitting in the house without a fence around it. I wanted a fence. So I filed.
She contested it. That is her right. A good attorney would have advised her to. She went before the judge and gave her version of what had happened in our house.
I did not fight the contest hard.

By the time the contest was before the judge, the marriage was already coming apart in every other dimension. The check was being negotiated. The talaq was being prepared. The divorce, formal and final, was within reach. The fence I had wanted at the moment I filed was being built, more permanently than any court order, by the divorce itself.

So when the judge weighed her contest, I did not push back hard. The hearing was held over Zoom, the way hearings were being held during that period. Both of us on screens. The judge on a screen. I let the truth speak as the truth. The order was vacated. The record reflects no protective order. The record does not reflect — because records do not reflect such things — that a man had filed because a woman had cursed his progeny into the cosmos, and he had wanted, for a moment, to put words from the state of New Jersey around words she had spoken in Urdu.

It cannot. The words remain where they were spoken. The order is vacated and the words are still out there. I let the order go because I had learned, by the time the contest came up, that no piece of paper was going to do what I had wanted that piece of paper to do.
After the garage day, the divorce was inevitable. Whether it took two weeks or two months to formalize was not the question. The question was only who would say the word first.
She said it. Then just give me the divorce. Let's finalize this. Let's go.

There is a kind of person who plays games with the word divorce. They throw it on the table to see what the other person will do. They want to be chased. They want to be begged. They want the partner to break first so they can keep the upper hand. There is a whole sub-language of marriage built around this, and I think most marriages I have watched up close from a distance have a version of it running underneath them.

I do not play that game. I never have. I think the boy who refused to attend Hina's first wedding at twelve and the boy who slept in a stairwell at fifteen and the man who built a flower shop and eleven Edible Arrangements stores has one thing in common across all those versions of himself: he is not bluffing. When he says a thing, he means it. When you say a thing to him, he assumes you mean it.
She said give me the divorce. I said okay.
That was it. There was no negotiation. No three-day cooling-off. No friend pulling us back into a room. She had asked. I had agreed. The word was out in the cosmos.

I called Kamal. Brother Kamal, who had been a steady voice in both our lives, who had tried to speak with her and tried to speak with me before any of this. I told him it was not working. He tried. He did what a good man does when two people he cares about are coming apart. He spoke. He listened. He suggested. He came back. I think — and I am only guessing, because I cannot read another person's heart — that ego got in the way of it on her side. I do not know that for certain. I know that the conversations did not change the direction we were already moving in.

I gave her money. I signed a check. I did the talaq formally — said it, did it in writing, gave her the paper that says this marriage is over and she is free. It was not a happy moment. It is not a happy moment now to write about. But I did not want to carry a burden where there was no goodness left. I did not want her to carry one either. The bridge had been built. She was already most of the way across it. The kindest thing I could do was step aside and let her walk the rest.

She has since gone to friends of mine. I have heard the words. It was a mistake. I do not understand exactly what happened. He is such a nice person. His family is such a nice family. I believe her when she says that now. I believed her then too. People in extremity reach for what they reach for. The thing that is broken in the reaching is usually the thing the person was trying to protect.

I wish her well. I always have. The bridge is hers. She is walking it. The work I did inside those fourteen months was real, and the fact that it could not save the marriage does not mean it was not real. Junaid is a young man. Her family is in Binghamton. The Philadelphia house is rented. The savings exist. Whatever I was supposed to do in her life, it seems I did. Whatever she was supposed to do in mine — I am still working that out.
The bridge is hers. She is walking it.
The work was real, and the fact that the marriage could not survive does not mean the work was not real.
A widower, looking back · on Zahira
— IV —
The Empty House

December 2021 surgery. I do not even remember what it was for. Shahbaaz's marriage in autumn 2022. The two-couples-under-one-roof season. The slow careful plan to find someone, take it slowly, two to three years, possibly never cohabitate. None of that survived August 2023.

After the divorce, I was not actively looking. The talaq was done in July of 2021. I was not, in the months that followed, sitting at a computer scrolling profiles. I was sitting in a house with two of my sons in it. Moaaz and Qurat-ul-Ain (Anna, the name we use) were upstairs, newly married. Shahbaaz was back home after his mother's passing. The household had a shape again, even if the shape was new.
There was a surgery in December of 2021. I do not remember what it was for. That much is true.

Where the mind began to turn, after Zahira was out of the picture, was toward Shahbaaz. My second son. The middle one. The one who gets squeezed in a way only middle sons understand. He was beginning, on and off, to look for a possible spouse. I was bringing him some prospects. He was doing his own search. There were a couple of girls I liked enough to introduce him to. None of mine landed. One of his own did.

Shahbaaz married Zuha in the autumn of 2022. The nikah was in September. The mehndi was in November. The shadi was in December. That marriage got done during the tail of COVID, with all the constraints that came with that, and I did the best I could attending the functions and being there and helping with the communication between the families.

Hina's siblings — her family, my in-laws of thirty years — did not attend my marriage to Zahira. None of them came, though I extended the invitation. I did not expect them to come. It was obvious from the sentiments, or from whatever was in the air, that they would not. For Shahbaaz's wedding, Zarrar came to the nikah. The other Beg siblings did not attend his functions.

The warmth had not been there before Hina's death either, not in the way it should have been, and it was not there in the months after. A piece of what was going on was the Franklin Road property fight — Amina and Karrar on one side over the house, the older three siblings unable to contain it, the manners by which the whole thing was handled. The fight technically resolved before Hina passed. The rupture inside the family did not. The egos remained. The foolishness remained. The stupidity remained.

And underneath the property fight was the older pattern. The pattern was a lifetime habit: the family I am describing never knew how to deal with anything real, anything serious, anything that mattered. Whole lifetimes got spent on the surface — laughing, joking, mocking other people. That was the muscle the family had built. The muscle for substance, for gravity, for grief, for naming the actual thing in the room — that muscle had not been trained. So when a real thing came along, the property fight or the death of a sister, the family did not have a way to meet it. The laughing and joking and mocking kept running, because that is what kept running, but the laughing did not pivot to grief and the joking did not pivot to repair. The pattern did not change because the events demanded it to. The pattern kept being the pattern.

This is not an indictment. It is a description. They are who they are. They had built what they had built. And what they had built was not a vessel that could hold the weight of a sister dying or a brother and sister fighting over a house. So they did what they could, which was mostly to stay scarce. Scarce in the months I needed them. Scarce at the wedding to Zahira. Mostly scarce at Shahbaaz's wedding. Their sister Hina had been the one in that family carrying the substance. Nothing of substance was required of them and nothing of substance was offered. Nothing of gravity. Nothing of meaning. Nothing of grace like Hina, who had been the one carrying all of it.

By January of 2023, my house had two couples in it. Two sons. Two daughters-in-law. It was the closest thing to a structured family I had had since Hina's passing. I was not in their way. The house was big enough. Shahbaaz and Zuha had the master side, their own bathroom, their own space. Moaaz and Anna had the other side, three bedrooms — their own room, an office, a third room they were not really using — and their own bathroom. The kitchen on the first floor was shared. I had the basement. I had my room. I was, in the most literal sense, getting out of their way.

From January through the summer of 2023, I started to think — slowly, and at first only as a thought rather than a plan — that this was the moment when I could begin to look for someone. Not a wife in the old sense. Not someone to bring into this house. Someone to talk to. Coffee once every two weeks. A conversation. A person who had her own life and was not looking to inject herself into mine. Not from the traditional community pattern I had grown up watching — the women who police every other woman's marriage and clothes and spending, who carry the news of one household into the kitchen of the next, who measure their worth by their access to other people's business. Someone professional. Someone independent. Someone whose self-worth came from her own life and not from inserting herself into other people's lives.

The plan was to take it slowly. Two years. Three years. Possibly, eventually, a marriage that did not require us to cohabitate. I had become open, by this point in my life, to the idea that a marriage or a relationship can take many forms — not just the form where the woman moves into your house and your family becomes hers. I had done that form twice. Once for thirty years that had been a true marriage. Once for fourteen months that had not. I was not eager to enter that same shape a third time without being very, very sure of who was on the other side of it.
That was the plan. I was going to start a conversation, take my time, and let the timeline be the timeline.
Then Moaaz and Anna moved out.
The Hotel Bill

First week of messaging. Connecticut. Two children in a hotel that could no longer be paid for. I had not seen her in person. I had not heard her voice. I paid the bill. It felt the right thing to do.

The decision had been seeded earlier. Qurat-ul-Ain — Anna, the name we use — had been applying to jobs at colleges and universities. One of the applications was Rowan, down in the Trenton-Philadelphia area. I had been told it was a possibility — a possibility in the way a son tells his father something when someone else is doing the actual deciding. Because Moaaz is kind. Moaaz is gentle. Moaaz is simple in the deepest meaning of that word — uncomplicated, straightforward, without strategy. He told me it was a possibility because that is what he had been told to tell me, and the person who had decided it was a possibility was the same person who had decided most of the things that were getting decided in their household. Anna was pulling the strings from behind. Moaaz was put out front, where the family could see a face it loved and could not push back against.

I knew this at the time. I did not say it then, because Moaaz is my eldest son and I do not undermine my eldest son in front of his wife or in front of his own face. The story that follows — the empty rooms, the cleaning, the rupture — is going to look like a story about a father and an eldest son. It is partly that. But the wires running underneath it run to a different switchboard, and the honest read on what happened requires naming the switchboard.

By July of 2023 the possibility had become real. By the last week of August they were moving. There was no moving truck. They did the moving themselves, in their own car, in stages, over a stretch of days. I wanted to help. I wanted to be of use. I offered. I was told no. So I watched them go in and out of the house with boxes, doing it the way they had decided to do it, and I sat with what it is what it is. Or better yet: whatever.

That word does a lot of work in the language I have been using inside my own head these last few years. Whatever. It is the word a person reaches for when they have stopped being able to use the word fine. When something is not fine but you also do not have the energy or the standing to fight it. Whatever. A son does not want help moving his life. A daughter-in-law does not want a father-in-law's hands on a box. Whatever.

But things have meaning, if we have a compass. The proper compass. There is a thing ladies do in our households — in many households — that is plain and simple, that is visible to anyone whose eyes are open, that bends the air of a home in a particular direction. The thing has no name in our language because the people who could name it have agreed not to. The question worth asking, the only useful question, is: who is going to name it.

I had not expected the timing. I had expected, vaguely, that the two-couples-under-one-roof season would last another year, maybe two. Long enough for the slow conversation I was having with someone else to take its own time.

By the spring and summer of 2023, I had been messaging with a woman named Kaltoum. We had met on a Muslim matchmaking app. She was in Connecticut. She had two children. She was looking for a husband. Our first interactions were the usual back-and-forth — hi, hello, photographs, the cautious early choreography of two strangers who think there might be something to talk about. The order of what happened next is what matters.

The first thing that happened, before anything else, was that within the first week of our messaging I learned she was in a dire situation. She and her two children — Idriss, her son who was fourteen, and Zoubaida, her daughter who was nine — were not in a home. They were bouncing from hotel to hotel. The current bill had come due and she did not have the money to pay it. A Muslim sister with two children in the streets, in the most literal sense the phrase will bear — no fixed address, the kids' belongings in suitcases, the next night's roof an open question.
I paid the bill.
I paid the bill because it felt the right thing to do. To do some good in the world. That was the whole of it.

A few weeks later she came to New York for paperwork at her consulate. She called me from the consulate and asked if we could have lunch. We met at Maggiano's in Hackensack, at the Riverside Square Mall. That was the first time I saw her in person.
She was lively. She had energy. She took care of herself. She was Moroccan, and that mattered to me. Here is why.

In 2015 I went to Hajj with Brother Kamal — not with the Pakistani groups, not with the Indo-Pak masjid configurations, but with Kamal's group. There I met a Moroccan brother named Hisham. The entire Moroccan group I met that Hajj had a quality I still cannot quite name in English: salt of the earth, easy in their skin, warm without performance, modest without rigidity. The whole Moroccan cultural texture — the mix of East and West, the French inflections of fashion and ease, modesty held inside a larger comfort with the world rather than against it — I had found, on that Hajj, more progressive in the truest sense than most of the cultures I had grown up inside. Not progressive as a political label. Progressive as a description of a culture that could hold tradition and modernity in the same hand without either one strangling the other.
That memory was sitting in me when I met Kaltoum at Maggiano's. The lunch went well. There was good energy. We agreed to keep talking.

The plan we shaped together over the next few weeks was sensible. She was thinking, on her side, that her son Idriss was about to start his freshman year of high school. She wanted to pick a place where she could move and let him do all four years in one school. New Jersey appealed to her — she had heard about it, visited it, knew it had more land and greenery than where she had been. She would come down, get her own apartment, get Idriss and Zoubaida into a school somewhere in North Jersey or a little further west, and we would see what happens. Two separate households. Two separate lives in the same state. A slow conversation conducted on the same time zone instead of across one.

This was not just a hypothetical. The plan was already underway. I was driving up to Connecticut to see her. She was coming down to Jersey. We had begun the apartment search together — I had taken her to look at a couple of places, walked through them with her, helped her think about location and school district and what her kids would need. The slowness I had originally wanted for myself — coffee every two weeks, two to three years — was already, by July, accelerating naturally into the shape of two adults helping each other build a structure they could each live inside separately.
That was the plan. It was a good plan. It was the plan I should have stayed inside.
Then Moaaz and Anna's move-out became real, and the house emptied, and crazy abrar's clock began to run.
— VI —
The Cleaning

I cleaned three empty rooms because I love my son and I wanted to save him a Sunday drive. The cleaning was the spark. The fire it lit had been built up over years from a wood I did not know was stacked against the wall.

By the week Moaaz and Anna were finishing their move-out, Kaltoum and her two children had been living in the basement for about two weeks. They had moved in shortly after our nikah. The basement was their space while the upstairs was still being vacated. The kids were settling into a school routine. Kaltoum was settling into a household. The household, in its quiet way, was already holding two families at once: the one leaving on the second floor, the one settling in below.

The decision to collapse the slow plan had already happened by then. I wrote earlier in this chapter that I jumped. This was the jump. Kaltoum had been showing signs — emotional ups and downs, medication, antidepressants, communication swings, the small moves that do not quite add up to a pattern you can name but accumulate into a feeling in the chest. My small circle of friends had picked up on some of it. There had been suggestions. There had been intuitions, gently offered. I had heard them and set them aside, because I do not know what is wrong with me but I have never been able to look at a person who is struggling and conclude that what they need is to be discarded. I had not been able to do it at fifteen when I was the one struggling. I had not been able to do it for Hina when Hina was the one who had been broken. I was not going to start doing it now.

So instead of letting Kaltoum move into her own apartment somewhere in North Jersey as we had been planning together, the both of us made the decision that she and Idriss and Zoubaida would move into my house. Into the basement first, with the rest of the second floor opening up as Moaaz and Anna moved out. We collapsed two timelines into one. We turned the slow plan into a fast plan. We did it because the logistics presented themselves and because crazy abrar's clock was already running and because, somewhere in me, I had decided that another woman with two children in distress was not going to wait a year and a half for me to be ready.
The day I am about to describe is the day all of this collapsed into a single afternoon.

Moaaz and Anna had been moving for days. Carload after carload — furniture, boxes, the smaller things — done by the two of them in their own vehicle, no help asked for, none accepted. They were essentially done. Eighty miles south, their new apartment was filling up. The Teaneck house, on their side of the second floor, was emptying out.

What remained in those three rooms — Anna's office, the small middle room they had been using mostly as empty storage, their own bedroom — was the kind of straggler material that gets left behind at the tail end of every move. Pens. Pencils. Batteries. Rubber bands. Loose change. A stapler. Some papers nobody knew what to do with. Knickknacks scattered across desks and shelves. Nothing personal. Nothing intimate. Nothing emotional. They had picked through and taken what they wanted. What was left was, in the simplest description, garbage.

Moaaz called me. He told me they were essentially finished but there was this little bit of stuff he wanted to come back and clean up. He asked if it would be okay if he came back the following Sunday to handle it. Sure, of course, I said. It is not a problem. There is no deadline. Whatever you want to do.

After the call, I went upstairs to look at the three rooms. Kaltoum came with me. The kids were downstairs in the basement, in their own space. We walked into the rooms together. What we saw was what Moaaz had described on the phone — the straggler stuff, scattered. Pens. Stapler. Batteries. Loose change. A little bit of mess.

We started cleaning. Kaltoum worked alongside me. Two adults in a house that was emptying and filling at the same time, doing the work of three rooms that needed to be ready. Together we gathered the loose items into two or three boxes — two or three boxes, not bags of personal effects, not anything intimate. Boxes of leftover small items. We vacuumed the rooms. We dusted. I carried the boxes downstairs and put them in the garage, where Moaaz would see them the moment he pulled in on Sunday and would know without asking that the stuff he was coming back for was waiting for him, dry, organized, ready to be picked up or thrown out at his discretion.
What I was thinking, while we were doing this, matters — because the misunderstanding that came next turns on it.

I was thinking: My son has a long drive on Sunday. He is moving into a new apartment with his wife. He has work. He has a life. He has been doing this move for two weeks straight and he is tired. If I can save him one Sunday trip back up here for a job that takes us an hour, I should do it. I was not thinking I was invading their space. I was not thinking I was going into their belongings. I was not even in their belongings in any meaningful sense — the belongings were gone. I was cleaning a room that was no longer their room. I was cleaning a room that, in the calculus of a household, had reverted back to being part of the house I owned and lived in.

I was not in great physical shape doing it. I had pulled my Achilles a few weeks earlier and I could not walk too well. Kaltoum carried more than her share. We finished the work, came downstairs, I poured myself some iced tea, and sat down to rest.
Then I called Moaaz.

Just wanted to let you know, I said. I went through the rooms. Kaltoum helped me. We cleaned them up. We tightened it up. I made a couple of boxes. I put them in the garage. So when you come, whenever you want to come, you don't have to worry. The stuff is here for you.
There was a pause.
Okay, Abu, he said.

Something switched. I heard it in his voice on the word okay. The first okay was a son's okay to a father who has just done him a small kindness. The second part of the sentence — Abu — was already a different word, said by a different version of him, after some signal I could not see had passed across the room he was standing in.
We hung up.
Three minutes later he called back. His voice was curt and short. We're coming up. I had never, in his entire life, heard him use that tone with me. We'll be there in a little bit.

An hour later they pulled into the driveway. They walked into the garage. The looks on their faces were not happy. They were annoyed. Set jaw. Hard eyes. They looked at the boxes I had so carefully organized in the garage, and the boxes were now, in some way I could not understand, evidence of something.

Anna did not say salaam. She walked past me. She walked straight upstairs, alone, to go look at the rooms. To check what I had done. To verify with her own eyes that what she had been told had happened had in fact happened.
Moaaz sat down in the living room and called Shahbaaz over. I need to speak with you guys.

He was furious. The fury was directed at me. I told you I would be back on Sunday. You went and you did this anyway. This is the problem. You don't keep your word. This is just what you do. You couldn't wait two days. You couldn't wait.
I let him speak.

I did not interrupt. I did not argue. I did not raise my voice. I did what I do when something is happening in front of me that does not match any picture of reality I recognize. I sat back. I crossed my legs. I leaned back into the couch.

Shahbaaz, sitting next to him, may have noticed the posture. He has known me long enough to read my body. The crossing of the legs and the leaning back is, in our family, a particular gesture. It means: I am no longer in this conversation as a participant. I am in it as a witness. I am observing what is happening in front of me and I am not going to dignify it by entering it.
What I was saying to them inside my head, while sitting back and crossing my legs and not opening my mouth, was this:

Are you fucking serious. Are you out of your fucking mind. This. This is what you want to talk about. This is what you will call your brother over to discuss. For fifteen years — the entire duration of your adult lives so far — I have been begging and pleading for you boys to call a meeting. To sit down together. To plan. To improve the communication. To talk about the family. To take the assets and the work we have built and build on top of them. To make choices. To make decisions. To move things forward. I have been asking for this since you were old enough to be asked. And in those same fifteen years, what have I been watching. I have been watching you sleep until one in the afternoon. I have been watching you not take the reins between yourselves when no ladies were even on the scene. I have been watching you stay oblivious to what was happening with the in-laws back in 2018, oblivious to what had been happening for years before that, oblivious to the fact that your father had lost his wife and was holding the household up alone. I have been watching you fail to see what your mother and I were — what we are — what your mother gave you and what is still owed back. And the first time in fifteen god damn years that you finally call your brother and sit him down for a serious conversation across a coffee table — it is because somebody touched somebody's goat.

That is a phrase from our language. In Punjabi it sounds different than it does in English. Kisi ne tumhari bakri ko haath laga diya. Someone touched your goat. It is the phrase people use when a person becomes furious about something that is, in any honest measurement, nothing. The goat is fine. The goat has not been harmed. The goat is standing exactly where the goat was standing before. But someone has touched it and now we are at war.

In Punjabi the phrase carries a particular flavor — half mockery, half exhaustion, the way a tired uncle might say it about two cousins who have not spoken for six months because of something neither of them can really articulate. In English it sounds like a non-sequitur. In Punjabi it sounds like a diagnosis.
I did not say any of this out loud.

What I said out loud, when Moaaz had finished and was looking at me waiting for a response, was very little. Maybe nothing. I do not remember. I remember the crossing of the legs and the leaning back, and I remember Shahbaaz's eyes on me, and I remember the absolute clarity in my own chest that this was a moment I was not going to enter on the terms it was being offered.
They left. The rupture began that day.
Fifteen years of begging you to call a meeting
about something that mattered.
The first time you finally do —
it is because somebody touched somebody's goat.
Internal · what I did not say out loud
— VII —
Three Incidents

Three things that happened in the months Anna lived in our house. I felt the weight of them at the time. I knew. I had been knowing for months. The washing machine. The donkey. The picture frame. Each one a piece of the price.

Three things happened in the months Anna lived in our house. I did not need hindsight to feel them. I felt the weight of them at the time. I knew what they were. I had been knowing for months. That is the price of meaning. That is the price of conscience. That is the price of caring deeply. That is the price that needs to be paid for life. You do not get to live a life that means something and also be spared the moments when the meaning shows you what it costs.
The washing machine.

There were days when Anna had a load of her clothes in the washing machine, and someone else in the house needed to do a load. On one of those days, it was me that needed to do the load. The reasonable thing, in any household, is to move the finished clothes to the dryer or to a basket and use the machine.

That is not what happened. If anyone reached toward Anna's clothes, she panicked. The panic was real and immediate. It would send Moaaz running from wherever he was in the house, into the laundry room, to stop whoever was about to touch what should not be touched.

It was clothes. In a washing machine. In a family home. Anything even slightly suggestive of sexuality, in the world Anna had inherited, gets converted into one thousand percent sexual. A wet shirt is no longer a wet shirt. An undergarment, even unseen, even still under other clothes, becomes a charged object that no male relative in the household can be permitted to come near, including a father-in-law of years in his own house.

We were not in 1930 in Jalandhar. We were in Teaneck in 2023, in a country whose actual surrounding culture is twenty times more exposed than anything the panic was guarding against. Billboards. Television. Workplaces. The actual culture outside our front door does not whisper about underwear; it sells it on building-sized advertisements. And inside our house, in the same week the world outside was doing all of that, a daughter-in-law's washing machine had become a checkpoint. The panic did not match the environment. The panic was inherited.
The donkey.

Moaaz was carrying boxes from the second floor down to the basement. He was making trip after trip. I watched him for a while and I asked him — three times, four times — Yo, Moaaz, can I give you a hand? You need a hand? Each time he said no. He had it. He wanted to do it himself.

I was not in great physical shape. I had pulled my Achilles a few weeks earlier and I was not walking well. But I could have helped with the lighter loads. I also said to him please, ask your brother. Get Shahbaaz down here. Let him help you. He said no to that too. I got it. I got it. I'm almost done.
A short while later Anna came to me, separately, and said she did not appreciate Moaaz being used like a donkey. The work, in her telling, was being dumped on him. He was doing it by himself.

I had asked him three or four times. He had refused three or four times. I had specifically suggested Shahbaaz. He had refused that too. The thing I had actually done was the thing any father does when he sees his son working — offer help, repeatedly, and accept the son's right to say no. The thing I was being told I had done was something else entirely.
I did not argue. There is no arguing with this. Whatever had reached Anna's ears was not the events of the afternoon. It was a frame the afternoon was being fitted into.
The picture frame.
In Moaaz and Anna's bedroom, on the wall, was a picture frame with a printed message: Smile, you're on camera.

I did not know it was there. I had never been in their room. Since my children were small I have never gone into their rooms, never opened their phones, never read their computers. Their mother — Hina — would sometimes do that, and would occasionally come to me with something. I did not. I respected the space. Maybe that was a foolish thing. Maybe at fourteen I had the right. But it was not in me.
