So I did not see the frame. But Zahira had seen it. At some point during her time in the house — I never knew when, I was never told — she had been in Moaaz and Anna's room. Sometime later, in the period when our own marriage was coming apart, she began accusing me of installing cameras throughout the house to record her. You have cameras in here. You are watching me.

I was bewildered. What are you talking about? I do not have cameras in this house. I have cameras in the stores and I never even watch those — my managers want them, my managers install them. I am not the kind of person who watches people on screens.

I did not understand the accusation until much later, when the picture frame surfaced and I realized what had happened. Zahira had walked into a bedroom that was not hers. She had seen Smile, you're on camera on the wall. She had not asked. She had not checked. She had treated a piece of dorm-room décor as forensic evidence of a watching male presence in the house. And then she had carried that evidence into our arguments without ever raising it as a question.

Two women under the same roof at different times, neither of them in conversation with each other, each one converting an ordinary object into a different kind of male threat, each one routing the conversion through me.
Three incidents. The clothes. The boxes. The picture frame. What they add up to is in the next section.
— VIII —
What They Add Up To

A culture sitting under our households. Three waters: Hindu cultural inheritance, colonialist Islam, and the older fact that men are not pristine. The Bahishti Zewar is one artifact of this water, not its source. The work is to name it, not to fight it from grievance.
The thing I am about to name is not one thing. It is several things stacked on top of each other over a long period of time, and the names matter.

There is, in our community, a culture. By our community I mean the Indo-Pak Muslim community I grew up in and that my parents and in-laws grew up in before that. By culture I do not mean Islam. I mean the cultural water Islam has been sitting in, in our part of the world, for a very long time.

Some of that water comes from Hinduism. The Muslim communities of the Indian subcontinent did not live next door to Hindu civilization for a thousand years and emerge untouched. Concepts about purity, about women's bodies, about the ritual fear of contamination — these are not Quranic concepts in their indigenous form, but they entered our households and put on Muslim clothes and stayed for centuries. By the time my grandparents were children, the difference between Islamic and cultural was difficult to see from inside the household. Most people did not try to see it.

Some of that water comes from what I have called, in earlier chapters, the colonialist Islam — the version of the religion that adapted itself, often without noticing, to the conditions of being a colonized people. A colonized people becomes obsessed with the small. The small policing of women's bodies. The small policing of dress. The small management of who looks at whom and how. When the large things are out of your hands — your government, your economy, your military, your dignity — the small things become the territory on which a community proves to itself that it still has authority. The women's bodies in the household become the last battlefield because they are the only battlefield left.

And some of the water is not specifically Muslim and not specifically subcontinental. It is older than that. Men are not, as a category, pristine creatures. There are things in the human heart — male and female both, but I will speak about the male side because I am one — that propagate this kind of culture wherever it grows. Possessiveness disguised as protection. Surveillance disguised as care. The conversion of every neutral act into a sexual one. These things are not unique to any one community. They are human things. Naming them as cultural is partly accurate and partly an evasion. They are also human.

So when I look at the washing machine and the donkey and the picture frame, I do not see a single book operating on a single household. I see all three of these waters meeting in the bodies of two women who did not know they were carrying them, in a house in New Jersey in 2023, with a father-in-law trying to live in it without understanding why the air was so thick.

I have a name for what runs in that current, but a name is just a name. There is a cultural water that the Indo-Pak Muslim community of the subcontinent has been sitting in for a very long time. Some of it is Hindu in origin — the purity reflex, the contamination reflex, the conversion of every neutral object into a charged one. Some of it is what I have called, in earlier chapters, colonialist Islam — the obsession with the small policing of women's bodies and clothes and movement, which is the territory a colonized people retreat to when the larger territories have been taken from them. And some of it is older than that and not specific to us at all. Men, as a category, are not pristine. There are things in the human heart that produce possessiveness disguised as protection, surveillance disguised as care. These things are human before they are cultural. Naming them only as cultural would be an evasion.

The Bahishti Zewar, which I have named earlier in this memoir, is one artifact of this water. It is not the source. The water was there before that book was written. The book is one of many books that gave the water a form, and there are Hindu books and colonial-era guides that gave it a form too. I name the Bahishti Zewar because it was the one that touched Hina's family directly and the one I refused at twelve. But to call it the source would be too clean. It is one channel of something larger.

To my children, and to anyone else's children who read this: do not take any of this from me as a finished idea. A seed from another person is just a seed. The seed has to be owned through your own effort, your own observation, your own research, your own awareness, your own practice. Live your life from a certain perspective — with awareness — and when things happen around you, you will begin to see the epistemology of them and the source of them. You will start to feel, before you can articulate, when something happening in the room is not really about the room. When the washing-machine panic is not really about the washing machine. When the donkey accusation is not really about labor. When the camera in a picture frame is not really about cameras.

The work is not to fight these things from grievance. The work is to know they exist and to know where they come from. To know that they entered our households long before any of us were born. To know that some of them are Hindu in origin and some of them are colonial and some of them are simply human, and that the inheritance is mixed and the responsibility is ours.

I do not blame Anna. I do not blame Zahira. I do not blame the women in my family or in Hina's family who carried different versions of this water in their own bodies through their own lives. The blame question is not the useful one. The useful question is whether the people who inherit this — my children, their children, the next generation of cousins — will know enough to recognize it when it shows up. And whether someone in the room, when it shows up, will be willing to name it. Plain and simple. Who is going to name it.

Hina and I were a bit different. We built a household that did not run on this current. Not because we were superior to the people we came from — that is not the point and it is not true — but because we had each, on our own, made decisions long before we were married that put us on a different path. Hina refused the line she came from in her own quiet way, every day of her life, by being who she was — the radiance, the grace, the way of holding a room without ever raising her voice. I refused it in the loud way at twelve, in 1983, on the day of her first wedding. The two refusals met in 1989 and built a marriage that ran on different water. Our children were raised in that water. That is the air they breathed for thirty years. When Anna came into our house, she came carrying a different water, and the difference between the two waters was the thing that showed up in the washing machine, in the boxes, in the picture frame, and eventually in the eighteen months of silence with Moaaz.
Late is better than never. What I can still do with the time I have left is leave a record: this is what was in the water. Drink carefully. Filter it. Pass on what is clean.
— IX —
Kaltoum

A formal nikah, larger and more public than the one with Zahira. The ring Kaltoum wanted. The wedding she had not gotten the first time. Her family surprised by what it was. The third time under the canopy. Events are easy. The daily work after the event is where we came up short.

My nikah to Kaltoum was done formally, larger and more public than the one I had done with Zahira three years before. Kaltoum wanted it that way. She wanted the ring she had not had in her first marriage. She wanted the wedding she had not had. She wanted the public moment that says this happened, this is real, this is being witnessed. I understood why. A woman who has carried two children from hotel to hotel does not want her next marriage to be a quiet thing done in a corner. She wants it on a record, with people in the room, with the ceremony given its proper weight.

So we did it that way. Formally. Publicly. With the proper functions. Done in the Moroccan and Pakistani-blended way that her family and mine could each recognize. Her family was surprised, on the day, by what it was — they had not expected something that formal, that arranged, that fully hosted. I had set it up that way on purpose. If we were going to do it, we were going to do it right. That is what I do. The event side of things, I know how to do. I have been doing events for thirty years — weddings, openings, holidays, milestones. The event is the part I can hold.

Underneath the event, though, something else was happening. The event was real and the photographs are real and the ring is real and the witnesses were there. But the event is not the marriage. The marriage is what comes after the event — the daily work, the slow, unphotographed, unwitnessed work of two people learning each other, building something steady, doing the hundred small things that a marriage actually consists of. The wedding day is a single day. The marriage is the ten thousand days after.
We were good at the wedding day. We came up short on the ten thousand days.

That is the honest summary of the whole chapter. Across three marriages, across thirty-some years of trying, the place where I have done my best work has been the public, structured, observable layer. The event. The function. The bridge built. The hotel bill paid. The wedding hosted properly. The rooms cleaned. These are the things that can be done in an afternoon, a day, a week. They have edges. You can finish them and step back and see that they are done.

The daily work does not have edges. The daily work of a marriage is the asking-how-was-your-day every day for ten years. It is the sitting-quietly-together. It is the noticing-the-small-thing-and-saying-the-small-thing. It is the keeping-of-tempers-low when something annoying happens. It is the showing-up-to-be-known and being-willing-to-know. That work has no event around it. There is no hall, no music, no videographer. It is just two people in a kitchen, in a car, in a bed, doing the unphotographed thing.

With Hina, the daily work happened. Not because either of us was particularly good at it — I do not think I was — but because Hina was who she was, and she carried more than her share, and her water was the water of substance. With Zahira, the daily work did not happen, because the chatter ate it. With Kaltoum, the daily work also did not happen, but for a different reason. The reason is one of the long topics of the chapter after this one. The short version is that I had not built the stillness in me to do it. I was still in motion. The shark cannot stop swimming. The water in front of me was Kaltoum and her kids and a new household, and so I swam into it.

I knew, the night of the nikah, that this was not the marriage I should have entered on the timeline I entered it on. I knew it the way a person knows things underneath the level of articulation. I knew it and I went forward anyway, because the going forward was already in motion and stopping the going forward would have required a kind of stillness inside me that I did not yet have.

By the time Moaaz and Anna were finishing their move-out, Kaltoum and her two children — Idriss, fourteen, and Zoubaida, nine — had been living in the house for about two weeks. They were in the basement at that point. The basement was Kaltoum's space while the upstairs sorted itself out. The kids had their things down there. Their school routines were beginning. The household was already, in its quiet way, holding two families at once: the one that was leaving on the second floor and the one that was settling in below.

So the rupture I described in Section VI did not happen on Kaltoum's arrival day. It happened with her and the kids already in the house. When Moaaz and Anna pulled into the driveway that Sunday afternoon, Kaltoum was downstairs. Idriss and Zoubaida were downstairs. They heard what they heard. They saw what they saw. The new household witnessed the rupture of the old household from the basement of the same house.

That stillness, when it eventually came, came years later, and the cost of not having it yet was paid in the years between. Some of that cost was paid by Kaltoum. Some of it was paid by Idriss and Zoubaida. Some of it was paid by my own children. Some of it was paid by me. The full ledger of who paid what is a long ledger, and not all of it belongs in this chapter. Some of it belongs in the chapter after this one, when the stores started closing.
A du'a · for the one entering what he is not ready for
رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي
Rabbi’shraḥ lī ṣadrī wa yassir lī amrī.
My Lord, expand for me my chest, and ease for me my affair.

Surah Ta-Ha 20:25–26. The du'a of Musa alayhi'l-salam, before going to face Pharaoh. The man who is sent into something he did not choose and cannot refuse. I made this du'a many times in the period this chapter describes. The chest did not always expand. The affair was not always eased. But the asking was honest, and the asking is part of the record.
The Door That Stayed Closed

For eighteen months Moaaz and I did not speak. Then it was longer than eighteen months. The wound did not close inside this chapter. The chapter ends with a father, in a house that has Kaltoum and Idriss and Zoubaida in it now, looking at a phone that does not ring.

The chapter did not close on a wedding night and did not close on a moving day. It closed on the slow recognition, over the months that followed, that the rupture with Moaaz was not going to heal on its own.

For the first few weeks after the cleaning afternoon, I expected the silence to break. I expected Moaaz, given a little time, to call. He did not. I expected Anna, given a little space, to soften. She did not. I expected — because this is what I had expected for the first fifty years of my life — that the family would do what families do, which is bend back toward each other after a misunderstanding small enough to be embarrassed about.
The family did not bend back.

I asked Shahbaaz, more than once, to talk to his brother. He did. The talks did not produce a return. I asked my eldest brother Basit to talk to his nephew. He did. The talks did not produce a return. I asked because I have, by my own admission, an inability to articulate what this rupture actually was. I do not think Moaaz had the ability to articulate it either. We were two men of the same blood, both of us reasonable in most of our other relationships, both of us unable to find words for what had happened between us in a living room one Sunday afternoon over a box of pens and batteries.
So we said nothing. For eighteen months. Eventually for longer than eighteen months.
The silence is the end of this chapter. The silence did not resolve cleanly, and the chapter ends on the silence, not on a resolution.

I cleaned three empty rooms because I love my son and I wanted to save him a Sunday drive. The cleaning of those rooms was the spark. The fire it lit had been built up over years from a wood I did not know was stacked against the wall — the inheritance, the cultural water, the three waters of Section VIII. The fire was not really about the rooms. The fire was about everything that had been waiting for an excuse to burn.

I do not regret the cleaning. I would do it again. If I am sitting in a house and my son has a long drive ahead of him and there are three rooms that need an hour of work, I am going to do the hour of work. That is who I am. That is what Hina married. That is what raised those boys. To regret the cleaning would be to regret the man, and I am not going to do that, even for a son I have not spoken to in over a year.
But I do hold this in my chest, and I hold it as I write this chapter, and I will hold it until the day Moaaz reads these words or the day I die, whichever comes first:

I miss my son. I miss the version of our relationship that existed before that afternoon. I miss the calls. I miss the casual presence. I miss being able to say Moaaz into a phone and have Moaaz answer on the other end with the voice he had used with me since he was old enough to talk.

The chapter does not end with reconciliation. The chapter ends with a father, in a house that has Kaltoum and Idriss and Zoubaida in it now and not Moaaz and Anna, sitting with his iced tea in the kitchen and looking at a phone that does not ring. With a man at fifty-two understanding that the cost of being the kind of man he is, and has always been, is sometimes paid in eighteen months of silence from an eldest son. With a witness who has decided to record the cost without pretending it was worth less than it was.
This is who I am. This is what it cost. This is the chapter.
I do not regret the cleaning.
I would do it again.
To regret the cleaning would be to regret the man.
A father, looking at a phone that does not ring
