title: Chapter Eleven — The Stores Close (2022–2025)
paragraphs: The Stores Close

Eleven stores down to two. A heart that finally said enough. The mother and the daughter, two peas in a pod, and the mercy of the order in which Allah took them. A one-person journey, made by a man Allah built for it.
Part III — Rupture & Collapse
Walima Son
opening couplet · written 2018
Son you might win some,
but you just lost one.
May this defeat be sweeter than victory.

There is a thing that happens to a man who has spent thirty years building. The buildings start to come down. Not because he is doing the wrong things. Because the wrong things were done earlier, by him and by the world around him, and the bill comes due on its own schedule, and the schedule does not consult the builder.

This chapter is about the years the buildings came down. Eleven Edible Arrangements stores down to two. A flower shop already passed to other hands. Personal guarantees signed long ago, finally calling in what they had been quietly accumulating. A house still standing, with Kaltoum and Idriss and Zoubaida inside it, and a daughter four years unreached. A heart, in the middle of all of it, that gave out twice in November of 2025 and was put back together by people whose names I no longer remember and who do not remember mine. Silhouettes. That is what they were. That is what I was to them. That is life.
The Couplet

Son you might win some. But you just lost one. The couplet at the top of this chapter was written in 2018, before any of the stores had closed, before the heart attacks, before Moaaz stopped calling. It was a father’s line to his sons. It is the line this chapter is written underneath.

The piece is called Walima Son. I wrote it in 2018. Two lines at the top of a longer set of verses that did not all survive into anything finished. The couplet did. The couplet was the thing I kept coming back to, in the way a man comes back to a piece of his own writing when life keeps proving it true.
Son you might win some, but you just lost one. May this defeat be sweeter than victory.

I did not know, when I wrote it, what I was naming. I thought I was naming a small thing: a moment in a young man’s life when something he had counted as a win turns out, on second look, to have been a loss. The kind of correction every father wants his sons to make for themselves before the world makes it for them.

By the end of 2025 the couplet had grown into something bigger. I had lost more than I had counted on losing. Four stores in three years. A relationship with my eldest son measured in months and then in years of distance — the kind where the small talk holds and the deeper conversation does not. A daughter unreached for four years. A second wife in 2021. A heart that gave out in November. The list was longer than the couplet, and the couplet was still doing its work underneath it.
May this defeat be sweeter than victory.

That line is not a man pretending the losses do not hurt. It is a man asking that the losses be put to use. That what comes out of the losing be worth more than what would have come out of the winning. That is a particular kind of prayer. It is the prayer of a man who knows he is no longer in the part of life where things will keep accumulating. He is in the part where things will keep leaving, and the question is what he will be left holding when they are gone.
The chapter is the answer to that question, as much of an answer as I have so far.
— II —
The Stores, In Order

Fort Lee, December 2022. Midland Park, December 2023. Pompton Lakes, March 2025. Westwood, November 2025. Four stores in three years. Eleven down to two. Each one came off a different shelf in the same building, and each one took with it a piece of what I had thought I was.

Edible Arrangements began for me in 2001, with the franchise agreement signed in June and the first store opening in 2002 at 350 Main Street in Hackensack. Over the years that followed, I built up to eleven stores. The expansion went through Bergen County and Passaic County and into Rockland and other markets. Each store had its own personality, its own staff, its own holiday rhythm, its own complications.

For most of those twenty years I did not have a financial structure underneath the operation that was as strong as the operation itself. I had built fast. I had relied on cash flow. I had signed personal guarantees, because that is how a small operator gets a lease and a loan when he is starting out, and once you sign one or two of them you stop counting. The signatures pile up in a drawer. They sit there quietly until the day the operation slows down and the signatures begin to speak.

By 2022 the operation had slowed. COVID had been hard on the model. Labor costs had risen. The fruit costs had risen. Delivery economics had shifted. The smaller stores that had been marginally profitable in 2018 were now marginally unprofitable in 2022. The math was not subtle. The math was telling me, store by store, what could be carried and what could not.

Fort Lee, December 2022. The first one to close. Fort Lee had been a difficult store for a long time. The rent was high. The traffic was good but the conversion was not. We closed it at the end of the year, the way you close a store: notify the staff, hand back the keys, satisfy what could be satisfied with the landlord, walk away from what could not. The personal guarantee on that lease was something I would deal with later.

Midland Park, December 2023. A year later, almost to the day. Midland Park was a smaller store in a smaller town. It had been doing its job for years — not a strong performer, but steady. By 2023 the steadiness was gone. It closed the same way Fort Lee had closed, with the same set of motions, the same set of conversations, the same set of papers.

Pompton Lakes, March 2025. The third one. Pompton Lakes had been my own. I had opened it. I had hired the staff. I had spent years driving up to it. When it closed I drove up one last time, walked through it, and drove home. Some closings are louder than others. Pompton Lakes was a quiet one. The quiet was its own weight.

Westwood, November 2025. The fourth one. Westwood closed in the same week as the surgery and the heart attacks. The two events were not connected on paper but they were connected in the room where I was standing during both of them. I will write about Westwood again in Section V, because the timing matters.
Eleven stores down to two. Hackensack and Pearl River are what remain. They are smaller. They are leaner. They are not what I had built. They are what could be saved.

That is the operational summary. The numerical version is the kind of thing that goes in a P&L spreadsheet, and there is a P&L spreadsheet, and at some point in a later draft of this chapter I will put one of the actual P&Ls in the page so a reader can see what a store closing looks like in numbers. The cost of goods. The labor. The rent line. The royalty line to the franchisor. The net at the bottom that started positive in 2018 and walked itself down through 2020 and 2021 and 2022 until it went under. That is the visible part of the closing. The invisible part is what the closing did to the man who had been carrying it.
— III —
The Letter the Day Before

November 15, 2025. Ten in the evening, Saturday. A letter to the sons and to Younes about generations and the shifting of weight onto men. I sent it. The next day, Sunday, the heart attacks began. The letter sat unanswered on the day my body almost did not come back.

On November 15, 2025, at 10:19 PM, I sent a letter to my sons and to Younes — the young man who became, over years, a kind of semi-adopted son and a steady friend to our family. The letter was a few pages long. It was not about the stores. It was not about the heart. I did not yet know about the heart. The letter was about something else that had been working its way through me for a while: the way the burden of holding the social fabric of a family had quietly shifted, over my generation and my parents’ generation, off the shoulders of the women in our families and onto the men.

I wrote that this was not a complaint, and not an indictment, and not a thing to lay blame for. It was just an observation. The women in our families, going back to grandmothers and great-grandmothers, had once been the ones who kept the relationships alive, kept the connections going, kept the sense of belonging warm in the rooms they walked through. Over time that role had eroded. The work had not gone away. The work had moved. The men of my generation, and increasingly the men of my sons’ generation, were carrying it now, often without knowing they were carrying it. You and we — men — are paying a dear price for this. I dealt with it with your mother and then subsequent wives. It is not to lay blame, it is so you and the next generations understand the actual super hero efforts that are expected and required of you, while the women spectate.

I wrote that we should not beat ourselves up about it too much, because the burden was real and unavoidable, and Allah knew every intention and every effort. I wrote that we had to keep trying. I wrote that gratitude must never fade. I wrote that we had been born into families of decency, faith, and goodness, and that even when we fell short we remained on the side of striving for what is right — fighting the good fight, as best we can.
And then, at the end, I wrote the part of the letter that had been the actual reason for writing it:

Since childhood, one thing that has always troubled me — in our family and community — is how we tend to avoid dealing with things openly. We carry unspoken expectations, assumptions, and disappointments. I’ve seen how that silence can create pain, misunderstanding, and distance between people who actually love one another. Covert expectations and supposed understandings cannot be allowed to fester.

That was the heart of it. The thing I had been writing toward my whole adult life. The thing the previous ten chapters of this memoir have been, in their own way, trying to name. The covert. The unsaid. The understandings that everyone is supposed to have absorbed by osmosis and nobody is supposed to articulate. The structure of silence that allows people who love each other to live in the same house for years without speaking the thing that is actually in the room.

I closed the letter with a line about how, if Allah had allowed me to make one contribution, perhaps it was to help bring these hidden things to the surface. To make us see and face ourselves, even when it was uncomfortable. Perhaps that was my small role, despite my many shortcomings and missteps. I signed it Aboo.
I sent it at 10:19 PM on November 15. I sent some related forwards from earlier in the week. I went to bed.

The next day — November 16 — the heart attacks came. The first one at seven-thirty in the evening, after a salat ul tasbih in the morning that I had not prayed in ten years and a dinner with Kaltoum that ended in a ring-around-rosy conversation. The second one at five in the morning, in a hospital bed. The full account of what happened is in the next section. What matters here is the proximity of the letter to the attack. November 15, 10:19 PM, sent. November 16, the body broke. Twenty-some hours between them.

The letter, when I came back to it weeks later, had not been answered. There was no reply from Moaaz. There was no reply from Shahbaaz. Younes had replied with care, as Younes always does. My brothers and sister had received the related forwards and the tone of their responses, where there were responses, was reasonable and steady. But the central letter — the one written the day before my heart stopped working — sat unanswered by the people it had been most addressed to.

I do not include this to assign fault. I include it because it is the texture of the time. A father in his fifties writing a letter to his sons about the weight men are carrying, sending it twenty hours before his body confirmed the weight, and waking up after surgery to the same distance from the deeper conversation that had been there for years and was there still.
Covert expectations and supposed understandings
cannot be allowed to fester.
From the letter sent November 15, 2025, 10:19 PM
— IV —
The Heart

November 16, 2025. Salat ul tasbih, two and a half hours alone with God, the first time in ten years. Dinner with Kaltoum. The ring-around-rosy conversation. The first heart attack at seven-thirty in the evening. Drove myself to the hospital. The second attack at five in the morning. Angioplasty through the wrist. The surgeon they wanted to send me to was the one who had operated on Hina in 2019. I refused. Found another. The open-heart surgery was about ten days later, right around Thanksgiving. I did not announce it. I went about my business. Allah built me for a one-person journey through this life. That is how it has always been.

November 16, 2025. The heart attacks happened on that day. I know the date because I have gone back and checked it. The texture of the day is what I want to write down here, while the texture is still close enough to the surface to be recovered.

That morning I prayed salat ul tasbih. The salat ul tasbih is a long prayer — some accounts of it run two and a half hours, which is how long mine ran. It is the prayer of glorification, said with three hundred repetitions of the tasbih distributed across the rakats. I had not prayed it in ten years. Something in me had wanted to pray it that day and I had gone with the wanting. Two and a half hours alone with God. The first time in ten years that I had given Allah anything close to two and a half uninterrupted hours of my body and my breath.

I did not know, when I was praying it, what it was preparing me for. A man who is given a long conversation with Allah in the morning before a long conversation with his own mortality in the evening is being given something. I do not pretend to know exactly what. But the two and a half hours were not coincidence and I will not write them as if they were.

That evening I went to dinner with Kaltoum. It was a normal dinner. After dinner she initiated what I have come to call, privately, the ring-around-rosy conversation. Anyone who has been married long enough knows the shape of it without needing the details. It is the conversation that does not have a destination. It circles. It picks up a grievance, sets it down, picks up another one, refers back to a third, returns to the first, sets that one down again, picks up a fourth. There is no exit. The conversation is not designed to have an exit. The conversation is the exercise itself.

The first heart attack came at seven-thirty in the evening, right after that conversation. I do not draw a clean cause-and-effect line between the conversation and the attack — bodies do not work that cleanly — but the timing is the timing and the record is the record.

I drove myself to the hospital. That is not a heroic line and I do not write it as one. I drove myself because driving myself was what was in front of me. There was no parade. There was no convoy. There was a man with chest pain getting in his car and going where the chest pain told him to go. Allah built me, somewhere along the way, for the one-person journey. The journey was not modified that night by the chest pain. The journey was just being the journey it had always been.

I was admitted. They began the workup. At five in the morning, while I was already in the hospital bed, the second heart attack came. The hospital handled it the way hospitals handle these things, which is competently and without ceremony.

That morning they did an angioplasty through the wrist. I was sedated. After the angioplasty, while I was still under, they told me what they had seen and what they needed to do. The damage required open-heart surgery. Immediately. They wanted to send me to Hackensack Medical Center to the cardiac surgeon there.
I recognized the name.

It was the name of the surgeon who had done my wife’s surgery in 2019. The surgery that had not, ultimately, saved her. I do not blame him for that. Hina’s passing was Allah’s qadr and the surgeon had done the work he was capable of doing. But I was not going to put my body, on a sedated morning in a hospital bed, on the table of the same surgeon who had been the last hands on my wife. I do not have a fully articulable reason for that refusal. I have a refusal. The refusal was clear and immediate, even with the sedation still moving through me.
I said no. I checked myself out. I went home and made the calls that needed to be made to secure a different surgeon, with a different team, at a different hospital.

The open-heart surgery happened on November 24 or 25, 2025 — right around Thanksgiving. About nine or ten days after the first attack. By then the right team had been found, the scheduling had been done, the paperwork had been completed. The surgery itself I do not remember in any detail. I remember being prepped. I remember the lights. I remember waking up. The hours in between are not in my memory and they do not need to be.

The names of the people who did the surgery I no longer remember. I saw them written somewhere afterward and then I did not retain them. They were silhouettes. That is what they were to me. That is what I was to them. They had done the work and I had been the body the work was done on and the relationship was a professional one with a beginning and an end. They do not remember me either. That is fine. That is how those relationships are supposed to work. There is no failure in it.

Kaltoum was there. My sister Saima was there — she came up for about a week and a half, which was the kind of presence a sister provides for a brother in that kind of week. Moaaz and Shahbaaz visited a couple of times. The visits were what they were. I do not want to magnify them and I do not want to minimize them. They visited. They saw me. They left.

I did not make an announcement about the surgery. I did not post it. I did not call a circle of friends and family to alert them. I went about my business in the way I have always gone about my business: I did what needed to be done and I moved forward. Allah built me for a one-person journey through this life. That is how it has always been. I do not expect a parade. I do not look for one. It is not me.

My eldest brother Basit has said, in his own way over the years, that a person has to leave a mark on the world. Do the impactful work that gets remembered. Build something that stays after you are gone. I have heard him say it. I have respected the saying. I have given him my honest answer.

My answer is: that is not me. No one is going to name a hospital wing after me. No one is going to name a college after me, or a library after me. I know that. I have known that for a long time. I have not been seen in the way some men get seen, and I do not expect to be seen that way. Each of us has our own journey. This just happens to be mine. It would be nice if it were otherwise. It is not.
So I joke about it, because the joking is honest in its own way.

It is okay. I will do that myself too. I will build a statue of myself on my own front lawn. I will found a hall of fame and I will be the only member in it. The same way I have, for years, made plaques in calligraphy that quote myself and hung them on the walls of my own house. People come over. They see the plaque. They lean in to read it. They get to the bottom and see the author is Abrar, or Buyahka, or Aboo, and they laugh and smirk. Oh, you wrote that? Yes. I wrote that. I am the only one quoting me. I figured someone might as well.

It is not wise to take oneself so seriously. The whole world is busy worshipping itself. The whole world is busy being self-absorbed. The plaques and the imagined statue are my way, tongue and cheek, of poking it back. If the culture is going to insist on inflating itself, I will inflate myself in private, on my own walls, with my own quotes signed by my own pen names. The joke is on me first. That is how the best jokes work.

Underneath the joke, though, is the actual orientation. The one-person journey is the journey Allah gave me. I did not pick it. I have stopped resenting it. The body in November 2025 confirmed, in the most physical way it could, what the rest of my life had been telling me for decades: the driving, the hospital, the surgery, the recovery, the return to work — those things were going to be done by me, with whatever quiet help arrived from the people who happened to be nearby. The help that arrived was real. Kaltoum was there. Saima was there. The boys visited. Allah was there in the way Allah is always there. That was the whole company. It was enough.

Moaaz and the longer distance I have written about already. The eighteen months of silence that the previous chapter ends on had, by this point, softened into something else. Over the year leading up to November of 2025, there had been contact — phone calls now and again, drop-bys at the house, my going by his place. The small talk held. The touchy subjects stayed where they had been put. The deeper conversation, the actual reckoning, the desire and the effort to repair the thing that had ruptured in 2023 — that was not there. Not on either side, fully. The contact was present and the depth was not.

So when the heart attacks came and the surgery came and the hospital came, what happened was what happens in a relationship at that depth. Moaaz visited. Shahbaaz visited. A couple of times each. They saw me. They left. I do not magnify and I do not minimize. They came. They did what visiting looks like at the depth available. The longer conversation that the body might have opened, the body did not open. The pattern held.

Zanab and I have been in a different shape of distance since 2019. For the first six months after Hina passed, there was no contact at all. Then she got hurt — an accident on an electric scooter, I believe — and needed surgery. She reached out. She came to the house for a week and a half. I drove her to her appointments. The surgery happened. She got through it. She left.

A few months after that I invited her over with the young man she was seeing. David. I wanted to meet him. I wanted him to see that she has a family. I made dinner. We had dinner together. Then they went out with Shahbaaz and friends. That was the visit. That was what I could put on the table.
She came to Shahbaaz’s wedding in 2021. Since then it has been four years without real communication. I reach out now and again. There is no response. That is what it is.

I will write more about the Zanab situation in the section after this one, because there is a thing about her mother that needs to be on the page if the situation is going to be understood. For now I will say only that her absence at the hospital in November 2025 was not a surprise. It was the continuation of a pattern that the four years had established. The hospital did not change the pattern. The pattern changes when one of us decides to change it, and the deciding belongs to her and to Allah, not to me.

What the heart attacks taught was not that the family had failed me. The family is what the family is. What the heart attacks taught was that the one-person journey is the actual journey. The body said something in November. The journey kept being what the journey had always been. The journey was just made visible.
A du’a · for the body that gave out and the breath that was given back
الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانَا بَعْدَ مَا أَمَاتَنَا وَإِلَيْهِ النُشُور
Al-ḥamdu lillāhilladhī aḥyānā ba'da mā amātanā wa ilayhi'n-nushūr.
All praise is for Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the return.

The du'a said upon waking, every morning. I said it for forty years without thinking very much about it. In November 2025 it landed for the first time as a description of the actual situation. The body had been one thing, and then had been allowed to keep being a thing, and the keeping of the body in being from one breath to the next had always been the work of Allah. The hospital just helped.
Westwood, the Same Week

Late November 2025, right after Thanksgiving. A store closed in Westwood in the same week as the heart attacks and the surgery. The fourth one in three years. I drove past it later. Someone else’s sign was on it within weeks. That is how stores close. That is how the world fills back in.

Westwood closed right after Thanksgiving of 2025, in the same week as the surgery and the recovery. I was not in any condition to be the one closing it. The team handled what needed to be handled. The mechanics of a store closing — the notices, the inventory, the staff transitions, the landlord conversations — do not stop because the owner had heart surgery the week before. They keep moving on their own timeline, and the people around the operation kept them moving.

I drove past the location a few weeks later. The Edible signage was already coming down. The space was being prepared for whatever the next tenant would be. That is how it works. A store closes on a Tuesday and by Friday someone is measuring the floor for the next operation. The world fills back in fast. It does not stop to mourn a store. Stores are not, in the long arc of a city block, the kind of thing the block remembers.

What the block does not see is what closed inside the operator when the store closed. Twenty-three years of Edible operations in my hands. Eleven stores at the peak. Two stores now. Fort Lee, Midland Park, Pompton Lakes, Westwood — the four that closed between December of 2022 and November of 2025. Each one a piece of a business I had built over two decades. Each one a piece of an identity I had built over the same period.
— VI —
The Statue on the Front Lawn

No one is going to name a hospital wing after me. No one is going to name a college. No one is going to name a library. I have known this for a long time. So I joke about it. I build the statue myself. I found the hall of fame and put myself in as the only member. I write plaques in calligraphy and sign them Abrar, or Buyahka, or Aboo, and hang them on my own walls. The joke is on me first. That is how the best jokes work. Underneath the joke is the actual orientation.

My eldest brother Basit has said, in his own way over the years, that a person has to leave a mark on the world. Do the impactful work that gets remembered. Build something that stays after you are gone. He says it because he believes it. He has lived his life by it. He has earned the right to say it.
My honest answer to him, every time, is the same: that is not me.

No one is going to name a hospital wing after me. No one is going to name a college. No one is going to name a library. I am not in the path of life that produces those namings. I have not been seen in the way the men who get those things are seen, and I do not expect to be seen that way. I have known this since I was young enough to notice the difference. Each of us has our own journey. This just happens to be mine. It would be nice if it were otherwise. It is not.

The recognition that the namings are not going to come is not, in my experience, a grief. It is a clarification. A man who knows the namings are not coming is freed from spending his life trying to earn them. He can do the work for the work’s sake. He can sign his name to his own plaques. He can be his own hall of fame. He can build the statue on the front lawn himself, if a statue is what he wants, and not wait for the city council to vote.
So that is what I do.

I have, for years, made plaques. I write the lines in calligraphy. The lines are mine. The lines are things I have said, in conversations or in writing, that struck me at the time as worth keeping. I write them out, frame them, hang them on the walls of my own house. People come over. They see the plaque. They lean in to read it, the way people lean in to read a quote framed on a wall. They get to the bottom and see the author. The author is Abrar, or Buyahka, or Aboo. They smirk. They laugh. Wait. You wrote that? Yes. I wrote that. I am the only one quoting me. I figured someone might as well be.
The joke is half the point. The other half is what is underneath the joke.

What is underneath the joke is the observation that the whole world is busy worshipping itself. The whole world is self-absorbed. Every celebrity, every politician, every influencer, every man who has rented a podcast microphone and a backdrop — they are all engaged in some form of self-monumentalizing. The culture is one long monument, built by the people inside it, to the people inside it. The hall of fame is everyone’s personal hall of fame, and everyone is the only voter, and everyone wins.

If that is the game, I will play it too. On my own front lawn. With my own statue. With my own plaques. Signed by my own pen names. Tongue and cheek. The joke pokes the world back. The plaque on the wall is the wink at the absurdity, and it is also, when it lands well, an actual line worth reading. Both at the same time. That is how the joke gets its dignity.

The underlying orientation is the one I want my children and my children’s children to inherit if they inherit anything from me. Do not take yourself so seriously that you wait for the world to validate you. The world is not in the validating business. The world is in the world’s business. If the work is worth doing, do it. If the line is worth writing, write it. If the plaque is worth hanging, hang it. Sign your own name to it. Hand the next generation a wall full of plaques you signed yourself, and let them know that the signing was part of the work.

That is what got built underneath, in the years the stores were closing. Not a monument. Not a legacy. A practice. The practice of the one-person journey, made visible in calligraphy on the walls of the house, with the man who walks the journey signing his own name to his own quotes and laughing when his friends figure it out.

The stores are closed except for the two that remain. Ironmark is beginning. The book is being written one chapter at a time. The plaques are on the walls. The statue is not yet on the front lawn but I have not ruled it out. Allah is, as ever, the One who decides whether any of this matters. The deciding is His. The doing is mine. That is the division of labor I have arrived at, after fifty-four years of trying other divisions and finding them all unworkable.
An aside · to the brothers and sister, eleven days before the heart attacks
The acknowledgments

On November 5, 2025, eleven days before the heart attacks, I wrote a separate letter to my brothers and sister. It was a short letter. It was not about business strategy or the stores. It was about acknowledging, in plain words, who had played what role in the original building of the flower shop and Edible.

I wrote that the Teaneck Flower Shop happened because of Assad as the catalyst, with Hina and Ali first and foremost, and Basit and Abajee and the whole family behind it. I wrote that Edible Arrangements happened the same way — Assad as the catalyst, the timing his, the initiative his, the early years carried by his presence. I wrote that I did not feel I had been shortchanged in either situation, but that I wanted to acknowledge, plainly, that both times Assad played the key role that got things moving. And that Basit, in his own intangible way, was the grounding energy without which neither thing comes together.

I wrote that I had caused Amee and Abajee and all of them my share of headaches and heartache, through my decisions and timing, and that I sought forgiveness. I wrote that Amee and Abajee were the foundation, and that for me Basit and Assad were the next pillars, and that Saima had been too young through most of the building years to share in the carrying of that weight.

I wrote it ten days before my heart stopped. I did not know my heart was about to stop. I wrote it because it had been time to write it for a long time, and I had finally written it. That is part of what I want the record to show: that the acknowledgments went out before the body broke. Not because of the body. Because the writing was overdue.
— VII —
Two Peas in a Pod

Hina and Zanab. The mother and the daughter. Two peas in a pod — the sons close to their mother but differently, the daughter under the mother’s wing. A theology of women, a theology of household, a theology of order — all of it stake-in-the-ground, all of it in Hina’s own voice. A nephew’s wedding in 2017 she could not bring herself to bless. A daughter four years out of touch by 2026. A question I hold for the chapter after this one. A mercy I have only recently learned to read as a mercy.

Hina and Zanab were two peas in a pod. Mother and daughter. The sons were close to their mother, but a little differently — my interactions with the sons were always more normal, more day-to-day. Zanab was always under Hina’s wing. The shape of that bond is the thing this section is about, because the shape of that bond is what makes what happened after Hina passed legible at all.

Hina had a theology of women. I do not use the word lightly. She had a stake-in-the-ground position on what a woman was created to be, what a man was created to be, and how Allah had honored each. She did not write essays about it. She did not give lectures. But on the page, when the moment required her to set it down, she set it down with a clarity I have rarely seen in anyone else who carried the same convictions.

In August of 2014, six weeks after the letter I wrote about in Chapter Seven, she sent me an email. The crisis of June was still moving through us. I had said something to her, in one of the long conversations of that summer, that had landed hard: I had accused her, in some form, of wanting to be the man. Of trying to occupy a role that was not hers. She did not let it sit. She wrote back, in her own voice, in the patient and tired way of a woman explaining her own existence to her husband, what she actually believed. The passage that follows is hers. Every word.

God knows and is my witness — I have heard many tongues and am unswerved with regards to HIS creation. I appreciate and honor this creation of the male gender for what he is meant to be. I don’t give a damn what any woman may think she is, she can not and will never be what was not intended for her. Likewise, nor will a man amount to the excellence of the created female gender. He (swt), the most wise and perfect, has indeed created in excellence and perfection; and freaking ungrateful insa’an is SO ungrateful.
Hina, August 16, 2014 · in her own words

Read those sentences twice. They are a complete theology of gender in four lines. There is such a thing as what a man is meant to be, and she honored it. There is such a thing as what a woman is intended for, and she did not give a damn what any woman thought she could be beyond that. The excellence of the created female gender is not something a man can reach. The excellence of the created male gender is not something a woman can claim. Both are perfect creations of Allah. The ingratitude is in pretending otherwise — in either direction.

This is not the soft, modern, equality-of-sameness version. This is not the patriarchal man-above-woman version. This is the older position, the deeper one: two distinct excellences, both honored by the One who made them, both betrayed by the ones who refuse to see it. The word she used three times in three lines — excellence, excellence, excellence — that word is the spine of her theology.

And notice the language. I don’t give a damn. Freaking ungrateful insa’an. Hina did not curse. Hina did not need to. Her grace was such that even when her blood was boiling she could not bring herself to the word she was substituting for. Damn instead of the word underneath it. Freaking instead of the word underneath that. The substitutions were the grace. The boiling underneath them was the truth. You could tell, when those words appeared on the page in her hand, that what she was naming had crossed into the territory she did not normally allow herself to enter. The territory was hers. The temperature was hers. The not-using of the underneath word was hers too, and the not-using was the dignity.

What she was saying, plainly: I am not trying to be a man. I have never wanted to be. I honor what a man is. I am content in what a woman is. When I use my heart, my mind, my strength, my capability, that is not me trying to be a man. That is me using the bounties Allah granted in my make-up. To call that wanting to be the man is to misread me and to misread Allah’s creation.

That was Hina. That was what she carried. That was the framework that everything else in her life sat on top of, including her marriage to me, including her relationship with her sister Naila, including her work at the flower shop and at Edible, including her raising of our three children, and including — the part of this section that is hardest to write — her position on what a daughter, raised under her wing, was being asked by Allah to be.

The theology was not confined to gender. It was a theology of the order Allah placed in human relations, and she applied it to every room she walked into. The household was one of those rooms. About seven months after the August 2014 email, with the worst of that summer’s crisis behind us and the slow work of recovery beginning, she wrote me another letter. The subject this time was our sons.

By 2015 Moaaz and Shahbaaz were in Boston for college — Moaaz at Babson, Shahbaaz at Northeastern. They were home on breaks. Their friends were appearing at the house. People were sleeping over. The household was running, in Hina’s phrase, as a free-for-all. The boys were doing what boys of their age do, and they were not exactly wrong to be doing it. But Hina, watching from the kitchen and from her room, was watching something larger than a behavior pattern. She was watching the family unit lose its shape.
She drafted a letter to send to them. Before she sent it, she sent it to me.
As I believe maturity has nothing to do with the number associated to years lived.
I feel, not till we get things in order, will we find order, peace and harmony in family, business and life over all.
Hina, March 8, 2015 · to the husband first, before the sons

Two sentences. Two distinct theological moves. The first says maturity is not the number of years a person has lived. Maturity is alignment with what was put in you by Allah. A twelve-year-old refusing a wedding in 1983 because something in him knows the wedding is wrong is more mature than the adults in that room. A twenty-three-year-old appearing and disappearing from his parents’ house without the courtesy of asking is less mature than the principle would require. The number is not the measure. The behavior is.

The second sentence is the one I want my children to read three times before they move on. Order, peace and harmony in family, business and life over all. Hina did not separate the three. In her mind they were one fabric. Disorder in the household was disorder in the business was disorder in her own breath. Order in the household was order in the business was order in her own peace. The boys appearing unannounced at the door was not a household matter that could be solved in the household alone. It was a piece of a larger pattern that, if not arrested in one room, would express itself in every other room.

This sentence, in particular, is the key to how she read our marriage. When she had written eight months earlier, in June of 2014, about stepping out of the business seat and toward looking for an apartment, she had not been describing three different concerns — the business, the marriage, the household. She had been describing one fabric. The seat in the business was the seat in the marriage was the seat at the family table. To step out of one was to step out of all of them. To restore one was to restore all of them. The theology was the same. The application was different.
And then the move that made this letter what it is.

She had the email drafted. To her own children. She did not send it. She brought it to me first. Not because she needed my permission. The letter she had written would have stood on its own. She brought it to me because the order she was naming for the household applied to her too. If the boys owed their parents the courtesy of consulting before making plans, then she owed her husband the courtesy of consulting before sending a letter to those parents’ children. The asking was not deference. The asking was the order itself. She was practicing, in her treatment of me, the same thing she was asking the boys to practice in their treatment of the household.
I was going to e-mail them this, but figured I should honor you and run it by you first. Please let me know what you think and if this is better relayed in person (I feel it may be).

That was Hina. The law applied to herself before it was the law applied to anyone else. The theology she carried was not a stick she used on other people. It was a stick she had picked up first for her own back, and only because she was already carrying it did she have the standing to ask anyone else to carry it too.
She signed the letter your honith. An endearment that lived only in our private language. I will not translate it. The not-translating is part of the record.

What happened with the letter after that — whether the conversation with the boys happened in person as she had suggested it should, whether some version of her message reached them, whether the household pattern shifted — the answer is that the pattern did not, in the end, shift. The boys grew older. They came home less. They moved out properly. They married. The free-for-all of 2015 became, in its own time, the four years without real communication that Zanab is now in and the years of small talk without depth that Moaaz is now in. Hina’s 2015 letter named the disorder before it ran its course. The naming did not arrest the running.

But the naming is on the page. The wife’s voice, in her own hand, in March of 2015, calmly and patiently laying out what she believed Allah had ordered for a household and what she believed had gone missing from ours. That voice is the voice the rest of this chapter is sitting on top of. The voice the next subsection is going to walk into the territory of, because the same voice that named the household disorder in 2015 had, two years later, to navigate her own sister’s son’s wedding to an outsider — and what she did there is the second pillar of this section.
Two years after the household letter, in July of 2017, the theology met its harder test.

Hina’s sister Naila had a son named Rabi. By 2017, Rabi was preparing to marry a young woman named Jade. Outside the community. The wedding invitation arrived at our house and put a question on Hina’s desk that she did not know how to answer.

I drafted a polite note, in our joint voice, declining the invitation. The note thanked them for the courtesy of inviting us. It wished them the best in what life had to offer. It said warmth, care, and compassion should always accompany the two of them in their journey together. It closed with a small line about how truth and clarity should always exist between family. I sent it to Hina to review before sending.
Her response to me, that same afternoon, is the second pillar of this section. I will not quote it in full. I will say the shape of it.

She told me my note was very nice. She said it was much better than she could have done. She said in her current state of mind it was beyond what she would have done — she would have left it at will not be able to attend the wedding and stopped there. The grace I had managed to write was, she said, beyond what she had access to in herself at that moment.

Then she opened up. She wrote that she was grappling with her own thoughts. Her own reasons, her own choices. Whether she was making the right choice. Whether she could find peace inside it. She said she could empathize with Apa — her older sister, Naila — up to a point, but that the anger she was feeling on her sister’s behalf was, in the end, less defensible than the principle her own note had named: truth and clarity should always exist between family.

And then the line that mattered. Matrimony has meaning to me. It is not a game, not an ‘IN THING,’ nor should it be done to ‘show face.’ What defines marriage? Before us we have two unknowns — Rabi and Jade. At least we married to make our haraam into halaal, and we both understood this.

That is the theology applied. What defines marriage? with her own answer underneath it: marriage is the conscious making of haraam into halaal by two people who both understood what they were doing. The form of a ceremony is not what makes a marriage. The intention and understanding are what make it. Anything outside that, regardless of how festive the wedding looks, is something else — something she could not, with her grace and her stake-in-the-ground theology held together, find a way to bless.

She closed with a supplication for Rabi and Jade. May Allah place peace and harmony between them and guide them to goodness. May He open the doors of His mercy and knowledge so they may get to know HIM. May the light of His deen attract their hearts and grant them deep inner satisfaction. Ameen. She handed me the pen for the note, and she handed Allah the rest of the burden. She did what she could and gave what she could not carry to the One who could.

We attended the Rabi wedding in the end. We went because I made the call, on my own, that we should go. My mind in those years was, as I have said elsewhere in this book, more flexible than hers about the layers and the angles and the burdens family members carry. Hina agreed to go because I had taken the responsibility and the weight of the going. She could not have functioned at that wedding under her own steam. She did not have to. The husband took the weight. The husband walked beside her. The husband absorbed what she could not absorb. That was the marriage, on that day, doing what marriages do.

I tell my sons this now — and I will tell them again in the chapter after this one. What Hina felt about Rabi’s wedding is what she felt about Naila’s own choices going back to 1979, when Naila had married in a way Hina also could not, in her heart, bring herself to celebrate. The pattern was older than 2017. The pattern was older than Hina herself. The pattern was the gap between what Hina understood matrimony to be and what the surrounding world kept asking her to attend ceremonies for.
Now sit with what I am about to say next. Because this is the question this chapter has been walking toward, and the question is the answer all at once.

If Hina could not bring herself to bless a nephew’s wedding to an outsider, with her theology of matrimony fully intact, with the grace to write a supplication for the couple but not to attend the ceremony in her own strength — what do you think she would have felt about her own daughter doing something along the same lines?

Not in the abstract. In the actual. Zanab, raised under Hina’s wing for twenty-three years. Zanab, who was Hina with another face. Zanab, who had been formed by the same hands, in the same household, with the same theology in the air around her from the day she was born. Zanab, who, in the four years after her mother died, moved into a life and a relationship that her mother, were she alive, would not have known how to bless.

I am not going to describe Zanab’s life as it is now. It is not mine to describe. I will say only the shape of it: the boyfriend named David, who I met when I made dinner for them and Shahbaaz, the move out, the four years without real communication, the messages I send that do not get answered. That is the shape. The substance belongs to her.
But the question I am asking is not about the substance. It is about Hina.

If the woman who wrote those four lines in August of 2014 — the woman who would not bless a nephew’s wedding in 2017 even with my pen and her supplication at the bottom of the page — if that woman had lived to see her own daughter, the pea-in-a-pod, the one she had raised under her own wing for twenty-three years, walking a path that her own theology could not accommodate — what do you think would have happened?

I have asked myself that question more times than I can count over the four years since the contact with Zanab fell away. I have answered it more times than I can count, too. The answer does not change. The answer is that Hina could not have borne it. Her grace would have held the surface, the way her grace held the surface of every difficult family situation she ever moved through, but underneath the grace something would have broken. The break would not have been at Zanab. The break would have been inside Hina herself. The mother who had carried the theology, the mother who had raised the daughter inside the theology, watching the daughter step outside it — that mother would have been carrying a weight her body and her heart could not have carried at the same time.
And Allah did not ask her to.

Hina was taken in May of 2019, before David, before the move out, before the four years. She was protected from the thing she could not have borne. The mercy was that the test did not arrive in her lifetime. The test arrived in mine.

I am still working out how to bear it. The bearing of it is part of what this chapter is about. But the bearing of it is also, in a way it took me years to see, a mercy in itself — because the bearing fell to the husband, who has more tolerance for the grey areas, less judgment, more practice in carrying what cannot be resolved. The bearing fell to me because I could bear it. Hina could not have. So Allah, in His mercy, did not put it in front of her.

I have a thing I want to say to Hina about this. About the order in which He took her. About what I have come to understand about why He took her first. About what it means for the daughter she raised, and the husband she trained, and the conversation I am still trying to enter.

I am not going to say it here. It belongs in the next chapter, where the naming duty and the gentle-and-furious man and the seeking-forgiveness all sit. There is a passage I am writing for the close of Chapter Twelve. The passage begins Sweetheart, do you see it now? and I do not want to spend it here. I want it to land where it lands.

What belongs here, at the close of this chapter, is the recognition itself. That Hina was the one in our family carrying the theology with the stake in the ground. That Hina handed me the pen when she could not deliver the words herself, but the conviction underneath the words was always entirely hers. That I was, more often than I realized at the time, the voice for things she could not say plainly — not because she was less clear than I was, but because she was more graceful than I was, and the grace would not let her say the underneath word even when her blood was boiling.

And that Allah, knowing all of this, ordered the events of our lives the way He ordered them. Hina first. The hardest tests for the children later, in my hands, where they could be borne. Both of us where we needed to be. Neither of us where we could not have stood.

The barzakh conversation continues. I will join it when I am called. Between now and then, the husband’s pen is still in his hand, and the husband is still writing what the wife handed him to write, with the wife’s grace and the wife’s theology underneath every line.
Sweetheart. The pen is still moving.
— VIII —
The Letter After

January 7, 2026. Two in the morning. A long letter to the sons and to the brothers and sister, naming what six years of grief had actually done. The collapse-as-purification. Not punishment. The slow work of Allah dismantling a man who had been trying to power through what could not be powered through.

In January of 2026, about seven weeks after the heart attacks, at two o’clock in the morning, I wrote a longer letter. This one was to the sons, the brothers, the sisters, and a few of the people who had been close enough to need to read it. It was the letter the November 15 letter had been pointing toward but had not had room to say.

I wrote that I was about to say something that had taken six years to understand and even longer to express. I wrote that this was not a letter of blame or excuses. It was a letter of honesty, of clarity, of vulnerability, of accepting Allah’s qadr.

I wrote that when Hina passed, my life had not just lost a person I loved deeply. Something inside me had collapsed. I had not fully realized it at the time. I had not known how to process it. I had believed I had to be strong, that I had to stand up, that I had to keep moving.

So I had done what I have always done my whole life: I had tried to power through the grief. Not because I had been healed. Not because I had felt normal. But because slowing down had felt like falling apart, and stopping had felt like disappearing.

I had not grieved properly. I had not healed. I had numbed myself, distracted myself, and pushed forward in a state of emotional shock. And when a person tries to push through life while he is deeply wounded, the wound grows — quietly, silently, powerfully.

I wrote about the layers that had compounded the collapse. The loneliness after Hina’s death. The emotional absence I felt from the in-laws. The distance from Zanab. The crushing weight of trying to hold a family together while I could barely hold myself.

I wrote about the two remarriages. Zahira and Kaltoum. I wrote that my intentions had been stability, companionship, the rebuilding of a family structure. And that both times I had entered the marriage with a broken heart, and both women had come into my life with their own unprocessed trauma and emotional histories. None of us had been healed. None of us had been stable. None of us had been clear. What had resulted was more emotional turbulence, more misunderstanding, more pressure — not because anyone was a bad person, but because two wounded people cannot hold each other up.

I wrote about my sons. About how, when each of them married, their wives naturally came with their own emotional needs and expectations and backgrounds and traumas, as every human being does. And how, because I had been already emotionally weakened and exhausted and grieving and unstable, I had struggled to manage those new dynamics with patience or clarity or consistency. I wrote that I had never become distant from them in my heart. My communication had failed, not my love. I had assumed too much. I had expected them to read what I had not said. I had thought their stage of life meant they did not need me as much. I had believed giving space was the right approach. I had been wrong in those assumptions.

I wrote to my siblings. That if I had seemed distant or silent or unavailable, it had never been lack of love. It had been shame, overwhelm, exhaustion, not wanting to burden anyone, not knowing how to explain what I had not understood myself, the lifelong belief that I had to carry everything alone. I had not had the strength to reach out. Not because I had not wanted them. Because I had not known how to let them see how lost I had truly been.
And then I wrote the section that was the actual work of the letter.

I wrote about what collapse looks like, from the inside, when a person collapses internally. They do not fall to the ground. Instead they avoid responsibilities because even small tasks feel impossible. They withdraw from calls and communication. They disappear from the masjid. They make impulsive decisions to avoid emotional pain. They lose clarity and judgment. They react instead of respond. They feel guilt and shame for everything. They shut down emotionally. They live in mental fog. They become inconsistent. They appear like they do not care when they actually care deeply. They run from anything that triggers grief or failure. They try to manage life with only ten percent capacity.

I wrote: This was me. Not a man who did not love his family — but a man who was drowning quietly. Not a man who stopped caring — but a man who could not carry his responsibilities anymore. Not a man who abandoned anyone — but a man who was utterly collapsed inside.

And then I wrote about Allah’s qadr in those six years. For a long time I had thought those years had been punishment. Now I saw they had been purification. Allah had been humbling me. Breaking my ego. Freeing me from illusions. Teaching dependence on Him alone. Showing me that life is not in my control. Removing attachments that were harming me. Cleaning my heart through pain. Redirecting my path. Bringing me closer through loss. Shaping me for something beyond my understanding.
Nothing that had happened had been random. Every mistake, every loss, every breakdown had been written with purpose. Allah had not abandoned me. He had been rebuilding me.

I closed the letter with an acknowledgment of the blessings of my life before the six years. My parents. My siblings. Hina. The children. Uncle Ali. The countless blessings of health and wealth and opportunity and safety that I had done nothing to earn. I asked Allah to forgive me for every moment I had failed to honor those blessings properly. And I wrote that, for the first time in years, my heart was awakening. I was understanding my past and my wounds and my qadr and my need for Allah in a way I had never understood before. I was trying to heal. I was trying to rebuild. I was trying to reconnect. I was trying to walk slowly and sincerely toward a better version of myself.
I asked for understanding. For patience. For forgiveness. For du'a.
I signed it Aboo/Abrar.
Not a man who stopped caring.
A man who could not carry his responsibilities anymore.
A man who was utterly collapsed inside.
From the January 7, 2026 letter
— IX —
What the Collapse Taught

The stores closing was the external version of the internal collapse. The heart attacks were the body finally telling the truth the rest of me had been managing not to tell. Between the two, a small clearing opened. The clearing is what this section is about.

The closing of the stores and the closing of the heart, three years apart in the visible timeline, are the same event from a slightly higher angle. A man had been carrying more than the body and the operation could carry. The body and the operation had each, in their own way, told him so. The body did it loudly. The operation did it quietly, store by store, over thirty-six months. Either way the message was the same.

I had not known how to slow down. I had spent thirty years moving fast because moving fast was how a homeless fifteen-year-old had become a married eighteen-year-old, how a married eighteen-year-old had become a flower-shop owner, how the flower-shop owner had become an eleven-store Edible operator. Moving fast was the only mode the body and the mind had learned. Slowing down had not been part of the training.

What the collapse taught was that slowing down was not optional. The body had stopped giving me the option to choose. The operation had stopped giving me the option to expand. The choices were narrowing. The narrowing was, in its own painful way, a gift. A man who has been given fewer options has fewer places to hide.

I did not learn this gracefully. I do not want to write into this chapter the kind of language that would make the learning sound clean. The learning was not clean. The learning involved a hospital. The learning involved a son not calling for two years. The learning involved a third marriage that, by the time of the heart attacks, was not the marriage it had been at the wedding. The learning involved every part of a life turning slightly in its mounting and the mounting holding only because of the people who happened to be on hand.

What I can write honestly is that, by the spring of 2026, when I started building this memoir in the form it now takes, something inside me had begun to settle. Not finished. Not resolved. Settled. The settling was the thing that made the writing possible. Before the settling, the writing would have been performance. After the settling, the writing could be witness.

The two are not the same. A performance is what a man does when he wants to be seen a certain way. A witness is what a man does when he wants the record to be accurate. I had spent most of my life in performance mode — building things to be seen building them, being the head of family to be seen being the head of family, holding the household together so that the household could be seen as held together. The performance had its honest moments. It also had its costs. The costs are in the chapters before this one.

The witness mode is newer. The witness mode is what the collapse opened. A man whose stores are closing and whose heart is breaking and whose eldest son no longer goes deeper with him is a man for whom performance no longer works. The performance has no audience left. What he is left with is the witness. The witness records what happened without trying to make it look better than it was. The witness is what this memoir is.
What Is Left to Do

Two Edible stores still bearing the name. A house with Kaltoum and Idriss and Zoubaida in it. Three children, each in their own version of distance. A book being written one chapter at a time. A plaque on the wall, signed by the author. The list is short. The work is daily. The work is not finished.

As of the writing of this chapter, in the spring of 2026, the list of what is left to do is shorter than it has been at any point since I was eighteen. That is a strange thing to write. For most of my adult life the list of what was left to do was the longest list in any room I walked into. The list was the operation, the family, the community, the building, the expansion, the next thing. The list never finished, because every item on it produced two more items. The list ate every hour of every day for thirty-some years.

The list is shorter now. It is shorter because four stores have closed and I am not opening replacements. It is shorter because the two remaining stores no longer need me in them daily. It is shorter because the body has been told, by November of 2025, what its operational ceiling is, and the operational ceiling no longer permits the kind of list-keeping I was good at.
The items that remain are the ones that always mattered and that I had not, in the longer list, given proper room to:

The relationship with Moaaz. The deeper conversation is still not where it needs to be. The small talk holds. The drop-bys happen. The phone calls happen. The reckoning underneath the contact does not yet happen, and the reckoning is what would make the relationship into the relationship it was before 2023. The repair is not in my hand alone. The repair is in the hands of two men who both have to decide to do the deeper work, and the timing of that deciding belongs to Allah. What is in my hand is to remain available. To not close the door on my side. To keep my own house in such a way that, when Moaaz is ready to go deeper, the door is open. That is the work. It is a small daily work. It does not look like work from outside.

The relationship with Zanab. Older and harder than the distance with Moaaz, and shaped by the question I named earlier in this chapter. The work, as far as I can tell, is the same work: stay available, do not close the door, keep the house in a condition that allows a return. The return is in her hand and Allah’s hand, not in mine.

The relationship with Shahbaaz. This one is alive. It is not without strain. It is a working father-son relationship, the kind that takes work and is worth the work. The work here is not about reopening a closed door. The work is about keeping an open door open.

The marriage to Kaltoum. The next chapter will say more. What I can write here is that the marriage is a third marriage, entered fast, on a timeline I should not have accepted, and that what is left to do inside it is the daily work of two adults who did not get to do the courtship correctly and are now doing the courtship inside the marriage. Some of that work is going well. Some of it is not. The honest summary is that we are working on it. Both of us. With the imperfections we each bring.

The book. The book is the structural project of my late fifties. The chapters get built one at a time. The Ledger gets updated session by session. The book is for the children. The book is also for the readers who do not yet exist, who will pick this up in 2050 or 2080 and find a record of what it was like to be a Muslim man of my generation trying to live a marriage and a household and a community in the world we have lived through. The book is the part of my work that does not depend on the body. The body can fail and the book will still be there. That makes the book, in some small way, the most secure of all the things I am building.

Allah. The relationship with Allah is, more than at any prior point in my life, the actual relationship rather than the inherited language for the relationship. The collapse forced this. I have written about it in the January 2026 letter and in the previous chapter and I will write about it more in Chapter Twelve. What I want to record here is just that the relationship is present in the daily life in a way it had not been when I was forty or when I was thirty. The collapse, whatever else it did, did that.
That is the list. It is shorter than the lists I have carried before. It is the list I can actually do. It is the list that, if Allah wills, I will keep doing for whatever time I am given.
A du’a · for the years that are left
رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا وَتَوَفَّنَا مُسْلِمِينَ
Rabbanā afrigh 'alaynā ṣabran wa tawaffanā muslimīn.
Our Lord, pour patience upon us and let us die in submission.

Surah Al-A'raf 7:126. The du'a of the magicians of Pharaoh, after they had believed and before their execution. The du'a of people who have run out of options and have, in the running out, found the only option that mattered. I said this du'a a great deal in the months after November 2025. The patience did not always come. The submission did, in fits and starts, slowly, in the small daily work of accepting what could not be argued with.
— XI —
The Couplet, Answered

Son you might win some, but you just lost one. May this defeat be sweeter than victory. The chapter opened on the couplet. The chapter closes on the answer the years gave to it. The defeat was sweeter. Not because the losses did not hurt. Because the losing taught what the winning had not.
The couplet at the top of this chapter was a father’s line to his sons. I wrote it in 2018. By 2025 it had been answered, not in any way I had planned, by the years themselves.

The losing was real. The stores closing was real. The distance from Moaaz and the longer distance from Zanab were real. The heart attacks were real. The third marriage in something less than a fully settled state was real. The list of losses is long enough that, written out in order, it is the kind of list a man would not want to read about himself in someone else’s memoir.

And the couplet’s closing line was answered too. May this defeat be sweeter than victory. It was. Not in the way a sweet is sweet. In the way a lesson is sweet to a man who has been refusing to learn it. The defeats taught what the victories had not. The victories had let me keep believing the operation was the man. The defeats had not allowed that belief to continue. By November of 2025, with four stores closed and a heart in surgery, the belief that the operation was the man had been fully retired. What was left was the man. The man without the operation, the man without the eleven stores, the man whose identity had to be something other than the building of things or the running of things.

The something other is still being assembled. The assembly is the work of the next chapter and of whatever years come after. I do not know how many years that will be. The body has been informed, in a way it had not been informed before, that the number is not unlimited.

What I have learned, between the couplet at the top of this chapter and the closing of it here, is that a man can do the losing well or do the losing badly, and that the doing well is the choice that is actually available even when the losses are not.

I have, by my own honest assessment, done some of the losing well. Some of it I have not done well. Where I have done it well, the credit is not mine — the credit is the inheritance of decency from my parents, the inheritance of patience from Hina, the lessons that Allah taught me through the very losses that I am writing about. Where I have not done it well, the responsibility is mine. Both are part of the record.

The chapter ends here. The stores are closed except for the two that are not. The heart is steady, monitored, doing its work. The book is being written one chapter at a time. The sons are at varying distances and the variances are not in my hand. The third wife is in the house. The work continues. The defeat, as the couplet asked, is sweeter than victory would have been. Not by a wide margin. By the margin that matters.
That is the chapter. The next one is Chapter Twelve.
The operation was not the man.
The defeats made the difference visible.
What was left, after the defeats, was the man.
A widower, at fifty-four, looking forward
