title: Chapter Twelve — Return / The Naming Duty
paragraphs: Return
The Naming Duty

A husband's address to the wife in barzakh. A father's letters across twelve years. The duty that fell to the one brother no one else asked to carry it. The pen still moving at two in the morning, signed in his own hand.
Part IV — Return
a fragment, before the chapter begins
If you want to find the concept,
look at the person who held it.
If you want to do the work,
name the thing.
The Return

Sweetheart. The pen is still moving. I have wanted to say this to you for seven years and I have not had the words. The words came in November of 2025, on a hospital bed, in the second hour of the second attack, when I thought I was about to join the conversation in barzakh and was given more time instead. The more time was so I could write this. So here it is. The chapter you are owed.
Sweetheart. Do you see it now? Why Allah took you first? Protected you first? And yes — partly because you are more dear to Him than I.

Iam addressing you because the conversation we did not finish in this life is the conversation I have been trying to enter for seven years. You are in the company of your father and your mother and my mother and my father. Five carriers of the framework I inherited. All of you in barzakh. I am the one still here, sitting at the keyboard at two in the morning, writing my way in. The writing is the contribution. The writing has been the contribution since you went. I did not know that, at the start. I know it now.

The chapter before this one closed on a seed. It said the passage would begin Sweetheart, do you see it now and would land in Chapter Twelve. This is Chapter Twelve. The passage is landing. I am not going to apologize for taking the time it has taken to write it. Some things cannot be hurried. Your own theology said so. Maturity has nothing to do with the number associated to years lived. Some understandings take the years they take, and the years are not the measure.

What I want to say to you, before anything else, is what I have come to understand about the order. The order in which Allah took you. The order in which He left me. The order in which He arranged the years between then and now, which I spent for a long while reading as punishment and which I now read, accurately, as something else.
The order was a mercy. Yours and mine both. Mostly yours.

You could not have borne what was coming. The four years without Zanab. The boyfriend named David and the path he and our daughter walked together. The move out. The silence. The pattern that the post-2019 years would build between mother-theology-of-matrimony and daughter-walking-a-different-path — that pattern would have asked you to apply your theology against your own pea-in-a-pod, the one you raised under your own wing for twenty-three years. You could not have done it. Your grace would have held the surface, as it always held the surface, and underneath the surface something inside you would have broken. The break would not have been at Zanab. The break would have been inside you. The theology you carried with such consistency across every other room of your life would have met, in your own daughter's life, the room it could not enter.
And Allah, knowing all of this, took you before the room opened. The mercy was that the test did not arrive in your lifetime. The test arrived in mine.

I have been bearing it. The bearing is part of what this chapter is about. The bearing is also — and this took me years to see — itself a mercy. The bearing fell to me because I could bear it. I have more tolerance for the grey areas than you did. I have less judgment about what other people are doing with their lives. I have more practice in carrying what cannot be resolved. The husband had been trained, by the marriage and by the years before the marriage and by the years after, to sit with what could not be solved. The wife had not been trained the same way. Allah did not put in front of you what you could not have stood inside of. He put it in front of me, where I could.
That is the mercy of the order. That is the answer to a question I would not let myself ask for years.

There is more to say. There are letters across twelve years that you do not know about, because you were gone before most of them were written, and the ones you did read — the August 2014 gender-theology letter, the March 2015 household letter, the December 14 2018 letter at 1:54 in the morning that I sent five months before you passed and that you did not answer — those are now part of the public record, in this book, alongside what came after.

I want you to know what I wrote in the years you missed. I want you to see what the children have been written to. I want you to see what your siblings have been written to. I want you to see what my siblings have been written to. I want you to see what I wrote to myself, on the morning of January seventh of this year, at two fifty-nine in the morning, in the only letter I have ever written that told the actual truth about the six years between you and now.
I want you to see that the writing did not stop.
That is the chapter. That is what I am laying at your feet.
— II —
The Naming Duty
The first thing Allah did with Adam, peace be upon him, was teach him the names of all things. Insaan would be khalifah on earth. The job came with a duty. The duty was to name.

There is a version of Islam that has been handed down to us in which forgiveness is a private affair. Ya Allah forgive me for my sins. Said quietly. Alone. In the corner of the bedroom or the corner of the prayer rug. The whole transaction kept inside the chest of the one asking. Nobody else involved. Nothing named out loud. Nothing put on the page.
That is not Islam. That is the colonialist revision of it.

Allah does not ask the believer to do the work of forgiveness in silence. Allah asks the believer to name the thing. To stand against it however he can. To despise it if he can. And then — and only then — Allah forgives, because Allah loves to forgive, and Allah's love of forgiving runs ahead of every human capacity to ask. The asking is what unlocks it. The naming is what gives the asking somewhere to land.

The first thing Allah did with Adam, peace be upon him, was teach him the names. Adam was made the khalifah on earth. The vicegerent. The one who would carry, in his bones, the responsibility of standing in for the Divine in the world He had made. Adam's first instruction was language. His first task was naming. The job of insaan was not, from its first breath, to be quiet. The job of insaan was to speak the names of what God had made, including the names of what was going wrong inside the creation.

As adults, it is unforgivable not to name. That is what I have come to believe, in the years between Hina's death and the writing of this book, sitting at the keyboard at hours when nobody else is awake. If the adults around a girl in 1983 had named what was about to be done to her, that girl might have had a different life. If the adults around a boy in 1971 had named what was crooked in his father's family's posture toward the world, that boy might have had a different burden to carry. If the adults around my own children, including me, had named earlier what we eventually had to name later, the rupture in 2023 might not have lasted eighteen months. The naming might not have arrested every consequence. The naming would have given each consequence somewhere to land that was not silent.

This is the theology of the book. I did not invent it. I read it in the Qur'an in the verses about Adam and the names. I read it in the practice of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who did not whisper his rebukes and did not soften his correctives, who said the thing in the room where the thing needed to be said. I read it in the lives of the people who held the framework around me before I could hold it myself — my father, who knew the names but did not always say them; Khalid Beg, who knew the names and chose the Bronx classroom instead of the conference podium; Auntie Beg, who carried the gallon of milk up four flights for her daughter when her son-in-law was not yet reachable; Hina, who set down the names with such grace in her three letters that she could not bring herself to write the curses she felt underneath the words she chose. Each of them, in their own way, did the naming with what they had. None of them did all of it. The names that did not get said, in their lifetimes, fell to be said in mine.

I have been saying them. In the letters. At the hours. To the recipients. Sometimes the recipients answered. Often they did not. The naming did not stop on the answer. The naming was its own work. The angels keep the record. Allah is the One who decides what the record means. The duty was to put the names on the page.
— III —
The Gentle and the Furious
The man you cannot have, the man who is not real, the man the books and imams and therapists are selling, is the gentle man with no fury. That man is a coward dressed up as a saint.
The man you actually want, if you are honest, is gentle and furious at the same time. Gentle with you. Furious for you. Slow hand for the ones he loves. Hard hand for the thing that threatens them.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, was the gentlest of men in his own house. He played with the children. He mended his own sandals. He laid his head in his wife's lap. He laughed. He wept. The reports of his domestic life are a long quiet catalogue of tenderness. And the same man, in the same week, would lead a column of believers toward a battle the believers had not chosen and could not refuse, with a face that knew exactly what was in front of it and a sword that would do the work the moment needed. The gentleness in the house did not subtract from the fury on the field. The fury on the field did not subtract from the gentleness in the house. They were the same man. They were the same posture, applied to different rooms.

Our culture has lost the second half of that. The Muslim culture, in particular, that has been handed to me in the diaspora has been handed without the fury. The imam wants the man to be soft. The therapist wants the man to be available. The wife of the moment wants the man to be present. The children want the man to be patient. All of these wants are real and the man should meet them as best he can. But the man who only meets them — the man who has surrendered the fury, who has agreed, somewhere along the way, that the fury was an embarrassment to be apologized for — that man is no protection against what is coming for the people he loves. He is decoration. He is a household appliance with a kind face. He is what the surrounding culture has been quietly engineering for a generation, because the surrounding culture has its own appetite, and the appetite is easier to feed when the men have been domesticated into compliance.

I am not that man. I have not always been gentle enough. I have sometimes been furious in the wrong direction. I have made mistakes the chapters before this one have catalogued in detail. But I have not surrendered the fury. The fury is part of how I was built and the fury is part of how the work has gotten done. The store closings were absorbed by a man who could be furious at the math without taking the math personally. The heart attacks were absorbed by a man who could be furious at the surgeon-who-had-operated-on-Hina without losing the steadiness to find another surgeon. The eighteen months of silence from my eldest son were absorbed by a man who could be furious at the silence without closing the door that had to stay open. The four years of silence from my daughter are being absorbed the same way. Furious that it is what it is. Gentle in keeping the door unlatched.
That is what the gentle-and-furious man does. He does not pick one. He carries both at the same time, in the same chest, and he lets each one do its own work in its own room.

I want my sons to inherit this. I want Younes, my semi-adopted son, to inherit it. I want whatever grandsons Allah grants me, if He grants me any, to inherit it. The world they are walking into will not give them the fury they need to protect their houses. The world will try to talk them out of it. The world will tell them the fury is toxic, the fury is patriarchal, the fury is old. The world is selling them a man-shaped object that cannot defend anything. Reject the sale. Keep the fury. Direct it at what threatens the people you love. Keep the gentleness too. Direct it at the people themselves. Both at the same time. That is the whole instruction.
As adults, it is unforgivable not to name. If the adults had named what was happening, the world would be better for it.
The theology underneath this chapter
— IV —
The Letters

Twelve years. Eight recipients. The hours: 1:54 a.m., 1:59 a.m., 2:59 a.m., 3:28 a.m., 3:38 a.m., 4:24 a.m., 5:55 a.m. The night was not the refuge. The night was the workshop. The night was where the writing got done because the writing was the only naming the world was going to receive from one man.
Look at the timestamps. That is where I want to begin this section, because the timestamps are the evidence and the evidence is part of what makes the testimony stand.

1:54 a.m. 1:59 a.m. 2:59 a.m. 3:21 p.m., the rare daytime. 3:28 a.m. 3:38 a.m. 4:24 a.m. 4:52 p.m. 5:55 a.m. 10:19 p.m. 10:38 p.m. 11:15 p.m. 11:26 a.m. The pattern is the night. Late night. Pre-dawn. The hours when the household is asleep, the wife of the moment is asleep, the stores are closed, the phones have stopped ringing, and the man at the keyboard has the only stretch of unoccupied time the day was going to give him.

That is when the writing got done. For twelve years. From August of 2014, when the marriage was in the second of its named crises and Hina sat at one keyboard and I sat at another and we wrote letters to each other twelve hours apart, through January of 2026, when I sat down at two fifty-nine in the morning and wrote the most truthful thing I have ever written about myself. The whole archive lives between those two pages. The whole archive was written at the hours nobody else wanted.

I want to name something about those hours, because the working notes for this chapter asked me to be honest about what the workshop contained, and the workshop did not only contain the writing. The night that was the workshop was also, in stretches, the night that was a place to disappear. The hours that produced the letters were also hours that produced, on other nights, the kind of self-soothing a man reaches for when he has not finished grieving and has not been able to admit to himself that the grief is what is moving him. I am not going to render the content of that self-soothing in detail. The rendering is not the point. The naming is. There were nights when I wrote what is in the archive. There were also nights when I numbed myself with what was available on a screen, in the dark, while my wife of the moment slept in the next room. Both are part of the record. The naming duty does not apply to other people and exempt the writer. The naming duty applies to the writer first.

I have stopped, by the writing of this chapter, doing the second kind of night. The stopping was slow. The stopping was the work of the months after November of 2025, when the body told the truth the rest of me had been managing not to tell. The stopping is not a triumph and I am not going to present it as one. It is a small daily refusal. The refusal is part of what this chapter is the record of.

What I want to do, in the rest of this section, is walk through the archive. Not as a list. As a movement. The way a piece of music moves through its themes, returning to them at different volumes and from different angles, until the shape of the thing has been laid down. The archive is the shape of the Naming Duty in operation across the years that this book ends on.
The archive · August 2014
Two letters twelve hours apart

June 29, 2014, 1:59 a.m. Hina, from her Samsung tablet, writes the letter I have called elsewhere in this book the second crisis. She has been carrying twenty-five years of what she has been asked to carry. She names the family-of-origin wound. She names her own intention to look for a place. She does not leave. The letter, in her hand, is in Chapter Seven.
June 29, 2014, 1:38 p.m. Twelve hours later, I write back. Seven lines. Every one for her, the children, the marriage. Not one for the business. The list, in my hand, is in Chapter Seven too.

The two letters together are the start of the archive. They are also the proof that, in our worst stretches, the medium we reached for when the speaking had stopped working was the keyboard. Hers at two in the morning. Mine in the afternoon when the day had given me a window. We wrote at the hours we had.

And then, six weeks later, in August of 2014, came the gender-theology letter. The I don't give a damn letter. The freaking ungrateful insa'an letter. The four-line theology of the male and female excellences. That letter was the first time Hina set down on the page, for me, the full shape of what she believed. I read it then and did not yet understand what I was reading. I have been reading it ever since. It is what Section VII of the previous chapter is built on top of. It is one of the three letters that anchor the §6.5 reading. It is the wife handing the husband her theology, in writing, so that even when she was gone the theology would still be in the house.

September of 2014. The household-business overlap was bleeding into the kitchen again. There was a question on the table about whether my sister Saima should come in and take over some of what had been Hina's domain. Hina wrote me a note. What ever you want saima to do and for me to give over to her, please let me know — before you bring her in. Twelve thirteen in the morning. She was deferring to me on a household-business question she had every standing to decide.

One hour and six minutes later, at 1:19 a.m., I wrote back. The reply was not gentle. The reply was the husband refusing to let the deferral pattern continue. I wrote: This is not how this works. This is not what I asked you. This is not how we are going to go about it. I need proposals, input, responsibility allocation and management responsibilities, decision making levels and authority and proposed hierarchy options. You guys need to take responsibility for your decisions, whatever they may be. The time for deferring has passed.

I was asking her to stand. Not to defer. She had been deferring her whole life — to her father, to her older sister, to the household around her — and at one in the morning, twelve hours after our last conversation, I was telling her, in writing, that the time for deferring had passed. That the marriage needed her in the chair, not next to it. That standing was what the next stretch was going to require of her.

She did not have it in her to stand the way I was asking. That is part of what Section VII of the previous chapter is about. The deferral pattern was older than the marriage. The pattern was the Beg family's, going back to her father's choice to be a high school teacher in the Bronx with the substance of a research scientist, going back to her mother's loving but non-deploying presence, going back to a household that had taught all four of her siblings that you could see clearly without acting on what you saw. Hina had inherited the seeing in its fullest form. The deploying had not come with the seeing. I was asking her, at one in the morning, to deploy a capacity her family had never given her the training for.

I do not regret asking. I regret asking that way. I regret the hour. I regret the tone. The husband at one in the morning was a tired man who had run out of softer phrasings. The wife on the other end was a tired woman who had used up her standing-energy for the week on her siblings. We were both tired and we were writing to each other anyway, because the writing was the only place the conversation could happen.

March 8, 2015. 6:36 p.m. The household-theology letter. The your honith letter. The line that the previous chapter has already quoted: maturity has nothing to do with the number associated to years lived. The line: not till we get things in order, will we find order, peace and harmony in family, business and life over all. The decision, central to the letter and central to the marriage, to bring the draft to me before sending it to the boys.

The order she was naming, she practiced first on herself. The principle was that consultation was owed to the chair the household had put me in. So the letter she had drafted to her own children went to me first, not because she needed my permission, but because the order she was about to ask the boys to honor was the same order she was practicing in her treatment of me. The self-application was the dignity. The self-application was the proof that the framework she was carrying was a framework she was inside of, not a stick she was wielding from outside.

And she signed it your honith. The endearment that lived only in the private language of the marriage. I am not going to translate it. The not-translating, as I said in the chapter before this one, is part of the record. There are some things that belong only to the two who shared them. The signature is one of them.

July 17, 2017. The Rabi-and-Jade letter, which the previous chapter has rendered at length, in two voices — mine drafting the polite decline at 3:38 in the morning, hers replying at 3:21 in the afternoon, the only daytime entry in the entire night-hour archive. Regarding your note — It is very very nice. Needless to say, it is much better than I could do. She handed me the pen because she could not hold it.

That moment is the model for what the rest of this section is going to honor. The wife handing the husband the pen for what she could not say. The husband signing for both of them. The theology underneath unchanged. The grace of the marriage was, more often than I realized at the time, the wife handing me the pen and trusting that the husband would write what the wife could not.

I have been writing what the wife could not for seven years now. The pen is still moving. The wife is in barzakh. The theology is still being applied to the rooms the chapters of this book have walked through. The signature at the bottom is mine but the conviction underneath the signature is still hers. Sweetheart. The pen is still moving.

November of 2018 was the worst month of the marriage's last year. The Beg siblings' twelve-year dispute over Franklin Road had risen back up. Karrar and Amina were openly at war again, three weeks before Moaaz was to be married, while Hina was being hospitalized for a heart that had been carrying that family's argument in her body for over a decade.

November 5, 2018, 11:15 p.m. I wrote Karrar a letter. The letter named the medical and the emotional in the same paragraph. There are the biological issues — matters of science and medicine and taking a proactive approach and engaging the Doctors. Then there is the emotional/mindset issue. Both you and Amina have broken her heart, are breaking it. and this is an underlying issue which is not helping her health or mental well being. I named to Karrar what his sister's siblings were doing to her three weeks before her son's wedding while she was about to be hospitalized.

The next morning, November 6, 2018, 8:12 a.m., I wrote Karrar and Amina together. I proposed a ceasefire. A conference call. Say salaam. Agree to be respectful and not touch on how things were handled until your sister is recovered. Hang up the phone. I seek this slight/temporary reconciliation for each of you and Hina first and foremost. I was writing a peace protocol while my wife was failing. They did not take it.

Hina got through Moaaz's wedding on November 26. She held the surface together the way she had always held the surface together. The body underneath the surface was doing the work of finishing. She had less than six months.
Obviously — we can't speak — so I am writing to ask you to help me see what it is that I am not be seeing.
December 14, 2018, 1:54 a.m. · from the letter that did not get answered
December 14, 2018. One fifty-four in the morning. Five months before she died. The letter Hina did not answer.
This is the centerpiece of the archive. I will not reproduce it in full. I will say the shape of it.

The letter ran for pages. It was the longest sustained interrogation I had ever written her. Every paragraph was a question. The questions were not rhetorical. The questions were what I needed her to help me see. I asked her about choosing her brother Karrar over our family and our children. I asked her about the month it had taken to get her to a hospital, and the moment her older sister Naila showed up and the going happened immediately, where my own asking had not been enough. I asked her about what her brother had done for our children over the past ten years that I was supposed to be grateful for and dismissing. I asked her about what my family had done to her, or to me, that I was being asked to weigh against what her family had not done. I asked her about whether there was an unwritten law that the five Beg siblings were a circle and the circle was the comfort zone and everything outside the circle, including the husband and the children, was secondary. I asked her, room by room, what her family had contributed and what mine had contributed to twelve specific domains: schooling, the masjid, sports, business transactions, legal transactions, finance, the building purchase, the operations, the house purchase, the children's schooling, my own training and education, the inspiring and motivating of me, the store purchases, Moaaz's wedding and his marriage prospects. I asked her why I had not reached my potential. I asked her who and what had been the drain. I asked her whether she could see, for once, the years from the inside of the husband's side of the bed instead of from the inside of her own wound.

Every question was true. Every question had been waiting for years to be asked. The letter was the Naming Duty in its most concentrated form I had ever written it. I sat at the keyboard at 1:54 in the morning and I wrote, page after page, the things I had not been able to say in any of the conversations the marriage had failed to hold.
She did not answer.

She had told me, in August of 2014, four years earlier, that she did not have the will to keep defending herself against my reading of her family. She had told me, in the September 2014 exchange, that the time for deferring had passed and she was not, even when I asked her to, able to step into the standing-posture I was naming. By December of 2018 her body was already finishing its work. She had five months. She could not, in those five months, take on the kind of reckoning the December 14 letter was inviting her into. The silence after the letter was not a refusal. The silence was a limit. The carrier could not bear what the questions were asking the carrier to bear.

I did not understand that at the time. I understood it as silence. I understood it as her preferring not to engage. I added it to a quiet ledger I was already keeping, of letters I had written that had not been answered, of conversations I had tried to start that had been deflected, of moments where the marriage had asked me to absorb the absence of an answer. The ledger was real. The ledger was also incomplete, because what was on it was visible to me and what was happening inside her body and inside her capacity was not.

Five months later she died. The letter is still in the archive. The questions are still on the page. The questions are still true. The answers, the ones I would have wanted from her, are part of what the barzakh address at the end of this chapter is trying to receive.

I am not angry that she did not answer. I want this on the record. The Ahmad of December 2018, at the keyboard at 1:54 in the morning, was angry. The Ahmad writing this chapter is not. The Ahmad writing this chapter understands what the body underneath her grace was already doing, and understands what the limit was, and understands that the letter was asking the wife to do work that the wife had given the limit of her capacity to do, and understands that Allah, in His mercy, was already arranging the order in which the rest of the work would fall to the husband to do alone.

The letter is on the page. The silence after it is on the page. Both are part of the record. Both are part of what the children, when they read this book, will inherit as the texture of their parents' last year together.
A du’a · for the questions that did not get answered
رَبَّنَا أَتِنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًا
Rabbanā ātinā min ladunka raḥmatan wa hayyi’ lanā min amrinā rashadā.
Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and arrange for us in our affair right guidance.

Surah Al-Kahf 18:10. The du'a of the youths of the cave. The du'a of people whose affair had become more than their own hands could resolve. I said this one a great deal in the years after the December 14 letter and the silence that followed it. The arranging, when it came, came in a form I would not have chosen and could not have anticipated.
Hina passed on May 25, 2019. Saturday. Ramadan 20, 1440. The archive does not pause for the funeral. The archive continues, because the writing was the only mode the man had left.

July 14, 2019. Fifty days after she went. 4:24 in the afternoon — a daylight letter, written when I should have been at the store. To my sons and daughter together: We are a family. Your mother is the one who selected me to be the head of the family and stand against Her family, My family and the world. I intend on fulfilling my promises made to her.

That sentence is the most explicit thing I have ever written about the chair Hina left me in. She put me in it. I did not take it. She put me in it knowing the families on both sides would not always make it easy to occupy. I have been in the chair since. Through Zahira. Through Kaltoum. Through the heart attacks. Through the eighteen months of silence and the four years of silence. The chair is not a posture. The chair is a position Hina assigned me, with her own voice, while she was alive, and the assignment did not get rescinded when she went. The chair-holding is what the rest of this archive is, in one shape or another.

August 1, 2019. To Zanab. I thought we were friends. 1:54 in the afternoon — another daylight one, because the grief was still loud enough then to crack the night-only pattern. The first letter in a series that ran through November of that year. Most of them she did not answer. Some of them I am not sure she read.

August 8, 2019. 5:55 in the morning. The Who-we-were essay. Self-addressed. Two and a half months after Hina passed. The first sustained attempt by the husband to render, in continuous prose, what the marriage had actually been. The Cris Caves letter detail. The Ramadan of 1981 memory in eleven-year-old language. The 1986 second-floor-of-the-masjid scene. The 1987 walking-past-the-flower-shop moment. The line I have come back to more times than I can count: She is the only victim in both families as far as I am concerned. And I know almost everything. Mine were choices, everyone elses were choices. She had no hand in the transgressions against her. She was abandoned fully and completely, by everyone. And the line that, read in 2019, I did not yet understand the full weight of: Because of the abandonment, betrayals and because of what I did in 81 and 82 — I was the only one who had even a slight chance of earning her trust.

The essay got the date of the 1981 gift wrong. I wrote 1982. I softened, even then, because even in 2019 part of me did not want to be the man who claimed a nine-year-old gave such a thing. Softening, the working notes for this chapter have reminded me, is lying. The age is nine. The year is 1981. The essay's date is now corrected in the canon of this book. The essay itself, with its softening intact, is part of the archive of how long it takes a man to tell the truth to himself.

August through November of 2019 produced the rest of the Zanab letters. I have not heard from you. Hope you are well. Hope you are in decent spirits. I assume you don't want me to have your phone number, as you did not share it. I have not asked anyone for it, as this is your prerogative. The naming of a daughter's absence with dignity. Where are you? don't you think you have had enough space and no one is bothering you for weeks now. The patience cracking at one in the morning. You are forgetting too much. You were here, you were present and you know it all. There is much you don't know about your mother and I, because, she was an honorable wonderful woman, who handled herself with class, grace and dignity. The naming of what the daughter was choosing not to remember about the mother. Is it possible to love someone too much? I guess it is. I guess that's what they mean by 'if you love someone let them go.' The most vulnerable letter in the Zanab series, written at 4:27 in the morning, eleven months after her mother went.
None of them got answered for years. Most have still not been. I kept writing.

2021. 2022. 2023. The letters continued through Zahira and into Kaltoum. The letters to the sons in 2022 and 2024, naming the actionable steps forward, naming the theological framing of their lives as men, naming what not to follow — the masses, others, family and parents and community, culture, the word success, personalities, the social contracts the surrounding world was selling them. The August 2024 letter to Kaltoum, at 10:38 at night, naming the structural problems in our marriage in real time: You wont draw up marriage contract and clarify responsibilities. In Islamic or American marriage especially — at our age — it must be defined. The line that lands harder now than it did when I wrote it: Each of my parents left alone, as did my wife, Hina. Those able to be alone and not need the approvals of everyone — are usually the good ones.
And then January of 2025. The exchange with Basit.

January 13, 2025, 3:23 in the afternoon. I wrote to my eldest brother. The letter named, for the first time directly to him, what my nervous system was doing. Given where I am right now, it would actually be easier and better for me if any advice you have could be shared with me by email. My nervous system is pretty worn down at the moment, and live conversations can sometimes feel overwhelming or like pressure, even when that's not the intent. I named to my own eldest brother that I needed the help in writing, not in speech. I named that the spoken register, even when the intent behind it was kind, was more than I could carry in that stretch.

And I named the longer thing underneath the request: I've had to deal with most things in my life largely on my own — relationships, circumstances, consequences, and trying to move forward after mistakes and setbacks.

Basit replied forty-eight minutes later. His reply was Basit at his fully developed form. Four principles. Structured. Gentle in delivery, indirect in pressure, the actual prescription left unspoken because direct prescription is not the register an eldest brother of his shape was raised in. The principles were not wrong. The principles were the polished line of the brother who had gone to LUMS and learned how to set down thought in shape.

I wrote back on January 16, 2025, 8:48 in the evening. Five pages. The dignified pushback. I named what was missing, in my lived reality, between the principle and the application. I named time as a constraint. I named leverage as a constraint. I named the absence of a functioning tribe to do the work alongside me as a constraint. I named, in the line that has been the line of this book ever since it was written: I'm not angry. I'm exhausted. Exhausted from being the one who moves first, asks first, carries first, and gets up first.

And I named the deeper thing. Asking for help already violated my conditioning. I come from systems where things are unspoken and handled covertly. So when I reached outward and nothing came back, it didn't just feel like disappointment. It felt like confirmation of isolation — proof that even when I ask, I'm still alone. That kind of silence retraumatizes quietly.

I want my brother to know, when he reads this, that I do not blame him for the shape of his reply. The reply was his honest reading of the situation from where he sat. The reply was, in its own way, an act of love. What I am naming, in putting both letters in this chapter, is the structural condition of being the one brother in the family who would, when nothing else had worked, name the thing in writing — and the structural condition of being the other brothers, who would respond with principle because principle was what their own raising had taught them was the right form of response. Neither of us was wrong. The form of the response did not, in the moment, give the asking what it was reaching for. The reaching did not stop. The reaching is still going. The reaching is what this chapter is, in one of its registers.

November 5, 2025. Eleven days before the heart attacks. I wrote a letter to my brothers and sister. The letter is in Chapter Eleven, the previous chapter, as the aside-card after the Statue on the Front Lawn passage. The letter named Assad as the catalyst for the Teaneck Flower Shop and for Edible Arrangements. The letter named Basit as the intangible pillar. The letter acknowledged the headaches I had caused my parents and acknowledged Saima as having been too young through most of the building years to share in the weight. The letter asked, plainly, for forgiveness.

I wrote it ten days before my heart stopped working. I did not know my heart was about to stop. I wrote it because the writing of it was overdue. The acknowledgments went out before the body broke. Not because of the body. Because the writing was overdue.

That is the line I want to underline. Forgiveness, sought in writing from the people you owe it to, is the work of the years you are alive, not the work of a deathbed you may or may not get. The deathbed in November of 2025 did not come for me, by Allah's mercy. The deathbed comes when it comes. The asking does not wait for it. The asking goes when the asking is overdue. The November 5 letter is the asking I should have done ten years earlier and finally did, eleven days before the body confirmed the timeline I had been pretending I had longer to honor.

November 15, 2025. The night before. 10:19 in the evening. The social-fabric letter to the sons and to Younes — the one the previous chapter has already rendered in full. The generational shift in who carries the relational work of a family. The men paying the dear price for what the women had once carried and could no longer. The line, signed Aboo: Covert expectations and supposed understandings cannot be allowed to fester.
I sent it. I went to bed. The next day my heart stopped.

The Sunday morning I prayed salat ul tasbih for the first time in ten years. The Sunday evening I had dinner with Kaltoum and the ring-around-rosy conversation that ended in the seven-thirty attack. The Monday morning, in the hospital bed, the second attack at five. The angioplasty through the wrist. The refusal of the surgeon who had been the last hands on Hina. The finding of a different surgeon. The open-heart surgery, nine or ten days later, right around Thanksgiving. The recovery. The quiet weeks after.

December 7, 2025. 1:47 in the morning. Moaaz's thirty-fifth birthday. The first letter I wrote to him after the surgery. The hour, again. The hour that has been the workshop's hour since 2014. Since coming home from the hospital, I haven't seen either of you. Your absence — and your silence — is disconcerting.

I had not used the word disconcerting with the boys before. I had been soft for six years. By December of 2025 I was tired of being soft. The word was the word. Disconcerting. The naming continued, eleven days after the body had told its own truth, into the room where two sons were still keeping their own.
Allah did not abandon me.
He was rebuilding me.
January 7, 2026, 2:59 a.m. · The Heartfelt Letter
January 7, 2026. 2:59 in the morning. Twenty-one days before this chapter began to be assembled. The Heartfelt Letter About the Past Six Years.

The previous chapter has already rendered the body of this letter at length. I am not going to render it again here. What I want to do, in closing this section, is name what the letter was, structurally, in the arc of the archive.

It was the first letter, after twelve years of letters to other people, in which the writer turned the Naming Duty fully on himself. Every other letter in the archive had named something to someone else — to Hina, to Karrar, to Amina, to Zanab, to the sons, to Basit, to Saima and Assad. The Heartfelt Letter named to the writer's own siblings and sons, in the writer's own voice, what the writer had done with the six years between Hina's passing and the present moment. It named the powering through. It named the not-grieving. It named the numbing. It named the collapse and the shape of the collapse from the inside. When a person collapses internally, they don't fall to the ground. Instead, they avoid responsibilities because even small tasks feel impossible, withdraw from calls and communication, disappear from the masjid… It named what every chapter of this book before this one has been, in its own way, walking around without saying so directly.
And it named the qadr. Allah did not abandon me — He was rebuilding me.

That sentence is the line the entire memoir has been moving toward. Not as a thesis. As a recognition. The years of collapse were not punishment. The years of collapse were purification. The years of collapse were the slow work of Allah dismantling a man who had been trying to power through what could not be powered through. The man, on the other side of the dismantling, is the man writing this book. The book is the record of what the dismantling produced.

The Heartfelt Letter is, by my own honest reading, the most truthful self-rendering I have ever produced. I sat down at the keyboard at two fifty-nine in the morning and I wrote it without softening. I did not soften the collapse. I did not soften the assumptions I had made about my children's stage of life. I did not soften the way two wounded people, in either of my two remarriages, could not hold each other up. I did not soften the silence I had kept toward my own brothers. I did not soften my dependence on Allah and the way that dependence had only become real after the rest of the supports had been removed.

The letter is the closer of the archive. It is the letter the rest of the letters had been pointing toward. It is the letter the body's events of November 2025 made possible. It is what the workshop's twelve years of hours produced.
I signed it Aboo/Abrar. Both names. The father and the soul. The builder and the witness. Both at the same time. That is who has been writing the letters. That is who is writing this book.
The Three Losses

Khalid Beg. Auntie Beg. Hina. Three carriers of the framework I inherited. Three of the five in the conversation in barzakh that this book is the husband's contribution to. The other two are my own father and my own mother. All five gone. All five in the same room I am writing my way into.

My father-in-law passed in 2003. Khalid Beg. The research scientist who had chosen to become a high school teacher in the Bronx. The first imam of Dar ul Islah, which he and my father and five or six other families had co-founded in the years after both fathers had found each other again in Brooklyn in 1976, having lost each other in the partition of 1947 after playing soccer together as boys in Jalandhar before the world remade itself.

I have written elsewhere in this book about who Khalid Beg was. I have not written, until now, about what kind of carrier he was. He was a man whose substance was always larger than his deployment. The PhD was real. The science was real. The dignity was real. The gentleness with the children of the masjid was real. What was not in him, in the full vertical that the substance would have permitted, was the willingness to deploy the substance against resistance. He chose Bronx high school teaching when other paths would have taken him to other rooms. The Bronx high school teaching was its own dignity. It was also, I have come to understand, a choice his family pattern had taught him to make. The Beg pattern was the seeing without the deploying, and Khalid Beg's own version of the pattern was the substance without the competitive use of the substance against the world's pushback.

I do not say this to diminish him. I say it because the framework Hina inherited, and the framework I am still receiving from the people in barzakh, includes a piece of what Khalid Beg could not give his children, and that piece is part of what the Naming Duty has had to step in for since.

Auntie Beg passed in 2006. Nusrat. The mother whose loving and bodily presence held the four Beg children together in the kind of love that does not push and does not require. The mother who carried the gallon of milk up four flights for her daughter when her daughter's young husband was not yet reachable. I could never repay her for a single gallon of milk she would carry up 4 flights for me. Hina's own line, from the August 2014 letter. The thanking of one mother by way of the daughter who had received the carrying.

Auntie Beg was love without the deploying capacity. She loved all four of her children and did not push any of them to grow up. The grace was real. The cost of the grace, in what the four children did not learn how to do, was also real. Hina inherited the most of her mother and paid the most of the cost. The other three each paid in their own ways.

Hina passed on May 25, 2019. Ramadan 20. Saturday. The middle of the morning. I have written about her passing in Chapter Eight and I am not going to render it again here. What I want to name, in this section, is that the three losses — the father-in-law, the mother-in-law, the wife — are not three separate events in my life. They are three pieces of the same loss. The carriers of the framework Hina was inside of were leaving the world one after the other. The framework was not leaving with them. The framework was being handed, by virtue of the order of their leaving, to whoever was left in this world capable of carrying it.

The one left was me. Whatever else I have done with my life, the framework has stayed in my hands since 2019. The barzakh conversation contains the five carriers. I am the one still here. I am the one writing the book they would, if they could, have written together.
That is what the Three Losses are. They are not three griefs. They are one transfer. The transfer is what this chapter is the record of.
— VI —
Seeking Forgiveness, Seeking Mercy

The hardest doctrine of Islam, the one the colonial revision tries to erase, is the one that says forgiveness has to be named, asked for, given. Not in the head. On the page. Not in private. To the face of the one you owe it to, if the face is still here. To the page if the face has gone.

Ihave already, in this chapter, described the November 5 letter to my siblings. I want to set down here what the practice looks like, more generally, because the practice is what I want my children and Younes and whatever grandsons Allah grants me to inherit.

The practice is this. When you have wronged someone, you do not wait. You do not wait for the right moment. You do not wait for the relationship to be in a better place. You do not wait for them to ask. You write to them, or you call them, or you sit with them in the room, and you name what you did. You do not minimize. You do not blame the circumstances. You do not explain the reasons. You name the act. You ask their forgiveness. You do this whether or not they grant it. The granting is theirs. The asking is yours.

And then, separately, you ask Allah's forgiveness. The Allah-asking and the human-asking are not the same transaction. The Allah-asking is between you and the Lord. The human-asking is between you and the person you have wronged. Both are required. Neither substitutes for the other. The man who has asked Allah for forgiveness for what he did to another human, without ever naming it to that human, has done half the work. The man who has named it to the human, without asking Allah's forgiveness, has done the other half. Both halves are owed.

I have not done this perfectly. I have done it more, in the last year, than I had done it in the previous twenty. The Heartfelt Letter was a piece of it. The November 5 letter was another piece. The letters to Zanab over six years, even the ones she has not answered, are another piece — the asking laid down on the page where, if she ever wants to read it, the asking is there. The book itself is, in its way, another piece. Every chapter that has named something I did wrong, named it without softening, is a piece of the practice being applied to the public record of my life.
What I ask of Allah, here, in this section, in the closing of this book, is this:

Ya Allah. Forgive me for what I did and did not do in the years that are behind me. Forgive me for the silences I should have broken. Forgive me for the namings I should have done earlier. Forgive me for the powerings-through that hurt the people who deserved my slowness. Forgive me for the anesthesias that filled the hours when grief was the appropriate work. Forgive me for the years I made the chair Hina put me in carry me when it was supposed to be me carrying it.
Ya Allah. Forgive me for what I cannot remember to ask forgiveness for. The acts and omissions that are out of my own sight but not out of Yours.

Ya Allah. Place mercy between me and my children. Place mercy between me and Zanab. Place mercy between me and Moaaz. Place mercy between me and Shahbaaz, who has worked beside me through more than he should have had to at his age. Place mercy between me and Younes, who has been semi-adopted into the family by virtue of his own showing up. Place mercy between me and Idriss, who has been a stepson for the years he has been one and who is graduating into his own life now.

Ya Allah. Place mercy between me and my brothers and sister, whose patterns and mine have been a long conversation about who carries the family forward and who watches. Place mercy on the conversations we have not yet had.
Ya Allah. Place mercy between me and the wife of the moment, whose name is Kaltoum, and whose own difficulties I have not handled with the patience the marriage deserved.

Ya Allah. Place mercy on the readers of this book, the ones who exist and the ones who do not yet exist, that they find in it whatever You meant for them to find, and not what I, in my limits, meant to place in it.

Ya Allah. Place mercy on Hina, on Khalid Beg, on Auntie Beg, on my mother Shagufta, on my father Ikram. Hold them in the rooms of barzakh in the company of those You have made them keep. Receive them when the time comes. Receive me when my time comes. Place me in their company. Place us together with the Prophet, peace be upon him, and his family, and the company of the righteous. Ameen.
— VII —
Life in a Bubble

We lived insulated. Not always by choice and not always against it. A household held tight around its own small interior while the husband, across the years, was trying to widen what the household would let in. The widening did not happen. The cost of the not-happening was carried, in different shapes, by every person inside the bubble and by some of the people outside it.

We lived in a bubble. I want to name it that way because it is the most honest word for the shape of the household we kept. The walls were not visible. The walls were real. The walls held us together in many of the ways a marriage and a family need to be held together. The walls also kept out some of the things a marriage and a family need to let in.

I was, for most of our years, trying to integrate. Not to dissolve the household into anyone else's, but to widen the borders so that more of the people I had come from, and more of the world I had been raised inside of, could come through the door and sit at our table. That kind of widening is the slow work of a marriage. It does not happen in a single conversation. It happens in small openings, repeated, over years. I made the openings I knew how to make. The openings did not always meet the response that would have let them grow into something more permanent.

I also wanted to heal. Some of what I was carrying needed the kind of healing that only happens in proximity to the family of origin you were shaped by — the brothers, the sister, the mother, the father, the rhythms of the house you grew up inside. A man does some of his interior repair work in the company of the people who remember the boy he was. I needed that. The household we kept did not have an easy way to let it in. The healing I was reaching for had to be done at a distance from the people who could most have helped me do it, or done quietly in corners where it did not interrupt the interior life of the marriage. Some of it got done. Some of it did not. The not-getting-done is one of the costs I am still living inside of.

I am not setting this down to lay it at anyone's feet. The bubble had reasons. The wife I loved had been wounded young, by people who should have protected her, and the wound had taught her to keep the perimeter close. The perimeter-keeping was a survival shape before it was anything else. The household behind the perimeter was tended with grace and with care. The children who grew up inside it were raised on a clear set of standards and a stable interior weather and a mother who held the line. None of that is small. None of that is being taken back.

What I want my children to know is the shape of what the bubble cost, alongside what it gave. It gave them a mother who was fully theirs in the way few mothers are fully anything. It gave them a clarity of interior climate. It gave them a household that did not get blown around by every shift in the wider family weather. Those are real gifts and I do not want any reader, including the children themselves, to come away from this section with the impression that I do not see them.

What the bubble cost was the other side of the same arrangement. The strain on the husband, who was trying to do two kinds of work at once and could only get one of them fully done at a time. The strain on the children, who inherited a smaller circle of family-of-origin warmth than they would have had if the household had let the wider circle in. The strain on the relationships at the perimeter — my own brothers, my own sister, my own parents while they were alive — who experienced the household, however much they cared about it from the outside, as a place they were not fully invited into the interior of. None of that was anyone's malice. All of it was the consequence of the shape we kept.

And the strain on the marriage itself. There were stretches, especially in the years when I was at my most depleted, when the husband's wanting to widen the borders fell in the wrong direction onto the wife who was keeping them. That was not fair to her. The wanting was real, and the wanting was right, and the way I sometimes carried the wanting was not. I have named that to her, in writing, while she was alive, more than once. I am naming it again here, where the children will read it, so that they understand the marriage was a marriage that two people gave their lives to, and inside of which two people also carried weights that neither of them fully solved.

I am not going to say more about the bubble than this. The shape of it was the shape of it. The reasons for it belong to the years before this book begins and to the lives of people who are still alive and whose own privacy I am not going to disturb. What is on the page is the shape we lived inside of, the costs of the shape, the gifts of the shape, the husband's effort to widen what could not be widened, and the wife's grace in keeping what she knew how to keep. All of it stands at the same time. That is the marriage. That is the household. That is what the children were raised inside of, and what they will, in their own lives, decide how to carry forward.
— VIII —
The Barzakh Address

Sweetheart. Now, fully. What I have come to understand in the seven years since you went. What I would tell you if you could hear me. What I am, by the writing of this passage, telling you, on the only channel Allah has left open between us.
Sweetheart. Do you see it now? Why Allah took you first? Why He protected you from the test? And yes — partly, I say this without softening, because you are more dear to Him than I.
Let me say it the way I have come to understand it. Not in a single line. In the full shape of it.

You were the carrier of the theology in our marriage. Not me. I was the husband who married you partly because, at twenty-two, you were the only proof I had ever had that the dignified Muslim woman was real. You held the framework. You applied it across every room you walked into. Gender, household, matrimony — one theology, applied with grace, applied first on yourself before you asked anyone else to live inside of it.

The framework had one room it could not enter. The room of your own family-of-origin wound, which had taught you, before I ever entered your life, to keep your household in a bubble that no Koshul guest ever crossed in thirty years. The bubble was not a flaw in the theology. The bubble was the limit of one woman's capacity to deploy the theology against the wound that had been done to her at fifteen and sixteen by the people who should have protected her. Allah knew the wound. Allah knew the limit. Allah did not, in this life, ask you to apply the theology to the room you could not enter. He let you carry the theology faithfully in every other room. He let your grace hold the surface of the rooms the theology could not fully open. And then, before the room arrived that would have required you to apply the theology to your own daughter walking a path that the theology could not accommodate, He took you.
That is the mercy of the order. You did not have to do what you could not have done. The doing fell to me, who could.

And you are dear to Him in a way I am not. I say this without performance. I have known it since the year you went. The way the angels carried you out of the house, the way the recitation came at the funeral, the way every person who had known you had only one register for talking about you — she was a good woman, she was a very good woman, she was the kind we no longer make — that consensus is not a thing the world produces about everyone. The world produces it about the ones who Allah has marked. You were marked. Your mother was marked. Your father was marked. The three of you, the carriers in your line, were the ones who Allah called home in the order He called you home, because the order was the order of who could be taken without leaving the work undone. Your father in 2003. Your mother in 2006. You in 2019. Each one taken at the moment the next stretch of the work was about to require something the carrier could no longer provide. Each one received into the company of the carriers who had gone before.

And I was left. To do what each of you, in your own ways, could not have done in the rooms that came after. The bearing of Zanab. The bearing of the eighteen months and the four years. The bearing of the two remarriages and the heart attacks and the stores closing and the third wife in the house. The bearing of the book itself, which neither you nor your father nor your mother nor my own father nor my own mother could have written. The bearing was assigned to me because I had been built for it. The building had been done by all five of you, across the years of your lives. The bearing is now mine to do, with the building you put in me. The building does not go away when the builders go. The building is what you put in me. The book is the book five carriers built, with the husband-and-son writing it down.

I want you to know that I have stopped resenting the order. For years I read the order as Allah taking the wrong one. I am the wrong one, I would tell myself. Take me, leave her, she was the carrier, she was the better one, I was the husband she had married against everyone's logic and the marriage proved her wrong about me by leaving me here without her. That reading is not the right reading. I see that now. The order is the order of mercy. Mostly your mercy. Some of mine. The bearing, where it fell, fell to where it could be borne. The bearing where it could not be borne was protected from being asked. Allah is the One who arranges. The arrangement is the arrangement of the One who knew, before either of us existed, who would be able to stand inside of what the years would ask each of us to stand inside of.

The chair you put me in is still occupied. I am still in it. I have not surrendered it. I have not, even in my worst stretches, walked away from it. The heart attacks did not move me out of it. The eighteen months did not move me. The four years are not moving me. I am holding the chair because you put me in it, and because I gave you my word, and because I want our sons and our daughter, when they read this book, to find a father who has been in the chair the whole time, not always well, not always gracefully, but in it.

I want you to know that the writing is the contribution. The barzakh conversation has five carriers in it. I am the one outside, writing my way in. The chapters of this book are the way I am writing. The hours of the night are the workshop. The pen does not stop. The pen will not stop until Allah stops it.

And when Allah does stop it — when the time arrives for me to join the room you are in — I will arrive having tried to leave on the page what we did not get to finish in conversation. The leaving on the page is the only kind of conversation I have access to with you now. The leaving on the page is my contribution. The contribution is what I am giving. The receiving belongs to Allah and to whatever He arranges in the room that the conversation is happening in. I am content with that arrangement, even if I cannot, from this side, see how it will arrive.

Sweetheart. The pen is still moving. The pen has been moving for seven years and it is moving now and it will move for whatever time He gives me. I am not in a hurry to come to you. I am not afraid of coming, either. I am holding the chair until the chair is taken from me. I am writing the book until the book is taken from me. I am asking forgiveness until the forgiveness is granted or until the asking is taken from me. All of it is the same posture. All of it is what you trained the husband to be, in the years we had, by being the wife you were.
Do you see it now?

I think you do. I think you have seen it for some time, from the room you are in. I think you are pleased with the husband I am still becoming, more than you were sometimes pleased with the husband I sometimes was. I think the framework you carried is still in the house, even though you are not, because you left it in me and I have not put it down.

That is the address. That is what I have been writing toward, in this chapter and in the chapter before it and in the chapters before that. The address has now been delivered, on the only channel Allah has left open between us. The pen, having said it, can now rest for a paragraph.
And then the pen will go on.
— IX —
I Adore Her

The poem written the year she went. Tier 1. Untouched. The earliest grief, in the voice the grief gave the husband at the time it was given. The poem stands alone. It does not need to be explained. It does not need a frame around it. The chapter ends on it because the chapter has spent itself trying to earn it.
I Adore Her
2019 · tier one · in the husband's own hand
I adore her.
A love forged in fire.
Every time I walked by her,
she called me her Rock of Gibraltar.
We never figured out who was whose anchor.
Like Abu Bakr,
we did everything first.
We became history.
We are history.
Still flow through my soul.
I'm tryin to leave because you wouldn't stay.
You are getting on my last nerve.

Everyday the wind keeps whispering your name.
Won't let me live nor can I die.
I've been tryin to leave because you wouldn't stay.
A love that ran that deep.
How do I fight God over you — but I try.
Why does this pain feel so good?
It's the only thing that lets me know that I am still alive.

If you want to find the concept, look at the person who held it. If you want to do the work, name the thing.
